speechtext: The House resumed, from Tuesday, June 8, consideration of the motion of Mr. Allmand that Bill C-84, to amend the Criminal Code in relation to the punishment for murder and certain other serious offences, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-84 proposes the abolition of capital punishment. I shall vote against the bill. By so doing, of course I shall vote to retain the death penalty for those who commit premeditated, first degree, coldblooded capital murder, call it what you will. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, and to my colleagues in this House that no single issue, certainly since my election over two and one-half years ago, has caused me more personal concern and torment than the issue of capital punishment.
Some complex issues have been discussed during this period. I think of the efforts to deal with the economy, inflation and of course the frustrating issues of unemployment as well as the energy crisis. There have been more heated issues. We have only to recall to the judges' affair to establish this fact. However, in over-all terms the death penalty or its abolition contains such a tremendous mixture of values and considerations that the subject defies, at least for me, a logical or rational approach, and frankly, in my judgment, presents a problem that is incapable of a solution that will continue to be acceptable to all segments of our Canadian society and all regions of our country.
Likely by now most of us have had for some time a definite opinion on this issue. But the considerations that prompted us to formulate this opinion are not nearly so definite. A great deal of opinion has been based on religious considerations, and I think quite validly so. Much of my mail and the personal representations I have received have this basis. What is difficult for me, and I am sure some of my colleagues share this difficulty, is that we find different church groups taking diametrically opposite views on the retention or abolition of the death penalty. Similarly, I have many constituents, and I am sure I am not unique, who are members of a certain church who will disagree firmly and openly with the official view that the Church has taken. I suppose, therefore, I should not be too confused or even too surprised when I see two individuals
in support of completely opposite positions quoting me the same Holy Scripture. That is the nature of capital punishment.
Another consideration involves the general concern regarding law and order, and in many cases it goes certainly far beyond concern. I detect a very real fear. People see an increase of some 25 per cent in the number of murders committed in roughly a five-year period, and they want a solution. Generally, people who are in fear look for a quick, simplistic and understandable solution. So the government has seen fit to bring in the peace and security package to this House for debate. It has tried to convince the people of Canada that this is one entire package, but really it is two different bills, Bill C-83 which deals at great length with gun control, wiretapping and other housekeeping amendments, and this bill. Bill C-83, the main thrust of which is gun control, has been debated in the House and it is now under discussion in the committee. Bill C-84 of course is the one we are debating now, and that deals with capital punishment. It also contains other provisions.
I wish to make another point regarding the conduct of the government in bringing in legislation such as Bill C-84. This bill has been highly touted as providing for a minimum 25 year prison term in place of execution. The Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) said this 25-year provision is harsh, that it may be counterproductive with respect to rehabilitation, that it may increase the problems in our prisons and for our prison guards. He does not know whether the 25-year rule in capital murder cases will act as a deterrent. In view of all this I, and others, must ask why we have the 25-year minimum rule? The only answer I can find is that the government, by instituting the 25-year sentence provision, may garner enough votes in this House to abolish capital punishment. It is the price it will pay to eliminate the death penalty which is unacceptable to it.
What happens then if this bill is passed? There are two classes of murder. A person convicted of either class may receive a sentence of life imprisonment. In spite of the sentence, is the murderer eligible for parole? Sure. In the case of first degree murder, the minimum 25-year rule applies. Does this mean that a murderer convicted of a cold-blooded murder has to wait 25 years to become eligible for parole? No, that is not what the bill provides. It provides that after 15 years a man convicted of first degree murder may have his case reviewed.
[DOT] (mo)
What does all this mean? It means that life imprisonment is not life imprisonment but 25 years, and it means that 25 years is not really 25 years, it is 15 years. Yet, the government wonders why the public is confused and angry. The government saw fit, in bringing in this legislation, to support it with a great deal of publicity and a high cost advertising program to try to convince the people of Canada that the peace and security legislation could

replace capital punishment in this country. We saw the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) on television and we heard them on radio. We received a great deal of literature, which must have cost the government a fair amount, and which was distributed to the people of Canada. Nevertheless I do not think that the government has been able to convince many Canadians to change their minds. I do not know what they have been able to accomplish so far as MPs are concerned. In their advertising they said that members of parliament should vote according to their conscience and not according to what their constituents want. They said this because they knew that a high percentage of the Canadian population is in favour of retaining capital punishment, according to the latest polls. In my riding the percentage in favour of retention is 84 per cent, and I believe it is 80 per cent across Canada. So, in their advertising the government is appealing to members of parliament not to vote in accordance with what the people of Canada want.
I do not believe they have been successful in convincing Canadians through this advertising program, and it is certainly not convincing many members of parliament to change their minds. In fact it seems that there is a hardening of attitudes among people in Canada with regard to this bill. We know, and much has been said and written on this, that there is to be a free vote on this issue. We also know that this is a government bill and that the peace package was brought in as government legislation. Bill C-84 deals not only with capital punishment, but with other matters as well. It is certainly the feeling of many of us that there will not really be a free vote on the government side, especially since we have been told that the cabinet will vote solidly for the bill.
Since I have been here we have had two votes on capital punishment in nearly two years, and since 1966 we have had four votes in the House on this issue. It appears to me that the vote will be quite close one way or the other, with the government making every effort that it can to ensure that the legislation is passed and that capital punishment is abolished in Canada, in spite of what Canadians want.
It is because of this conflict, and because I am not positive that this issue will be finally solved with the vote on this bill, that I am in favour of having a referendum on this issue. I do not favour government by referendum, but on an emotional issue of such importance it appears to me that if we are to solve this problem for any length of time we should let the people of Canada decide, not just the 264 members who are sent here to represent them. I would not want this practice to be extended to other issues, but I would certainly favour it in this case. If we have to bring forward bill after bill on capital punishment, eventually the government will be forced to carry out a referendum on this issue.
I made a speech on capital punishment in October of 1973 and at that time I outlined my reasons for being a reten-tionist. One is the fact that not much emphasis is placed on the relatives of victims of murder and all the attention is focused on the murderer after he has committed the deed. We hear a lot about the deterrent aspect of capital punishment. Many abolitionists say that the deterrent aspect of capital punishment must be proved beyond a shadow of a doubt. I really believe that capital punishment is a deter-

rent and I think I can use as many arguments as the abolitionists put forward to convince others that capital punishment is a deterrent. More emphasis should be placed on the fact that retentionists also have a conscience, certainly, this is true of a greater number than the abolitionists are prepared to admit.
Then there is the subject of parole. Here again, if the government really wanted to demonstrate that it is going to tighten up the law and order legislation by doing what Canadians really want, then murderers would certainly not be let out of prison on parole after only a short period of incarceration. I think that Canadians have come to the conclusion that capital punishment is necessary because of the large number of murders that have been committed by people out on parole.
[DOT] <U20)
The matter of second offenders is a matter which should be considered in detail because many murderers have committed the offence of murder a second time. These people, under the rules of law and order we have in Canada, are not doing very much to convince the people of Canada that we should not have capital punishment. Second offenders most certainly should not receive anything less than the death penalty.
Those are the reasons I feel that capital punishment should be retained in Canada. I think the courts should decide, when somebody is found guilty of the type of murder for which capital punishment could be the penalty, what the penalty should be. That penalty should be carried out, and the Cabinet should not be permitted to decide that capital punishment should not be carried out.
I will close by saying that I do not believe retentionists are cold-blooded, hard-hearted, cruel or have no regard for human life. I believe it is easier to be an abolitionist than a retentionist. If capital punishment is retained, each of us voting for retention will have to bear some measure of responsibility each time capital punishment is carried out.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have followed with considerable interest the debate on Bill C-84 to this date, and in particular, I paid very close attention to the statements made by the Solicitor General of Canada (Mr. Allmand) when he presented a brief on May 3, 1976 on the abolition of capital punishment. The Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) stated that the government of Canada, the ministry of the Solicitor General and he, personally, sees it as our first task in the field of criminal justice to protect the Canadian public against violent crime. I applaud the Solicitor General, as I am sure all hon. members of the House applaud this minister, since all of us in this House believe that the protection of the law-abiding citizen should be the first principle in the administration of criminal justice.
The minister further stated that capital punishment does nothing to protect the public, and those who argue that capital punishment does protect the public are using emotional, illogical and rhetorical remarks. Let me just pause at this point and quote from an interview with Ernest van den Haag, a psychoanalyst and adjunct professor at New York University. Professor van den Haag recently stated that he was in favour of the use of the death penalty for
June 10, 1976

certain types of crimes. He said that it is indispensable. He said that the federal prisons-and he was referring to the federal prisons in the United States-now have in custody a man sentenced to life imprisonment who, since he has been in prison, has committed three more murders on three separate occasions, and these murders included both inmates and prison guards. The professor said that there is no further punishment that man can receive and that in effect, he has a licence to murder.
Professor van den Haag dealt with another case and said that when a man is threatened with life imprisonment for a crime he has already committed, what reason has he not to kill the arresting officer in an attempt to escape? His punishment would be the same. In short, the professor said there are many cases where the death penalty is the only penalty available which could possibly deter.
In deference to the Solicitor General, that was not an emotional, illogical or rhetorical statement made by the professor. The professor disagrees with the Solicitor General. Therefore, I have come to the conclusion that the statement made by the Solicitor General regarding deference is open to question and interpretation, and that his statement that capital punishment does nothing to protect the public can be taken as a personal opinion rather than as a statement of fact.
In the statement on the abolition of capital punishment made by the Solicitor General there is a further reference to violent crime. Statistics have been brought in to show that the murder rate, as reported by the police in Canada, climbed since the last executions were carried out in 1962 from 1.2 murders per hundred thousand population to 2.4 murders per hundred thousand population by 1974. This is an interesting statistic because in the 12 years during which capital punishment was not carried out the murder rate has doubled. However, I must be careful because the Solicitor General states that those citing the increase in murder rates and concluding from those statistics that the lack of executions in Canada since 1962 is the reason, run the risk of deluding themselves and those who listen to them. I certainly do not wish to delude the House, because the minister went further and stated that the real problem is the growth in the rate of all violent crimes, and indeed, the growth of crime of all types both here in Canada and throughout the world in recent years.
I find little consolation in being told that I should not be incensed or distressed by the growth of the murder rate in Canada because violent crime has also been increasing. Could it be that the growth in the rate of violent crime in Canada and the doubling of the murder rate in a 12-year period just might be the result of a breakdown of deterrence in our criminal system, and that those who cause violent crime are very well aware of this breakdown?
Recently when touring the B.C. penitentiary, I and several of my colleagues were informed by the prison staff that approximately 80 per cent of the inmates were repeaters. In other words, they had not committed only one crime, but a succession of crimes. In all seriousness, is this an argument for making deterrence lighter or heavier? Are Canadians less law-abiding than they were 50 years ago, or are the same people perpetrating crimes, receiving minor sentences and being turned loose on society again?
Capital Punishment
It would be interesting to learn from statistics whether there are more people committing crime or whether the same people are being convicted on more than one occasion. Unfortunately, statistics tend to be rather dry in the reading, but to put the trend of murder in Canada in a better perspective, let me state that in 1955 there were 118 murders, while in 1974 this figure had risen to 539. I am afraid the trend of attempted murder is even worse than murder, according to Statistics Canada. In 1961 there were 74 attempted murders in Canada. In 1974 there were 524 attempted murders, so that in that 13-year period attempted murders increased seven to eight times, which I think is rather frightening.
It is not my intention to criticize the Solicitor General, but he stated that if those who suggest that capital punishment is an effective method of fighting crime were serious, they must argue that we should reinstate capital punishment for many more crimes and many more murders. I would only point out that in my humble opinion if the deterrents to all crimes were harsher, then those who prey upon the law-abiding citizen would have two choices. First, to be deterred by more stringent enforcement of the Criminal Code with longer sentences or, second, to be incarcerated for a period of time that would in effect protect the public at large. In those cases wherein the crime was so heinous and repugnant to our society that the ultimate deterrent should be provided, then the ultimate protection would be provided.
[DOT] (U30)
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to agree with the Solicitor General that the concentration on the issue of capital punishment does not serve Canada well and that ultimately the peace and security legislation embodied in Bill C-83 is of much greater importance. I realize that by stating this I will be in conflict with some of my colleagues and the general public in Canada, since they perceive the capital punishment issue much as a mariner would view an iceberg. The tip of the iceberg is an awesome sight and which can be clearly perceived; however, the main bulk and danger remains below the surface where it cannot be readily identified. Bill C-84 is a high profile bill. I would recommend that all hon. members of this House proceed with the speedy dispatch of Bill C-83 through the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs and third reading through this House, since the matters dealt with in this bill will ultimately have a greater impact on the protection of our Canadian citizens than will Bill C-84.
The hon. Solicitor General has quoted Professor Wilson who said: "It is a matter of dispute whether any penalty will have a deterrent effect on murderers, but surely the prospect of a long prison term will have as much as others." As a layman, I cannot dispute Professor Wilson but can only quote in rebuttal Isaac Ehrlich's recent article in the American Economic Review, where he stated: "Over the period 1933 to 1969 one additional execution per year may have resulted on the average in seven or eight fewer murders." My dilemma, Mr. Speaker, is that I do not know whether Professor Wilson or Isaac Ehrlich is correct in their statements and I doubt whether any of us in the House can make empirical judgments since experts disagree on whether capital punishment is a deterrent. Professor Wilson's thesis is that surely the prospect of a long
