prison term will have as much deterrent effect as capital punishment. The hon. Solicitor General has apparently heeded the words of Professor Wilson, since C-84 establishes the punishment for premeditated murder as life imprisonment with a minimum of 25 years incarceration as the answer to the protection of society from those who would commit premeditated murder.
If I may, Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote Mr. William F. Phipps, Chairman of the Penal Reform Task Force of the United Church of Canada who states:
We submit that the very extensive prison sentences will put even greater pressure on the penal system. The legislation seems to eliminate most of the current incentives, and when the incentives are lost, the pressure inside the institutions will be considerable.
These terms will also create a different class of prisoner, who will be living in a different "head space" from other inmates. Therefore, we would predict a negative impact on other inmates as they see their colleagues having no chance for parole. Some well informed people are predicting that these kinds of sentences will increase violence within the penitentiary system. A more isolated and dangerous "subculture" will surely develop.
Many of the programs within our prison institutions will be irrelevant because they are geared to inmates who are getting out of the institution. There seems to be no accompanying legislation regarding rehabilitation for such long term prisoners.
There will be an increase in prison population and therefore increased human pressures as well as increased cost.
He made a very interesting comment which struck me as something that I should certainly look into when he stated:
What happens to the inmate when he gets out of prison after serving 25 years? Most sociological data in this regard would say that the person would be more dangerous coming out than going in.
These are not my comments but those of William F. Phipps, Chairman of the Penal Reform Task Force of the United Church of Canada. I must say it is a rather chilling prospect to find that, according to his group, we are creating a dangerous situation within our penitentiaries and throughout our penal system if we adopt the provisions of Bill C-84 as they have been brought before the House. I think hon. members would agree that whichever way we vote on this, the object of the legislation is to not create more problems than we already have.
Mr. Speaker, I was going to quote further remarks made by Mr. Phipps but I think that is really the sum and substance of his remarks. I think the dilemma that we as members face in voting on C-84 is that we are told on the one hand by experts that life imprisonment should deter murders that are not crimes of passion. We are told again that by incarcerating a premeditated murderer we have removed him from our society therefore he is no longer a danger. On the other hand, Professor Van den Haag states that you run into an additional risk if you fail to execute the convicted murderer. In that case, since executions have had an additional deterrent effect, you have failed to spare the lives of a number of future victims. Mr. Van den Haag also states that between the two risks, first, of failing to impose the death penalty because it does not have an additional deterrent effect and thus by failing to execute the convicted murderer failing to spare the lives of future victims, he would much rather execute the convicted murderer than risk the lives of innocent people who could have been saved.
Mr. William F. Phipps, the Chairman of the Penal Reform Task Force of the United Church of Canada,
although not in favour of capital punishment, has clearly stated there is a disadvantage to long prison terms and that the pressure inside the institutions will be considerable. He predicts there will be additional violence. It would be fair to say that not only is there no concurrence regarding the deterrence of murder by the establishment of capital punishment, but that there are also varied views regarding whether life imprisonment or the 25 year sentence will protect our society or merely lead to acts of further violence by the establishment of long prison sentences. This, Mr. Speaker, is the quandary in which I find myself; the dilemma the government has to face and the decision that we, the members of the House of Commons must make and there is no clear evidence on either side.
Mr. Speaker, our system of criminal justice is based not only on deterrence but also on fairness. A person who has committed a crime, I believe, must be punished in proportion to the seriousness of the crime. When you kill a man or a woman with premeditation you do something which is irrevocable to the victim; his or her life is lost forever. The society which does not deal swiftly and justly with premeditated murder detracts from human dignity and in fact argues against the sacredness of life.
One paradox, Mr. Speaker, that I do not believe has been raised during this debate is why, in one of the most affluent countries in the world, during a time of almost undreamed of prosperity-undreamed of by our forefathers-are we experiencing a rapid rise in crimes of all types, including crimes of violence? In a society in which there is no class distinction, where anyone can rise to the potential of his or her own abilities, why should crime be increasing? Throughout the ages, the oppressed, the landless, poorly educated, those who have no material goods have traditionally taken to a life of crime because they could not obtain by honest pursuits what they could obtain by crime. Is this the case in Canada today? Are our children deprived of education? Are there oppressed people in our land? Is our society so stratified the people cannot succeed by ability? Surely, the answer is no.
[DOT] (U40)
Why has crime in Canada increased? I am sure there are many components to the answer. Could one component be that our society has turned the penal system and Criminal Code into an inconvenience rather than a deterrent. Should we not consider this? It is not our object, surely, to make the punishment for crime a mere inconvenience, which will leave the criminal free to pursue his course when he returns to society because we have not put road blocks in his way. I am no authority in this field. I merely bring to the attention of the House one of the causes for the breakdown of law and order in society.
In my opening remarks I agreed with the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand), that the first priority of any member of parliament when dealing with criminal law is the protection of the public. Since experts have expressed grave doubts about life sentences, I must vote against Bill C-84. As an idealist I regret that our society is in many ways barbaric and cruel, as evidenced by the murders taking place in society. As a pragmatic legislator I abhor the taking of life. Nevertheless, the penalty must fit the crime. The Canadian people must feel that the legal system does not condone premeditated murder.

June 10, 1976

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a philosopher rightly showed that the more education gives a man liberty in his judgment, the more complex and shaded every issue appears to him. He sees the valid reasons both for and against, and becomes all the more incapable of taking sides. Obviously, this is a position that many members of parliament find themselves in on the question of capital punishment. Unfortunately for the politician, while he may philosophize with the philosopher, he must take matters one step forward, to decision and action. For many months and years now I have maintained the philosopher's position without coming to a full and real decision. However, having been forced to make a decision, it is my intention today not to outline both sides of the issue, both of which I have sympathy for, but rather to rationalize the side of the decision I have taken.
First, most of us have our own visions of what Utopia our society should hopefully evolve toward; then we rationalize and legislate toward such a better lifestyle for mankind. In the Utopia, there is obviously no requirement for capital punishment, because man becomes a self-actuated, self-responsible individual, maximizing his individual capacities in a creative and productive way born of respect for himself and for the individual rights of others around him. Such a society would require fewer externally imposed laws by government, because enlightened reason would have replaced force and irrational violence. In view of the affluence of our society, virtually total literacy, a population which has, on average, more than 12 years of formal education, securely and firmly based churches and our democratic government, one might expect our society to draw close to the reality of such Utopian objectives. But the reality of the situation finds us straying far, perhaps even regressing, thereby necessitating an agonizing and pragmatic reassessment.
The question of retention or abolition needs to be considered in a common sense way fitting the time in which we find ourselves, a time, hopefully, leading to man's upward ascent. As we move through time and space there will be stages in social evolution when punitive factors need to be imposed; at other times of greater order and enlightenment punitive factors can be moderated or even eliminated. While I prefer to support an upward or progressive evolutionary movement, in order to uphold the fuller, long-term interest and approach Utopia sooner I must accept that at times it will be necessary to recommend backward, punitive, even regressive measures.
When a democratic society attempts to move beyond the commonality of its moral ethics at a pace too fast for the overwhelming majority, such a democracy or government deserves its own inevitable self-destruction. Therefore it is necessary, in my opinion, to take into account the contemporary moral ethics of our society. It does not take an oracle for politicians, who are moulding our laws, to recognize that the basic moral ethic of today's society is that the most precious value is human life and the safeguarding of the free continuation of such life. If one person takes the life of another without a just cause, and the just cause is commonly defined as approval by the state, as in war; and if these two lives are weighed equally before the court, the death sentence is inevitable for the murderer.
Capital Punishment
A regulation against capital punishment would necessarily value the life of the murderer more than the life of the victim, since the life of the murderer would become untouchable. This, in my view, does not conform with the aspirations of justice maintained by Canadian society. Hence, capital punishment should remain as a possibility, no matter how rarely used, in order to further safeguard our lives and preserve the ethical equality before the law of all human beings. The victims of brutal murders had a right to life. The crime of murder is equally on the hands of the state as it is on the hands of the murderer himself. An individual living in a non-state or a state of anarchy carries his own responsibility for his personal protection and security. In an organized state he subjugates and passes his right of self-determined security by any means, including murder, to the state. In transferring this authority the individual expects to gain from that society the guarantee of his right to life, personal safety and security.
The state by allowing, for whatever reason, the murder of the individual has become itself a party to the murder and thereby has an obligation, not only to the victim of murder but to those other individuals who remain in society, to demonstrate the equity of the value of life to the state by providing that the value of the life of the victum is no less than the value of the life of the murderer. Society owes not only the victim but other members of society who have abrogated their rights of self-determined security to the state a demonstrated expression of equity in the form of capital punishment. That the state has the right to take life is necessarily obvious in that, in order to defend the sovereignty of its law, a state must maintain the right to defend its territory and laws from an aggressor. If a state does not maintain the right to kill in a defensive war, the law and thereby the state itself has no force, authority, or security. If a state maintains, as it must, the right to take life, particularly in face of an external threat to its sovereignty, then it too has an obligation and a right to take life internally when the right to life has been violated within the state.
When the state or its individual components, basic security or right to life or law are violated, the murder of an individual component of the state is in fact murder of the state itself. The killing of a murderer by the state is not revenge, it is rather self-preservation and the ultimate statement of intent to guarantee, as far as possible, the security of both the individual component parts, the people of the state and the state itself. The strongest instinct that man is born with is the instinct of self-preservation which, in turn, formulates his understanding of his most basic right and that is his right to life.
If the state refuses to uphold his most basic right with the ultimate penalty for the ultimate crime, why should the individual within the state continue to abrogate his right of self-determined protection to the state? If the state will not protect his right to life, does the individual regain by default the right of self-determined protection? Will the policeman or the prison guard or the individual not take this law then back into his own hands?
Killing is a natural part of the balance of the environment. Murder, on the other hand, is offensive to the environment. Murder is wanton, wasteful killing that upsets

June 10, 1976
Capital Punishment
the social balance of the environment. One of the most basic reasons for man collectivizing to form a state is to ensure his own personal security in a balanced, lawful, and orderly society. Murder upsets the social environmental balance. The killing of a murderer stabilizes and re-establishes social balance and order within the environment of the society.
The acceptance and adherence to law is a matter of a broad and general public perception. Some enlightened people obey the law because they perceive the law to be right and just and because they know that because they live in a democracy, they have the opportunity for direct participation in the formation and changing of these same laws. However, the majority seem rather to obey the laws that they perceive; that should they break the law, justice will be certain and swift. I am more certain to be caught, more quickly caught and convicted for over-parking at the airport than caught and convicted for premeditated murder.
Unfortunately, the broad perception of law and order in today's society is that justice is unsure, uncertain and even improbable. This negative perception is enhanced when governments are either unwilling or unable to uphold and enforce their own self-made laws, or when the law makers themselves, even in a minority, are perceived to be dishonest and corrupt. Unfortunately, this negative perception is the perception that abounds in Canada today.
Through the focus of this debate, the problem is further compounded in that the broad perception in the minds of Canadians is that this vote on capital punishment is a symbol of the intent of the government to re-establish the upholding of law and order. If the retentionists win the battle by defeating this abolitionist bill, the abolitionists still win the war because the limitations of the existing act then remain in force, and while the government of the day remains temporarily in power it will, in all likelihood, continue its abolitionist stance through the commutation provisions still available to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his cabinet. The retentionists will, however, have some solace knowing that they have raised the level of perception of the intent of the government to uphold the existing laws and order in Canadian society.
Not only must the question of the state moral ethic of the nation attempt to be determined, but also the church moral ethic requires examination. This is a considerably more difficult position to ascertain because of contradictions between and within the various Christian denominations.
The Pentecostal assemblies of Canada quote, amongst other things, the Bible, Numbers 35, verse 33, and verse 31 which read:
Moreover ye shall take no satisfaction for the life of a murderer, which is guilty of death: but he shall be surely put to death.
They also quote Genesis 9, verse 6 and Romans 13. Ephesians 4, verses 31 and 32 and Matthew 5, verses 38 and 39 might well be cited by those on the other side of the question, the United Church of Canada which comes out clearly for abolition. They cite Matthew 5, verses 38 and 39 which read:
Ye have heard that it hath been said, An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth: But I say unto you, That ye resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also.

They may also quote Exodus 20, verse 13:
Thou shalt not kill.
I could list other examples.
In the face of such contradictions by the various church establishments, the individual member of parliament is, even on the moral question presented with both positions, left personally to make his judgment as to the broad consensus of the Christian Church.
In the research and consultation that I was able to undertake, it seemed clear to me that while the establishments and hierarchy of some church organizations speak strongly and clearly in favour of abolition, an interdenominational broad poll from coast to coast would show that Christians in general are in favour of retention of capital punishment and, taken as a group, would exceed the percentage reported by the various polls in the nation's news media. While I cannot fully substantiate this claim, I doubt that there are many neighbourhood church leaders who would refute this probability.
Abolitionists tend to centre their case around the question of deterrents and varying forms of empirical statistical analysis. Between the years of 1970 to 1974, during which time Canada was in a situation of de facto abolition, Statistics Canada provides the murder statistics as printed in the text I speak from today. While from these statistics I could claim that the murder rate had increased 25.9 per cent across Canada and claim that the reason for the increase was because the death penalty was in fact not invoked during this period, I reject that claim in the same way that I reject the claim of the abolitionists who will produce alternative sets of figures and interpretations to make their case. In my opinion, all these statistics indicate is that the murder rate is clearly up but the reason for the increase in the murder rate is not solely due to the effectual abolition of capital punishment, as currently practiced, but is rather only one factor in the increase in murder rate; the actual causes being the sum total of the many variants relating to the lifestyle, economics, morality and values prevalent in our society during any given period.
Similarly, comparing murder statistics in abolition countries and non-abolition countries of wide cultural and value differentials lacks considerable credibility or validity. Comparisons of different regions to ascertain the deterrent value of capital punishment must reckon with such factors as the homogeneity of the society and its traditions, and whether these have been lawless or law-abiding. Even regions within a country indicate variations. It is not surprising, therefore, to see that in the Northwest Territories the increase between 1970 to 1974 was 14 per cent, while in British Columbia the increase was 47 per cent. New England also, as another example, as might be expected, has had a low murder rate over the centuries. Rising racial animosity in Boston and its suburbs seems likely to change this tradition as it has drastically altered the social climate of Philadelphia and San Francisco.
I make these points, not to make a case for the retentionists but, rather, to question the cornerstones of the abolitionist argument. I suggest that the bric-a-brac of the statistical by-play game has little real value and is invalid, or at the least misleading and inconclusive.
June 10, 1976

Abolitionists often attempt to discredit retentionists by claiming that they are emotional and non-objective. I suggest that more often the opposite is true. If we were to shun emotional response and look for objectivity and reason, the argument might well follow in this manner: living on a small and delicately balanced life support system, mankind, through his unbridled consumption and over-population has embarked on the irreversible selfdestruction of his environment; the obvious end to this process is a lawless and chaotic struggle for depleting life support systems. Murder statistics show that where the population is extremely high, with extreme affluence at one end and extreme poverty at the other, the incidence of lawlessness, including murder, is also extremely high and increases rapidly. In order to restore a balance within the life support structure, society requires discipline, law and order and balance. If we could be totally objective and emotional, logic would accept the elimination of murderers from that society.
Those who argue against deterrence as being a factor in the prevention of murder seem, somehow, to categorize murderers as some sort of non-persons. We have become so preoccupied with distorted sensationalism in our thinking about criminals that we have almost succeeded in persuading ourselves that all criminals are radically different from other people; that they are utterly indifferent to rewards and incentives, and that they are capable only of response to fleeting impulses or passionately uncontrollable forces from within. As police superintendent Tom Flanagan said in an interview:
Don't believe for a moment that they do not prize their lives as much as you and I. They have families like you. They have jobs, albeit illegal ones. They enjoy living and put a high value on their lives .. . Anyone who thinks criminals do not weigh the possibilities of getting caught and do not understand that they could be executed is talking absolute balderdash. Every sane person thinks about the consequences of his actions. Some of these people are brilliant strategists and there isn't any way you can be that if you don't consider consequences and accept the risks involved.
Some abolitionists claim that no one in his right mind would purposely plan to kill another human being. There is an implication that all murderers must be depraved or insane. I maintain that in many cases not only is a murderer perfectly sane and rational, but also that he may well be highly intelligent. In such cases it is not a matter of sanity but, rather, a matter of moral values. If a murderer is sane and rational, he is also capable of considering consequences and of accepting the risks involved. In the case of murders of this type, capital punishment could well be one deterrent factor which would convince such a person not to commit murder.
Assuming the rationality of the criminal and his adherence to a set of values different from that held by "normal" persons in our society, the alternative to capital punishment is limited to some form of brainwashing or life imprisonment. Are the abolitionists suggesting total life imprisonment, or some form of mind alteration along the lines of the "Clockwork Orange" solution? Or, if the deterrent of capital punishment is removed, do abolitionists support the alternative of maintaining prisoners who pass their lives in drug-induced docility in root-cellar prisons?
Another favourite and typical statement made by abolitionists is this, "We must be very clear in our thinking and
Capital Punishment
our motives must be objective and unemotional." Then, in almost the same breath, they quote the line about Madame La Farge taking her knitting to the guillotine. Or else they hurry to this description of a hanging and its aftermath:
Two wardens would then cut the corpse down, lay it out on the table in the pit for the coroner to tuck the tongue back into the mouth, plug all orifices with cotton batten and then, while we stood around the body, proceed with the inquest.
It is interesting to note how on one hand an abolitionist will condemn emotionalism, while on the other using it for his own purposes. Mr. Speaker, murder is emotional and it is impossible to consider the subject without emotion. As a consequence, it is not my intention to discredit abolitionists who use this emotional approach. At the same time, I would not expect them to put down retentionists who use similar emotionalism to express the retentionist point of view. The question remains: What about the victim found in a bush area off the parkway who had been bludgeoned and stabbed several times with a screwdriver, or the two little girls who were raped and then strangled with their own blue jeans?
Those who hope that alternatives to capital punishment might have been found and presented to the House must be dismally disappointed in Bill C-84. There is nothing in this legislation to indicate that prisons will be changed so as to ensure that they are more than merely warehouses for convicts. There is no indication that the social and economic costs of locking people up for long periods have been considered. There is no indication that the government has a clear conception of the objectives it wishes to achieve in administering punishment by incarceration.
How can an abolitionist, who condemns capital punishment on the grounds that it is nothing more than revenge and an expression of the retributive urge support, proposed sentences of 25 years mandatory for first-degree murder, and ten years for second-degree murder? These proposals guarantee a prison system populated by men and women without hope. There is no evidence to support the notion that spending ten years in prison guarantees that a woman who shot her husband will emerge a better and happier person for that decadent experience.
If the abolitionists were truly humanitarian, they would call for indefinite sentences, recognizing that one man's rehabilitation might well take place in one year and that another's might never occur in a hundred years. They would call for punishment to fit the crime and the criminal, rather than a process of fitting the crime and the criminal to the punishment. They would recognize that one man's punishment might well be another man's pleasure, and vice versa. They would urge that those with maximum potential for rehabilitation should be identified and the full rehabilitative capacity of our society brought into effect; that justice be tempered with reason, emotion, mercy and love. The 25-year provision is arbitrary, illogical and self-defeating and I oppose it firmly in favour of the rehabilitative principles I have just enunciated.
In a complicated and diversified society such as ours, the 25-year provision will have little more effect than to restrict the parameters of justice by limiting the flexibility now given to judges to make allowance for the multiplicity of variants in the nature and individuality of the crime and the criminal. Our system requires a broad and full

June 10, 1976
Capital Punishment
range of options for punishment and rehabilitation-from pardon to parole, to prison, to solitary confinement, to capital punishment.
Like many other MPs, I questioned constituents regarding their views on the retention or abolition of capital punishment. While earlier questionnaires to the constituency elicited a return of approximately 8 per cent, the results of my last questionnaire showed that of 48,300 sent out, 7,885 were returned, for a percentage of 16.3. The tabulation indicated that 95.1 per cent of those who returned the questionnaire wanted capital punishment retained. Certainly, the value of such polls is not absolute. But whether the result showed 85 per cent or 98 per cent, the fact remains that it is a clear indicator of the broad, general feeling of my constituents and, in my opinion, of Canadians in general.
Like other members of parliament, I believe polls are only one of the factors which lead members to a decision on this subject. While I certainly did not agree with all the statements made in the hundreds of letters, telephone calls, conversations, interviews and public meetings, I might put on record a number of typical responses from constituents. Some thought there should be a national referendum and that the government should be bound by its results. Others pointed out that it cost between $10,000 and $15,000 a year to keep a prisoner in jail-money which might well be used to rehabilitate prisoners with a greater potential for return to the community.
Others say that we should strike a bold new step and bring back the noose; that until some better deterrent comes along we must retain the death penalty; that punishment must be swift and certain; that capital punishment is a deterrent. It is said there is a fundamentalist revival that recognizes revenge and retribution as valid motives for capital punishment; that we should vote secretly to avoid party pressure; that 25 years is a slow death; that capital punishment is justifiable homicide; that murder is an act of free will and the perpetrator must and should be held accountable with his life.
Others liken capital punishment to animal management and say that an animal that must be destroyed is destroyed without animosity or emotion but, rather, with cold, rational management. It is said that protection of the public is the most important consideration. Some ask, would the subject of capital punishment even have been raised if existing laws were enforced? Others say that responsible government is outmoded due to massive government intervention, that therefore there is confusion, and that consequently members of parliament should vote on a representative basis. Some feel the abolitionists should tell us how they will protect us. Still others claim that abolition has proved unsuccessful and they are tired of permissiveness, that now is the time to try severity. Some say that to propose the abolition of capital punishment for treason is treasonable; that we should not let the minority point of view of abolitionist members of parliament repress the will of the majority of Canadians. And so on and so forth, Mr. Speaker.
I could go on listing this typical kind of response that comes directly to all of us from our constituents. While I

certainly do not endorse all of the sentiments expressed by my constituents in letters to me, the mood of the country is frightening, yet clearly expressed. In the final analysis, the government must reflect, at least to some degree, the tenor of the times, however much this distorts the priorities of reason. After all, Mr. Speaker, democracy can prevail only if the law reflects the will and tolerance of the people. It does seem clear from any broadly based assessment of public opinion that the tolerance of the people for a humane and, in the short run, somewhat riskier penal system is being strained to the point of breaking.
In casting my vote for retention I do so with considerable regret. The responsibility of a judge is heavy when he finds a criminal guilty of premeditated murder. But how much heavier is the weight and pressure of responsibility on a member of parliament whose vote is cast for legislation that will put a man to death?
As I cast such a vote for retention, I feel regret and sorrow both for the criminal and his family. I feel anger at the failure of the institutions of our society and the inadequacy of my own efforts within these institutions. I feel anger that the schools, after 14 years of education, have been unable to teach the young people of our community self-respect for themselves, let alone self-respect for others in the community. I feel concerned that the church that has preached loud through the centuries has been unable to achieve its objective. I feel concerned and disappointed that the home that is supposed to provide the base of security and acceptance for the individual has, instead, in too many cases, rejected the individual; and with the community rejecting the individual, resulting in criminality, that we then allow that condition to continue.
It is with great regret and responsibility, Mr. Speaker, that I shall cast my vote thus; and it is with a pledge to work hard to improve our society, to move it forward so that perhaps another day another time will come when I, along with others in the House of Commons, will find that the time has come to vote for abolition.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel it is regrettable that members of parliament should be put in the position where this very serious matter is being debated once again. I feel this way because I think the responsibility for this must fall on the shoulders of the government. If the existing law had been upheld, as everyone in Canada expected it to be, we would not be discussing this bill in parliament today. When this bill comes to a vote, although I should not be prejudging the outcome, if it is defeated, then having spent many weeks debating this very serious issue we will again find ourselves in the position of having to live with the existing law and wondering whether the government is in fact going to obey it.
The second reason I am on my feet this afternoon is that I want to restate some of the views I hold about this legislation and to put forward a view that I think is held by the majority of my constituents. We are discussing Bill C-84 which seeks to amend the existing legislation, which provides that a murderer can be sentenced to death for the killing of a policeman or a jail guard and that all other cases of murder are regarded as second-degree murder. I say again that if the government had fulfilled its responsibility to the people of Canada, we would not be discussing this bill today.
June 10, 1976

The points I wish particularly to discuss this afternoon have to do with the arguments that have been presented on both sides of this issue; the arguments presented by the abolitionists from various articles available to us and to the public, and the arguments presented by the retention-ists. The abolitionists advance the argument that the death penalty is not an effective deterrent to prevent murder. The second point they make is that the imposition of such a penalty is contrary to all concepts of Christianity. Their third argument is that the hanging of a murderer is nothing more than an instrument of revenge. Their fourth argument is that all forms of capital punishment are objectionable and repulsive, and that the alternative to capital punishment is life imprisonment and a rehabilitative program.
To take the first argument of the abolitionists, that the death penalty is not an effective deterrent in the prevention of murder, I suggest that the deterrent effect of a certain punishment has two aspects: deterrence as it applies to the convicted prisoner, and deterrence as it applies to others who read about or otherwise learn of the imposition of such a punishment on a prisoner convicted by the courts. I suggest that such a penalty is the only deterrent that will guarantee that a murderer will not commit a murder a second time. Life imprisonment is certainly an assurance that for a given period a second murder will not be committed, but with the government doing some of the strange things it has done in the past, that is not much of an assurance.
Life imprisonment does not mean that a convicted murderer will spend the remainder of his life in custody. On the contrary, Mr. Speaker, all it means is a lengthy term in a penitentiary. But let us suppose that life imprisonment really does mean life imprisonment and that it would be enforced as presently proposed in Bill C-84. There is still a danger, and no guarantee, that a lifer will not again commit murder in attempting to escape from prison. Surely there is ample precedent for this view, and the possibility of prison murder increases as the number of lifers in prison increases.
The second argument that the abolitionists put forward is that the imposition of such a penalty is contrary to all concepts of Christianity. It seems to me that there is a conflict here. It appears to me that those who would make such a statement have not read three particular passages in the Bible to which I might refer. The first is Exodus, chapter 21, verse 12 which states:
He that smiteth a man, so that he die, shall be surely put to death.
The second passage, Leviticus, chapter 24, verse 17, states:
And he that killeth any man shall surely be put to death.
The third passage, Deuteronomy, chapter 19, verses 11 and 12, states:
But if any man hate his neighbour, and lie in wait for him, and rise up against him, and smite him mortally that he die, and fleeth into one of these cities; then the elders, of his city shall send and fetch him thence, and deliver him into the hand of the avenger of blood, that he may die.
Surely the aforementioned passages are the wish of God, who is the divine ruler of the world, and anyone who does not want to abide by his ruling should not say that he
Capital Punishment
believes in God, because if he does not want to abide by God's ruling how can he believe that God will save him from eternal suffering? Furthermore, as the Fifth Commandment says, "Thou shalt not kill". That tells you what not to do. The aforementioned Bible passages are warnings concerning what shall happen to anyone who kills a fellow citizen. It does not mean that they should get royal accommodation and royal service. Surely they should not receive the kind of treatment this government has been dispensing since the middle 1960s.
The third argument that is raised is that hanging a murderer is nothing more nor less than an instrument of revenge. I think the simple answer to that argument is that if the murderer has so little respect for the life of the victim, then it certainly does not appear to me that if society has no more respect for his life, that is revenge.
The fourth argument the abolitionists put forward in respect of capital punishment is that it is objectionable and repulsive. I must say that that statement is true. But, Mr. Speaker, so, also, are wars repulsive. Surely wars in the defence of one's country are not nearly as repulsive as wars fought to save political face, as has been the case in recent times where hundreds of thousands of "cream of the crop" young men have died to save the political image of politicians.
Yes, killing in any form is repulsive. It is as repulsive to take the life of a murderer as it is for a murderer to take the life of an innocent victim. But if that is the law of the land, then each one of us as an individual has the responsibility to abide by that law. So that is a valid point. Killing is repulsive. Killings by murderers are even more repulsive. In wartime, a Christian may kill an enemy in battle to prevent the enemy from killing other persons. Under the guise of self-defence, a Christian may kill an assailant who intends to kill another human being. Therefore, why may not a Christian government provide a law for the killing of a convicted murderer in order to protect its innocent citizens? I submit that killing of all kinds is repulsive, but capital punishment is not in the nature of revenge; it is, rather, a punishment justifiably prescribed by law, a punishment aimed to have effective deterrent results which I am thoroughly convinced it has.
As a retentionist, I believe that the repeal of capital punishment could unleash on society a greater number of criminals to murder innocent people, to rape, to maim, or to betray their country. I firmly believe that many the capital murder offenders are beyond the rehabilitative process. Surely not all, but many are beyond the rehabilitative process, and therefore the risk is too great. I believe that without the deterrence of capital punishment, the lifer would be much more violent toward policemen and authority, and there is a possibility that the people responsible in institutions would have to have their authority extended for the purpose of greater retaliation and this, reasonably, could lead to a greater upswing in violence and murder.
I suggest that 25 years in jail, as proposed by this bill, is less humane than the death sentence. Life imprisonment, particularly where there is little or no hope of parole, itself creates tension and anxiety. Custodial officers are forces to segregate or watch lifers most carefully. This places upon those officials an onerous and difficult responsibility, with a constant awareness of the danger to themselves.

June 10, 1976
Capital Punishment
I have on my file letters from people who have suffered through having lost loved ones who are prepared at this point in time to take the law into their own hands unless the government takes very serious action in this regard. To the extent that this government has not obeyed its own law, there has been, to a degree, a breakdown in our moral values. How does a government expect the populous of a nation to respect the laws this parliament passes, when the government fails to obey them?
It is true that in many instances the death penalty is not a deterrent. A person who is mentally deficient cannot conceive of his own death. Capital offences are usually of an emotional, spur of the moment nature. They are acts which are not planned. That, again, suggests temporary insanity, and in most cases that kind of murderer will not hang. It has been suggested that juries, in the knowledge that a man may die, are less likely to convict. Therefore, the culprit often is acquitted, which makes a travesty of justice. I have more faith in the jury system of this country than I have in a minister of justice or a solicitor general who will commute a death sentence when there is not a recommendation of mercy from the jury.
In conclusion, I wish only to say that my concern is not mainly in respect of murders of passion, murders that are not planned-because they cannot be controlled. They will not be controlled by Bill C-84. They will not be banned unless we ban the association of human beings one with another. What I am concerned about is the premeditated murder, organized crime, the hitman, so-called, and the destitute who deliberately plans to commit a robbery or a felony, and does so. I think to them it is a deterrent, because they are indeed very astute people in the pursuit of their trade. If weaponry is part of that pursuit, then the penalty for the crime should be the ultimate penalty.
I think the proposals in Bill C-84 are inhumane. Recent surveys have indicated that lifers who have been interviewed would prefer the death penalty to a 25 year sentence without hope of parole. The rehabilitation process is expensive, slow, tedious and uncertain. There is an everlasting risk of recidivism. Some way that capital punishment is archaic. Well, so is murder. The only thing modern about murder is the modern weaponry used to mow down a policeman or a bank teller. On the basis of that brief statement, I intend to vote against Bill C-84.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Skoreyko) and the members who spoke before him. They conveyed many of the sentiments that I wish to convey to this chamber. I am deeply concerned as I take the opportunity to participate in the debate this afternoon on Bill C-84. I do not propose to speak at great length on this legislation because, as I have said previously, many of my colleagues have already put forward many excellent arguments and any detailed remarks on my part would only prove repetitious on points that have already been made by these members.
However, I do wish to voice some of the sentiments and views of the constituents of Wetaskiwin on the extremely controversial issue of capital punishment. Nearly 90 per cent of the individuals who answered the recent question-
naire I sent out voted in favour of the reinstatement of the death penalty for all premeditated murders. Of the constituents who responded, 88.3 per cent said they wanted retention of capital punishment, 9 per cent favoured abolition of capital punishment, and 2.7 per cent agreed with the present law on the death penalty.
I found these results very interesting, particularly in light of a comparison between the current feeling and that of few years ago when we debated this issue. A poll of my constituency conducted in 1973 revealed that 74.3 per cent of the individuals who responded favoured reinstatement of capital punishment. Yet a large percentage-some 47 per cent-were willing to consider life imprisonment as a satisfactory substitute for capital punishment. Today, only 17.7 per cent believe that long prison terms would be an acceptable alternative to the death penalty.
Emotions in Canada are running extremely high because of the steady increase in violent crimes, in particular crimes in which the victims have been innocent, law-abiding citizens or law enforcement agents. Naturally, in view of the number of horrible murders and violent crimes committed recently in this country, the current major concern of all Canadians is the prevention and reduction of crime in order to protect our society. I believe that much of the strong feeling in my riding in favour of capital punishment stems from a concern over the lawlessness that individuals see everywhere today, and frustration over the fact that the law as it now stands has not been carried out by the present government.
I do not intend to involve myself in a discussion of the possible deterrent effects of the death penalty. Others have argued against the arguments of the abolitionists. The hon. member for Edmonton East recently put those arguments on the record. Rather, I would like to say a few words about the general scope of this bill. The government is presenting the citizens of Canada with an ill-formulated and, I believe, an unjust piece of legislation containing provisions on two aspects of conflicting principles which should more properly be dealt with in their own right.
The gist of the legislation is, first, to abolish capital punishment entirely in favour of lengthened imprisonment terms; second, to impose mandatory sentences of 25 years and 10 years to be served for first-degree and second-degree murder, respectively, without any consideration being given to the crime itself and the circumstances surrounding it. Little room is left for the exercise of judicial discretion. I think I am correct in saying that most retentionists would not advocate the death penalty for second-degree murder, say for a murder of passion resulting from a domestic dispute. The majority of these killings are unpremeditated, even accidental; the murderer would probably never again commit such a crime and therefore poses no threat to society or the safety of others.
While no one can condone the taking of life, for whatever reason, I believe that few people would maintain that a person who has no previous criminal record and who committed a crime of passion should be incarcerated for a minimum of 10 years. The punishment should be dependent upon both the individual's past behaviour and the circumstances surrounding the crime itself. To imprison a person who may contribute something of value to society and whose freedom constitutes no threat to the well-being
June 10, 1976

of others seems both unfair to society in general and to the individual in particular.
I believe in the premise that if you put someone in prison, he can be rehabilitated. The same can be said of individuals who commit first-degree murder. Will a mandatory 25-year sentence really prove of concrete value? During the 25 years in prison, the prisoner constitutes a burden to the Canadian taxpayer. He is a potential escapee and poses a danger to other prisoners and prison officials. On the whole, I think that a blanket 25-year sentence is not the answer for all first-degree murders. Some individuals deserve harsher treatment, others could be treated more leniently. Again I reiterate that the punishment has to be suited to the crime.
It seems to me that there are, indeed, instances where the death penalty is warranted: for mass murders perpetrated by organized crime syndicates, for treason killings, political assassinations, ritual slayings, killings of policemen and law enforcement officers. Even for some cold, calculated murders planned for financial gain, the death penalty would not be unreasonable, dependent upon the circumstances involved in the crime. But there may well be mitigating circumstances in some first-degree murder cases, and these should be carefully examined before sentence is passed.
Let us consider, for example, a man who plans to slay his wife's lover, or who plots the murder of a drunken driver who has seriously injured or killed his child or spouse. This man would be extremely unlikely to ever kill again, and could doubtless contribute more to society outside the prison walls, after he has been punished, than by being incarcerated for 25 years. Certainly he must be punished, but the punishment must suit the crime.
The Canadian people are indeed concerned, with justification, about the recent rise in our crime rate. They want action, and this is something the present government has failed to give them thus far. Even though the law at present calls for the death penalty for murderers of policemen and prison officials, the cabinet has commuted every death sentence. Likewise, rehabilitation efforts on the government's part have proved minimal, at best. Once again, with the introduction of this legislation the government has failed the citizens of Canada and has failed to show leadership in this very important area.
We are faced with only one alternative: abolish capital punishment and enforce lengthened prison sentences, with no regard for the nature of the crime. Imposition of the death penalty and prison sentences should be discussed separately. They should not be part and parcel of the same piece of legislation. The circumstances surrounding each crime must be carefully examined before sentence is passed, be the sentence the death penalty or imprisonment.
However, the enforcement of harsher penalties after a crime has been committed cannot, alone, lead to a lower crime rate. More effective correctional and rehabilitation programs are essential for both juveniles and adults which will, as much as possible, ensure that a prisoner upon his release from prison will be fully rehabilitated and declared fit to join society again. The government must concentrate
Capital Punishment
its efforts on providing valid, constructive rehabilitative programs in our prisons.
The entire peace and security package is supposedly designed to bring about a decrease in Canada's crime level. I fail to see how this legislation will prove effective in so doing, just as I fail to see how Bill C-83 will help in this area. Rather, I view this bill particularly as a thorn in the side of Canada's criminal law and jurisprudence system.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that capital punishment is a very difficult subject with which to deal. This has been amply demonstrated. There is the humanitarian standpoint and the standpoint of law and order in the state. A society without guidelines and ways and means of applying justice to those who would offend has nothing but anarchy and disorder. Justice must be meted out well and fairly to both the offender and the offended. Generally, in those cases the offender's peers sit as a jury and listen to all the evidence presented by both sides, and the judge sums up the case. The jury then carefully weighs the evidence to see that justice is done and that the judicial laws of this country are carried out. However, with this legislation I believe the government is trying to trade off capital punishment for long prison sentences to appease the people because of the long list of murders which have occurred since the government has failed to carry out any executions for the murder of prison guards or police officers since 1961. Let us look at the trend of murder from 1961 to the present time. We see that murders have doubled and that attempted murders have quadrupled. This is over a period of years when never have we given more to help social well-being in the community. Never have we spent more on housing, education and health. I am sure this is why the people of Canada have said they have had enough. They say that we have tried another plan and found it wanting. In my own constituency, people are overwhelmingly in favour of capital punishment. I feel that regardless of my own beliefs, I represent the thoughts of those people and in no way would I be responsible if I did not consider those wishes.
The carrying out of capital punishment should not be done by hanging. I think there are far more humane methods than hanging. A life can be taken in the quietness of a chamber with a minister or priest, prison officials and a judge present and giving the prisoner a period of time to make his peace. As an alternative, I could not be cruel enough, in any way, to sentence any man to 25 years in prison or a longer term if necessary-and that will be necessary because very few prisoners who receive a term of 25 years could be reformed or rehabilitated. All such a sentence can do is frighten or frustrate a man because of the long road ahead with nothing but hopelessness, walls and cells. Much better it would be to have the little white chamber and a quiet exit, than the Chinese water torture method of destroying a man's soul a little bit each day.
The minister states that cases would be reviewed in 15 years. At least all hope will not be taken away from prisoners. But 15 years is destructive in itself. A man going into prison at 35 years of age would be released at 50 years of age into a vastly different and rapidly moving world. Rehabilitation of this man would be beyond one's fondest dreams. Even if I was an abolitionist, there is no way I would have the heart or cruelty within myself to impose a

June 10, 1976
Capital Punishment
prison sentence of this length with the hope of rehabilitation, knowing full-well that rehabilitation would be nearly impossible. If we take an active individual and sentence him to 25 years in prison, he will become a robot with no hope for the future.
I want to substantiate that statement with the statement of Dr. Boyd, who is the head of the institution for the criminally insane. Incidentally, Dr. Boyd was an abolitionist, but he now says that he is forced into taking the position that we must have capital punishment and he has retired entirely from his position of being an abolitionist. He states that it would be absolutely impossible to control or to help a fellow who is facing that long prison term, and that bit by bit we would not only destroy him, but we would also destroy any chances of rehabilitation. Further, it would frustrate the man and he could very well become an incorrigible prisoner who might lead prison riots or lead others into grabbing hostages. As I said before, never before in the history of prison reform have prisoners been treated as well as they have over the last ten years, and never before have there been so many guards taken hostage. We have seen that in the west, and we have seen it across Canada. So here we have, as reported, a man of Mr. Boyd's stature, someone intimately associated with the criminally insane, saying that this long sentence will completely destroy any chance of rehabilitation.
I remember well once seeing a fellow in prison clothes standing outside Kingston penitentiary. I went inside and told a guard that there was a man out there on the prison walk, and I was told that that fellow had been released three years ago but he did not want to go out; he was absolutely unable to face the world.
I ask, which is kindest, cruelly destroying a person day after day in a cell over a period of years, or quietly letting that person meet his maker after he has had a good opportunity to see his priest or preacher, to set himself right after the criminal acts he has perpetrated in this world and to ask forgiveness in eleventh hour repentance?
I have heard people quote the Scriptures. I think the Bible can be used to back any stand. I have here an article by John Palmer, published in the Orillia Journal. John Palmer is the son of a minister. He states that this humanitarian standpoint started in the nineteenth century. He says it is a good standpoint. He continues, and says that people are quoting the Bible to back their stand, and one quotation they are using is, "Thou shalt not kill." He goes on to say that it is now known to be correctly translated, "Thou shalt not murder." There is one quotation which covers murder and which I think is very relevant. When Christ was asked about taxes, he answered, "Render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar's and unto God the things that are God's." What Mr. Palmer was saying is that you have to run this world by law and order.
I wanted to point out that it is probably a failure of society and probably a failure of the church that there is not enough contact with families who need help. Perhaps a young man could be saved from a life of crime, or a young girl from a life of prostitution. On the whole, society has treated its citizens well, but over the past several years we have had many prison riots and anti-social behaviour in
(Mr. Rynard.]
the prisons although social workers and others try hard to improve the system. How many prisoners have been killed within prisons in the last few years? This government imposes long prison sentences and total confinement for psychopaths, which just means that more prisoners will be killed. It just means that we will have to employ more security guards and this should be a priority.
At the same time as we are doing this, however, we are closing hospitals and firing staff, which means that we do not properly provide for the sick and severely afflicted. Some of the sick and afflicted are really under a sentence of death because they are going to die of the disease from which they suffer. On the other hand, the bank robber who laid plans and carried a gun with him at the time of the act, and knew that he might either kill a policeman or be killed by one, has in effect accepted the possibility of death. If he killed one or two policemen, the possibility is, today, that he would be sentenced to 25 years behind prison walls. But, Mr. Speaker, this also destroys a man day after day.
Many years ago, when I was a medical student, we took clinics in the penitentiaries and observed that long prison sentences destroyed any chance of rehabilitation. Many prisoners told us that they would rather have been shot when robbing a bank than land in prison. To me, the ultimate cruelty is 25 years behind bars. With a short prison sentence there is a chance for reform. If a prisoner gets out within five years, I believe there is a good chance of keeping him away from crime-and particularly if he is crime-free in five years.
Psychiatrists, doctors and social workers have never been able to determine what goes on in a man's mind. I remember the famous "Red" Ryan who escaped from Kingston penitentiary in 1922. He had killed someone during a bank robbery and was sentenced to life imprisonment. After his escape he was recaptured and returned to the prison under guard. For some time he caused all kinds of trouble, and then was put in the "hole", on bread and water. He started a whole destructive process in the penitentiary, through chants. I remember being in the prison hospital one day treating some prisoners, and the chanting was so loud that we could not hear ourselves speak. All the prisoners, even the one we were treating, were chanting.
That is not an easy thing to handle. Eventually, Ryan began to reform and he became an orderly. He was good looking, bright and intelligent, with an IQ of, I believe, about 150. He worked in the library and then in the works department and became a model prisoner. He was a Roman Catholic and the priest declared that he was reformed and could be paroled. I remember that R. B. Bennett was prime minister at that time. After "Red" Ryan's parole he went out speaking to service clubs and to boys' clubs, telling them that crime did not pay. He was a real success story. In time, a series of murders were committed in the Toronto area where Ryan lived. He also had a cottage at Jackson's Point. At Stouffville, which is near Toronto, a man discovered that his garage was being robbed and tires taken. His dog had been shot, so he went out himself to stop the robbery, and he was shot. He left a wife and three children. Some months afterwards, "Red" Ryan was shot dead in the process of robbing a liquor store in Sarnia.
June 10, 1976

What I am trying to convey, Mr. Speaker, is that there is no way a psychiatrist or anybody else can look into the mind of man and say what he is going to do. Man has a computerized brain and we do not know what starts the computer or what stops it. That just has not been discovered, so there is no way that we can predict a man's future.
Then there was the O'Donnell case in Toronto. A young school teacher had been murdered, her skull crushed. She had also been raped. O'Donnell was picked up. He had already served a term in Kingston for the same thing.
May I call it one o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had the file checked on this and am speaking from the knowledge conveyed to me by the file. I cannot claim to have a precise memory of what particular phrase was said at what particular time in the long sequence of events concerning the choice of an LRPA by the Canadian government. But, having checked the dates and, particularly, the statements made in the House by the Minister of National Defence, that he had become aware of this after his return from NATO in mid-December, I can only conclude that some time between December 15 and December 22 I became aware that the assurance that Lockheed could provide the bridge financing had been given verbally. It would be in that period when I became aware of that.
As for the second question, Mr. Speaker, as all the ministers involved have said repeatedly, they were aware some time in the fall and even before that, in the summer of 1975, of the difficulties of the Department of National Defence with financing the purchase of the long-range patrol aircraft. Indeed, we took a decision in the early fall, I believe, to increase the capital expenditures of DND in real terms by 12 per cent a year, in order to facilitate such purchases. So, we were aware of the cash flow difficulties with some precision toward the end of November, on November 27, when we realized we would have to do some borrowing-in other words, that there would have to be some bridge financing and that we would have to pay interest on it. At that time an approximate amount was established, but it was only'decided by Treasury Board in mid-December, on December 15, that $100 million-odd would be authorized for interest payments.
