speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON UN CONFERENCE ON TRADE AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
In reporting to the House on the results of the UN Conference on Trade and Development, I should like to say at the outset that its immediate results represent a major achievement in the dialogue between developed and developing countries on a new international economic order, and that the longer-term impact of Nairobi will be substantial. Obviously, UNCTAD IV-like all conferences where countries are required to make compromises in order to ensure agreement-did not achieve all that Canada or other developed and developing countries might have wished. But it was, without question, a most important step in the efforts to reduce disparities between developed and developing countries which were initiated at the seventh special session of the United Nations.
At that session I stated that Canada was determined to play a positive role, to use our resources and our influence to help bring about constructive change in the international economic system and thereby to reduce the gap between rich and poor nations. Governments committed themselves at that time to work together to make changes in the international trade and payments system in order to enable it to contribute to more rapid economic development in the developing countries and to permit them to obtain a larger and sustained share in world trade.
UNCTAD IV was the first major UN conference following the seventh special session, and in its disagreements as well as in its accords it reflected these new dimensions. There were efforts to address these questions at a practical level; there were some important new commitments; there was agreement to create a program, timetable and frame-

work for the central issues in which the many essential decisions can be taken.
In my statement to the conference on May 7, I touched on the four areas Canada considered would be the main issues to be dealt with: the problems of stabilization of commodity trade, the alleviation of the debt servicing difficulties of many developing countries, liberalization of trade to benefit developing countries, and the transfer of technology to developing countries. Of these, the commodities issue proved to be the central focus of the conference. Indeed, the adoption, by consensus, of a resolution which established an integrated program proposes a list of 18 commodities of particular interest to the developing countries for consideration, describes the international measures to be taken in the context of the program, and establishes procedures and a timetable for pursuing it.
On the important question of a common fund, the resolution provides for a negotiating conference to be held next year and for a series of preparatory meetings. As a major importer and exporter of commodities, we shall be actively involved in these international discussions and shall work with the other participants to resolve the problems of commodity trade which concern developing countries. These discussions and negotiations will provide the appropriate basis for examining the parameters of a common fund and for a decision regarding its establishment. As I stated in the House earlier this week, and as stated before that by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp), if we are satisfied in the course of these commodity meetings and negotiations that the common fund will be effective and useful, Canada will make a contribution to it.
The conference also took an important decision on the subject of the financial problems of developing countries by adopting, again by consensus, a resolution on the debt problems of developing countries. The resolution calls for appropriate international bodies to identify features relating to debt servicing problems which could provide guidance in the future for dealing with them. In addition, a ministerial session of the UNCTAD board will be held in 1977 to review this work and a group of experts will be established to assist in this review.
We had hoped that some further steps would be taken on the broader subject of financial transfers, which is of fundamental importance to many developing countries, but this was not possible. We had hoped, for example, that the conference would agree to improve the international standard for official development assistance so that developing countries would receive such assistance on softer terms than they do now. Although this was not agreed, we shall continue to pursue this objective.
Apart from these two issues of particular importance, the conference also adopted resolutions on trade liberalization, the transfer of technology and a number of other subjects. One remarkable, and encouraging, aspect of the conference was the fact that 12 of the 13 resolutions approved were adopted by consensus. No previous UNCTAD conference has reached such a broad measure of agreement.
Canada supported all of these resolutions, offering explanatory statements on a number of them. We also, together with other industrialized countries, supported a proposal for further study of the concept put forward by

the United States. Dr. Kissinger had proposed to the conference that early consideration be given to the establishment of an international resources bank to facilitate resource development in the poorer countries. While we have not reached any final conclusion on this idea, we believe that it fully merited further consideration and we regret that it was narrowly defeated by two votes, the great majority of developing countries abstained on the resolution.
Despite the difficulties which arose at the conference and the problems which still need to be resolved, I believe that the outcome augurs well for the continuing dialogue between the developed and developing countries. Most especially, the positive results of the conference, particularly in the commodity area, should provide a useful and constructive basis for pursuing the work of the Conference on International Economic Co-operation in Paris.
At UNCTAD IV, Dr. Perez Guerrero stated, on behalf of the developing members of CIEC, the Paris conference, that failure in Nairobi could bring into question the continuation of that dialogue. The 19 developing countries which are members of CIEC have now assessed the situation. In light of the progress made on a number of important questions at Nairobi, they have indeed judged it useful to continue the dialogue in Paris.
I fully share the view that there is a satisfactory prospect for balanced progress in CIEC during the remainder of the year. In July, the CIEC will be reviewing the progress it has made and setting its course for the second half of the year. I am confident that the results of UNCTAD IV will help the conference in Paris to pursue its essential objective-the strengthening of international cooperation for the benefit of all.
So far as Canada is concerned, we shall pursue the work outstanding from UNCTAD IV in UNCTAD, CIEC and other bodies. We shall pursue our interest in improving the international standard for official development assistance. Together with other countries, we shall consider further the balance of payments and debt problems of developing countries and the appropriate measures for meeting them. We shall continue to support the principle of joint producer-consumer financial responsibility, on a mandatory basis, for buffer stock financing within commodity agreements containing such stocks. We shall be actively involved in consultations and negotiations on individual commodities and on the common fund. We shall devote efforts to see that the developing countries achieve additional benefits in the course of the multilateral trade negotiations in Geneva. We shall take an active part in the elaboration of a voluntary code of conduct for the transfer of technology which is universally applicable.
While the decisions taken by UNCTAD IV mark an important stage in our common efforts to reduce disparities between developed and developing countries, our progress toward that goal, to which the government is fully committed, will not be easy and will require hard decisions. As we proceed along that course, there will be costs for Canada and for individual Canadians. Their support will be essential, but with it, and the support of this

House, we may approach these decisions in a confident and positive manner.

Mr. Speaker, first of all, why is UNCTAD IV so important as to merit this statement in the House?
UNCTAD'S purpose and principal aim is to transform a global economic environment that is most unfavorable for the poorest two-thirds of humanity. It seeks to do this through the process of negotiation, that is, hard bargaining as distinct from rhetorical expositions on the state of the world. It is, therefore, an essential forum to put into practice the trade reforms necessary to close the widening rich-poor gap in the world. But many nations are in great danger, and Canada is no exception, of becoming victims of procedural intricacies while losing sight of our real objectives.
The message of UNCTAD, the message of Habitat now in its closing hours in Vancouver, the message of the UN conferences in the past few years on the environment, population, food and the new economic order is that we must set in motion a process of restructuring the world economy. This will require more than an expansion of growth, more than better control over cyclical fluctuations. As the Secretary General of the United Nations, Kurt Waldheim, has said, this restructuring requires a well-defined time-table of economic cooperation to bring about-
-a more equitable share of developing countries in industrial activities beyond their present mere 7 per cent of the world's industrialization.
-self-sufficiency in food in developing areas.
-indigenous capacity in science and technology.
-serious progress in the eradication of mass poverty and unemployment.
All this is why the parliamentary subcommittee on international development issued an interim report, prior to UNCTAD IV, urging the Canadian government to exert leadership "in seeking creative solutions to the problems of commodities trade which will be acceptable to producers and consumers in both developed and developing countries." Canada's leadership is essential, not only because UNCTAD IV is itself a crucial element in international negotiations, but because Canada is a bridge between the developed and developing countries. This special role is reflected in the fact that Canada is co-chairman of the continuing Conference on International Economic Co-operation.
The subcommittee therefore suggested that Canada make a clear statement at the opening of UNCTAD IV committing this country to a phased, co-ordinated approach to increase and stabilize the prices of primary commodities exported by the developing nations. Such an approach would include the selection of an agreed list of commodities for action, the establishment of a timetable for negotiations, and emphasis on the possibilities for linkages among commodity agreements such as integrated or common buffer stock financing.
What the government did, however, at the opening of the conference was merely to repeat our worn-out position that "we are prepared to continue examination of the proposal for a common fund . .." In other words, continued
June 10, 1976

study but no action. Yet the Scandinavian countries and The Netherlands were able to go into UNCTAD and immediately pledge a commitment to the common fund principle around which the success of UNCTAD IV was clearly seen to turn. That was the kind of leadership that I expected from Canada. Why was that firm leadership, leadership we are capable of, not given?
Canada has a five-year strategy-between 1975 and 1980-on international economic co-operation, yet the government fails to implement it. In fact, most Canadians do not even know of the existence of this multidimensional strategy which recognizes that aid, as such, is insufficient in our relations with developing nations. The reason the strategy is not being implemented-and why we were so weak at UNCTAD IV-is that the government cannot get it all together. Some of the policy-makers want to participate in integrated commodity agreements, and others say that our domestic economy would be adversely affected and that we therefore cannot move on new agreements. But not to move is to perpetuate the economic discrimination which is at the heart of the problem. For this debate is not about charity, not about the $1 billion CIDA spends in a band-aid approach to poverty; it is about new, equitable economic relationships. This point is acknowledged by every serious student of the rich-poor gap. Last Monday, the Globe and Mail, expressing its disappointment at UNCTAD IV said:
The reality is that, setting aside the oil trade, the rich countries are taking out of the poor countries in excess profits from five to ten times as much as they are putting in foreign aid.
The Globe and Mail put its finger on the problem:
Thanks to grossly unequal access of capital, to the third world's lack of market leverage, the vulnerability of economies that depend on a single export, and to barriers set up by the rich against the manufactured products of the poor, it is the industrial world that takes most of the profit from what the third world has to sell.
So UNCTAD IV lumbered on as the pressure mounted. The Canadian NGO representatives kept sending back reports on the impending failure of UNCTAD IV. This group should be commended for its serious efforts to mount public opinion in Canada. Questions about Canada's commitment to a common fund were raised in the House. Finally, on May 27 the cabinet responded to the pressure and committed Canada to a common fund, if in fact there would be a common fund.
Why did this commitment have to be dragged out of the government? Why did the cabinet have to be pulled, kicking and screaming, to the reality of what UNCTAD IV was all about? Why does the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) talk about a "conspiracy of love" to solve the problems of the developing world, when the government cannot back up sentiments of love with a commitment to action? Are we to assume that if the NGO community had not escalated the pressure on the government, there would have been no final commitment at Nairobi? Are we to assume that Canada finally acted because it wanted to save face at CIEC but without alienating the United States which was more committed to a new bank than new rules of trade? What a sad way that is for the government to lead!
Finally, UNCTAD IV ended with Canada giving its approval in principle, along with 15 other countries, to an integrated commodities program which calls for a negotiat-

ing conference on a common fund to be held before the end of March, 1977.
We urge the government to play a more active role in these negotiations, and to do this by first of all building a climate of support within Canada for this action, which is clearly in the interests of our own country. We want to build better and more diverse trading partners, and this can be done by equalizing economic opportunities. This approach is a far more positive one than relying on the CIDA budget to do the job. When this policy is fully explained to the Canadian people, the government will find support for some brave, new action.

Mr. Speaker, we welcome the minister's statement and are glad that he has been able to make such an optimistic statement about the results of UNCTAD IV. We share the views that he has expressed, and action on the various aspects of the new economic order is urged. The well-known Swedish economist, Gunnar Myrdal, put it very well when he declared that we have been living during one of history's most abrupt reversals of political climate. UNCTAD has been an important step in that essential reversal of policy. The minister himself said at the UNCTAD conference that we need action with an unprecedented sense of urgency. He then went on to say:
I believe that we have passed that stage of analysis and assessment of issues. We must now get together to devise workable and dynamic solutions.
I must say I share, with the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche), the view that these bold words were not effectively followed up; there has been a degree of hesitation. I would give as an illustration the common fund, of which mention has already been made. The common fund is essentially a means of getting funds for a buffer stock to stabilize commodity prices, and this is one of the primary requests of the developing countries. Its purpose is to procure the exchange of commodities through which they can develop themselves so that they will not be dependent upon aid from the outside world.
Instead of our delegation taking a firm stand on principle, they put it off until the very last minute. Even in his statement the minister skated around any commitment by Canada, saying there were a lot of conditions and sort of backward steps. There is, in fact, no commitment at all. May I read what the minister said in this regard. He said that we shall be working with the other participants to resolve the problems of commodity trade which concern developing countries. He went on:
These discussions and negotiations will provide the appropriate basis for examining the parameters of a common fund and for a decision regarding its establishment. As I stated in the House earlier this week, if we are satisfied in the course of these commodity meetings and negotiations that a common fund will be effective and useful, Canada will make a contribution to it.
As has been pointed out already by the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona, many other countries were able to make a firm commitment. It is true that the details of the commitment still have to be worked out. Obviously, if a commitment was made which was impossible to carry out, or which Canada felt was a totally impractical way of
14370

June 10, 1976

solving the problem, we would not expect Canada to go ahead; but the making of a firm commitment is indeed perfectly possible. I wish the minister had used the same sort of language as was used by Mr. Hakkvard Bakke, the minister for commerce for Norway, who followed the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen). He said:
Only decisions which can be transplated into the realities of the daily life of the poor masses are real contributions. I am glad to say quite unequivocally that my government is in agreement with and supports the main elements of an integrated program for commodities... we have already declared ourselves ready to contribute to a common fund. In our view UNCTAD should have the central co-ordinating role in this important venture-
That language seems to me rather different from the language used by the minister in his statement. Perhaps the minister is just indulging in ministerial caution, which in many cases, I suppose, is befitting of his particular position. But as he described it, this is an urgent situation calling for action, not-to use his own words-analysis or assessment. I am disappointed that this caution, and perhaps the caution of some of his colleagues as well, seems to have so watered down his approach that I must agree with the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona that we have not had the real leadership we would have had. This common fund is not a backbreaking financial burden. It has been estimated that it would cost between $21 million and $29 million for Canada's share, which is about 3 per cent of Canada's aid budget.
Then there are other matters, Mr. Speaker. There is a vague reference in the statement to a resolution on liberalization of trade, but not a word more is said about that. Apparently the minister has overlooked the fact that the committee on development, which was approved by the whole external affairs committee, firmly recommended that if we are serious about liberalizing trade, we should get on with the business of planning adjustment assistance for those who might possibly be affected.
Has anything been done in this regard? I shall have to ask some questions of the minister about that later, but there is no mention of it in his statement. We are told that there was a resolution. Are we serious about this, or not? If we are serious, we should look once again at what the committee recommended, which was a tripartite body composed of government, employers and employees working together to work out adjustment assistance. This means that if, as a consequence of trade liberalization, we face competition from overseas which destroys job opportunities, something ought to be done about it. I am just wondering why so little is said on that particular question. UNCTAD IV is only a beginning, but an important beginning, leading to what may take months or years to hammer into shape so that practical action can be taken.
In closing, may I say there is needed a far greater and continuing effort on the part of the government, members of parliament and those who have the role of leadership in the community to make clear how vitally important is this whole new movement. If we are to build a stable world based on co-operation, greater justice and equality for men of all races, then we will have to start putting into practice some of the noble words we have been using for quite a while now.

I know that we are committed, but we need something to evidence that commitment a little more so as to arouse the Canadian people who must give it their support. If they do not do so, it will fail and fizzle. We have to do more to warn the people of Canada that we are in an era of drastic change; that justice as well as our own future stability and economic security depend upon a real change of opinions and upon action being taken in this field.

Mr. Speaker, first I should thank the minister for having been kind enough to send us a French copy of his statement before the opening of the House and we wish that this practice will continue in every other similar circumstances.
UNCTAD IV that was held in Nairobi in Kenya from May 3 to 28, 1976 enabled more than 2,000 delegates from over 150 countries to meet and try to find answers for the establishment of a new international economic order, which means that the old economic order that we knew is no longer appropriate.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) was very careful in his statements concerning our commitments to the developing countries and he was right because when we know the pressions between industrialized countries and poorer nations we realize how difficult it is to find an easy answer without offending one or the other of the countries that give or ask for help. Furthermore, an action program at the international level is highly impracticable because of important differences between the nations which can help and those which rely on that help. As the minister said, two particularly significant resolutions have resulted from this conference. One establishing an integrated program for basic products and the other concerning the debts of developing countries.
Mr. Speaker, it is unusual and it surprised me that even at the international level we discuss debts even before we talk about development. Even undeveloped countries have managed to get into debt. It is again an obvious sign of the illogicality of political economy principles which typify the financial management of those countries which have debts even before growing to maturity. Several external help programs have already been created by various international groups and by some countries, including Canada, the United States and others, and unfortunately the helping countries are too often criticized to the same extent as their generosity. But I am pleased by the minister's statement and I hope, as he said, that this conference will eventually give long term positive results.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs a couple of questions. Why is it that Canada changed its position during the course of UNCTAD? In the minister's speech during the opening days of UNCTAD he merely said we would give our assent to a study of the common fund principle around which the success of UNCTAD IV was turning. Indeed, on May 11 when he reported to the external affairs committee he said he was not yet convinced of the need for a common fund. Yet on May 27 the cabinet met and gave its assent to the principle of the fund, which was subsequently
June 10, 1976

announced in the House and relayed to Nairobi, enabling us to sign the statement of the resolution with 15 other countries at the conclusion of UNCTAD.
I ask the minister, now, what evidence was put before the federal cabinet to enable it to change its mind and give its assent to the principle of the common fund, evidence that was not available at the opening of this conference and which would have enabled Canada to go into the conference at the beginning and give the commitment in the opening stages so that we would have been able to give the leadership that UNCTAD so desperately needed?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not regard the comments made in the House by the President of the Privy Council as any change in the Canadian position. It was merely an evolution of a position that had been taken by myself in my opening statement when I said we were quite prepared to examine further the concept of the common fund. We merely advanced that proposition to the point where we stated that as a result of discussions and negotiations, if the common fund justified itself in terms of usefulness in the solution of commodity problems, then we would be prepared to contribute to it.
I do not regard it as a change of position, because these contingencies obviously were in our minds as we prepared for the conference and as we considered the various attitudes we could take. I do not regard it as any change. Our delegation, headed by Mr. Bruce, had been advising us of the developments in the discussion and it was in response to our own convictions on this point and the developments of UNCTAD that caused us really to carry forward the policy which had been indicated in embryo in my opening statement.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to see there was such a speedy evolution in the government's thinking during the course of UNCTAD IV, which only shows what can be gained by escalating pressure. That brings me to the question of public understanding of what this conference is all about and, indeed, the understanding and the commitment of the House itself.
I ask the minister why the report of the subcommittee on international development has not yet been tabled in the House, despite an expressed public desire by the minister that it be so debated in order to bring up the level of understanding by the Canadian people concerning the structural changes required in international relationships that are highlighted in the report. Those structural changes can be most significantly demonstrated by reference to two figures. Canada's aid to the ten leading recipient countries in bilateral assistance last year was $330 million, yet our trade surplus with those same ten countries was $368 million, which led CIDA to confirm today that there is a greater benefit to Canada in economic relations with these aid partners. In other words we gain more than we put into the developing countries, which is at the heart of the problem. The subcommittee reported on this, yet that report continues to be buried.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, perhaps I should correct a false impression under which the hon. member seems to be labouring, namely, that the whole matter of the common fund was escalated as a result of public pressure. Obvious-

ly, we had considered the view made known by the subcommittee. We had listened to views in the House of Commons. We were listening in Nairobi, and we acted in conformity with our own understanding of the realities and not as a result of any public pressure directed to us from Nairobi particularly.
I do not regard public pressure as distasteful or undesirable, but I think the hon. member would agree that there certainly was not an outcry among the Canadian public on the common fund that would cause the government to react to a groundswell in its favour. Unfortunately, the Canadian public up to the present time has exhibited only marginal interest in the subject we are discussing today. I had intended today, in my statement and in other ways, to draw to the attention of the House and the public these important questions that are so vital to the future of the world. I would be prepared to debate the subcommittee report at any time, but as my hon. friend knows, we are rushing pell-mell in this House to deal with all kinds of important matters and it is not easy to fit in every subject matter. That is the only reason.

I have a final supplementary, Mr. Speaker. The reason the Canadian public has a marginal interest in these questions is that the Canadian government has not laid before the public the full exposition of what this question is all about. I ask the minister specifically, with reference to the speech he made at the opening of UNCTAD, when he referred at page 5 of his speech to using aid funds to establish a trade facilitation office to assist developing countries seeking to export to the Canadian market, what did he mean by "trade facilitation office", and to what extent is the Canadian government prepared to move on that?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I thought that was a particularly positive proposal that was made in my statement. We did make several other important proposals that were not accepted by the conference, including a proposal to increase the grant threshold, including a proposal to have a debt conference and a proposal for support of mandatory joint producer and consumer financing operations. All these were distinct Canadian proposals which were not accepted and were, in my view, somewhat ahead of some of the proposals which were accepted. The purpose of the trade facilitation office is to assist developing countries to penetrate the Canadian market. We are taking that proposal seriously and it is being studied at present. It is a new proposal, but it has not yet been implemented.

Mr. Speaker, it is not easy, on the strength of 8V2 pages of generalities, to formulate questions: rather, this invites comment. There are two specific questions which I should like to ask, one relating to a comment that is made, and one relating to an omission. On page 5 the minister speaks in glowing terms of how happy he is that there was such a broad measure of agreement in that 12 of the 13 resolutions were adopted by consensus. I wonder if this is not a way, perhaps, of avoiding standing up and being counted. When you have reservations in a consensus procedure, you do not actually have to say you agree or disagree; you can virtually abstain.
9SS70-9y2

June 10, 1976

This is unusual in UN procedure. I wonder whether the minister would care to comment on this point, because it seems that the whole thing is a means of befogging the issue and, as two or three of my colleagues have suggested, there are no clear, positive actions aside from the decision to study something further. This matter has been studied for years now. On the matter of consensus, I wonder if the minister could comment on why he considers this more desirable than a voting procedure, because on the next page he says that something was missed by a couple of votes.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. With all due respect, the hon. member has no difficulty in putting precise questions. He has put this question two or three times.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I have not advocated consensus in preference to voting on the resolutions. What I have been saying is that consensus is much more positive than confrontation, which has been a real possibility in the course of the conference. It was only as a result of 48 hours of intensive negotiation that the developing and the developed countries agreed to go along with the negotiated resolutions by consensus.
In the case of the American proposal there was a vote. A vote was taken because the majority of those who voted were opposed to the American idea of a resources investment bank. We voted for that. I think it was a mistake to have turned that proposal down simply because it had not been fully explained or fully considered and it seemed to have been unwise for the conference to have turned down, without serious examination, a proposal made by the major industrial power whose co-operation is vital if we are to make any changes in the international economic order. I think that was a mistake.

My second question refers to an apparent omission. I believe that one of the objects-I may be misunderstanding the purpose of these ministerial statements-would be to make the Canadian public aware of what went on, not just to justify the position of the government. For example, there is complete neglect of the matter of the transfer of technology in agriculture with a view to improving or helping those countries which seek self-sufficiency in the matter of food, water and fertilizer-those three things together. They are basic even to the generation of commodities for trade, particularly renewable commodities. No reference whatever is made to this question. Would the minister care to comment either on the purpose of the omission or on the matter itself?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Three resolutions were adopted at the conference on the general question of the transfer of technology. I agree with the hon. member that agriculture is a very important item of development. My colleague, the Minister of Agriculture, through the world food council, through the world food conference, through the world food program, is addressing himself to the general question of agricultural production in the developing world. It did not receive special attention at this particular conference or in my statement because it was not a subject matter of special attention even though it is quite important. I did not omit it because I regard it as unimportant. As the hon.

member knows, it has been highlighted as one of the areas to which we attach priority in our international development strategy.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the minister about the resolution on trade liberalization. I have not seen the resolutions yet. I think the members of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence, and perhaps all members of the House, would like to see them. However, I think trade liberalization is a very sensitive subject and I should like the minister to tell us the nature of the resolution passed on that subject.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There were three resolutions passed by the conference on trade matters. One provides for measures to improve access to developed country markets for improvement of the generalized system of preferences and tariff reclassification. Another resolution calls for measures which will give added impetus to multilateral trade negotiations. The third resolution dealt with transnational corporations. I have received all of these resolutions. They require a good deal of study, and I believe it would be very useful for the standing committee to take a look at some of these resolutions which are cast in general terms. The three resolutions on trade liberalization were adopted, by consensus, at the conference.

I should like to ask the minister about another matter I mentioned in my remarks earlier today. What steps, if any, have been taken, in accordance with the recommendation of the committee, toward working out and developing adjustment assistance to help those who might suffer economically as a result of more liberal trade measures or, indeed, help those who are suffering because even now some industries are threatened by cheap imports?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I realize that the subcommittee of the standing committee did make proposals on the matter of adjustment systems, and if at a certain point the Canadian government, supported by the Canadian parliament and the people, decided that we ought to admit tropical products at the expense of Canadian production and Canadian jobs, then of course adjustment measures would be essential. But up to the present time, while we have an adjustment program in the textile industry, as have most other countries, we have not yet developed new adjustment policies with respect to other industries. I say this with the full realization that the responsibility for such a program and policy is that of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. I suggest that it would be useful, in the interests of the dialogue, to raise the matter with him.

Mr. Speaker, 1 have a question for the minister. In view of the record of commodity agreements and the great importance some of these commodities might have on our Canadian economy, how far did the Canadian commitment go in these commodity agreements?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
If I may attempt to abbreviate the Canadian position, we stated that we will support measures which have the effect of stabilizing commodity prices, and particularly of stabilizing the earnings of exporters. We accept, as one of the techniques, the negotiation of
June 10, 1976

commodity agreements, where they can be demonstrated as useful, on a case by case basis. For example, as a consumer we have joined the tin agreement. We made a voluntary contribution to the tin buffer stock because we believed that would be a useful approach. Some of the industrialized countries, including Canada, have supported the idea of a commodity by commodity approach and that each commodity should have its own agreement, with its own funding and with its own buffer financing formula. This has been our approach.
We then went on to say, like the French stated at the conference, that if a number of individual commodity agreements have been negotiated and are in operation, and if at that point there is a necessity for a common fund either drawing upon the individual funds or supplemented from other sources that would be useful, then we would consider it. In addition to that, we indicated at the conference our readiness to participate in the negotiations and the discussions on the common fund. But there seems to have been an idea abroad that we should create a huge common fund and that that would be an incentive, by the very creation of a large fund, for producers and consumers to enter into the commodity agreements regardless of whether the justification for these agreements had been carefully worked out. If a common fund is seen in that perspective, it certainly has dangers for the international economic system.

Mr. Speaker, on page 20 of the French copy of the fifth report of the Standing Committee on External Affairs, dealing with developing countries, it says in the third paragraph:
Debt
A crisis of accumulated debt has been brewing for years in many of the developing countries and the severe balance of payments of recent years have now brought a number of them to the brink of bankruptcy. It has been pointed out that the repayment of the capital and interests on former debts use up to 50 per cent of the total amdunt of financial aid received by developing countries. Some proposals consider drastic measures in all respects to alleviate the burden of debts in developing countries. Now, I do not see these proposals in the report.
Would the minister advise the House which proposals the government is prepared to make to those developing countries, since 50 per cent of the financial aid they receive are used only to service their debt?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member asked what proposals we had made with respect to the debt question. We supported the proposal in the Manila declaration that a debt conference would be convened to consider what action could be taken and what guidelines could be used in order to overcome the debt problem. We also made the proposal that it might be better to consider ways and means of preventing countries from getting into debt or from increasing their debt. It was for that reason we suggested an increase in the threshold of assistance to developing countries.
Now, of course, there have been various mechanisms established by UNCTAD-a review, the creation of guide-

lines, a group of experts to consider debt questions-and we have gone along with that.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this budget comes at a crucial stage in Canada's fight against inflation. Because of tentative-and I am referring to the period between now and October as compared with the earlier period-early signs of success in reducing the rate of increase in the cost of living, there are some who would abandon the fight now, before the anti-inflation program has had a chance to exert a deep and permanent effect upon the inflationary expectations of the nation.
There are others who would divert our attention from the battle by proposing that the government should spend its way toward full employment. Such a proposal would not only fatally compromise the government's adoption of spending restraint as an essential weapon in the fight against inflation, but by stimulating inflation would also impede the private sector's long-term ability to create jobs for the jobless.
It is a mistake to consider inflation and unemployment as mutually exclusive problems. The unemployment problem cannot be solved by abandoning the anti-inflation effort. If economists and the governments of the industrialized nations have learned anything from our post-war experience, we have learned that the cyclical switching of our attention from inflation to unemployment and back again has not only not cured either problem but has worsened both.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Hear, hear!
June 10, 1976

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is for just that reason that all our policies-spending policies, over-all fiscal and monetary policy, and the policies governing price and income restraint-are aimed at gradually bringing inflation under control without jeopardizing renewed growth of output and employment. The only way to bring down the rate of unemployment is to restore the economy to a state of health and vigour; and the only way to do that, in the present circumstances, is to remove inflation as a major obstacle to our economic progress.
And this is one of the reasons why we must strongly object to the diversion manoeuvres of our opponents.
When I announced the creation of the prices and incomes control board last October, I said clearly to the Canadian people that we were launching a three-year restraint program because it would take us that long to get back on our feet again, to return to steady prices and a balanced growth rate, and because we would need all that time to bring down inflation gradually and surely without putting the country in a situation of economic paralysis.
The government's viewpoint has not changed since then. We see no reason to give up our efforts today or in the near future, now that our hopes to bring down the inflation rate are just beginning to materialize. Despite the strong objections of some particularly restless unions and businesses, objections which their spokesmen in the opposition are echoing, we will not give up until we succeed in our attempt.

I am not surprised that some powerful interests are crying out for an early removal of restraints on the exercise of their free-wheeling power in the marketplace. But the plain, simple and hard fact of the matter is that there is no way in which inflation can be brought more quickly under control without resort to Draconian measures- measures which would seriously impede, if not abort, the present recovery of the economy and lead to substantially higher unemployment. Some may be prepared to pay that price. We are not. Nor do I believe the vast majority of Canadians are prepared to pay that price. I am surprised that the special interests of these powerful groups should be pleaded so blatantly by opposition members who have been elected to serve the powerless as well as the powerful.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are laughing; we are not; we are serious.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I must say, Mr. Speaker, that I am especially shocked by the New Democratic Party. In trying to give the appearance that it is serving simultaneously the incompatible interests of powerful unions, which oppose the controls program, and powerless low income families,
The Budget-Mr. Trudeau
who need and support the program, the New Democratic Party presents the absurd spectacle of having both feet planted firmly on the ground on opposite sides of the fence.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is a pretty low fence.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I had expected a little more courage and a little more honesty from the party which so often and so self-righteously has proclaimed itself to be the social conscience of the nation.
I am less surprised by the contradictory performance of the Progressive Conservative party, which in its predictable effort to identify itself with every competing special interest group in the country is not representing any interest very well, least of all the public interest. It is perhaps too much to ask the Tories where they really stand on the issue of controls and spending restraint. I would be satisfied if they would just tell us which fence they are currently sitting on.
For an example of the Tories' attempts to be all things to all men, we need look no further than the remarkable speech given in this House on May 27 by the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens). I am sorry he is not here. If he had known I was going to speak, I am sure he would have been here to understand the remarks I am going to make on the subject of his speech. After criticizing the government for the level of its spending and the size of its deficits, he proceeded, without so much as an embarrassed blush, to plead for more government financial assistance for farmers, small businessmen, energy consumers, exporting companies, job creation, industrial research, medical research, big business and the taxpayers in general.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Heward wrote that for him.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The next time I hear the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) complain about the damaged credibility of parliament, I will know exactly what he means.
It was to be expected that some business and labour leaders would object very strenuously to controls on their freedom of action. In fairness, however, it must be said that hundreds of thousands of union members have voluntarily agreed to settlements within the guidelines, and that the bulk of business criticism has not been directed against controls in principle but against the details of their application. That kind of criticism has usually been both constructive and welcomed by the government. It is more in sorrow than in anger-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, yes!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-that I listen to otherwise responsible people demanding restraint in government spending but objecting to restraint in programs in which they have a special interest. That kind of myopia has made the government's job more difficult than it need be. I have no quarrel with those who plead the special worth of one or other of the very many worth-while programs for people in which the government is engaged, whether it be regional development, housing, the Local Initiatives Program, museums, dairy subsidies, or many others. This afternoon we heard

June 10, 1976
The Budget-Mr. Trudeau
special pleading for UNCTAD. We have no objection to these; they are all worth-while programs and that is why this government is pursuing them.
But the harsh fact is that we do not have the billions of dollars which would be needed in order to give immediate and adequate support to all those and other priorities. We will have to learn to choose more carefully and pay for some things over a longer time period than we have been used to in the past.
I ask for public understanding and support of the hard spending decisions which are being forced upon us by economic circumstances. It seems to me that there comes a time in the affairs of the nation when a particular public policy is so much in the public interest, so crucial to the stability of the country, that it requires members of parliament and citizens generally to lay aside narrow private interests and stand up for Canada.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Now is such a time, and the anti-inflation program is such a policy.

For in this fight against inflation, we have only one alternative: success or chaos. A failure would be a gross injustice towards our most disadvantaged citizens and would jeopardize the hold we must have on our future. I urge opposition members to think about it when they are tempted to use the House of Commons as a forum for powerful economic interests. I said it many times, an effective control of prices and incomes is possible only with the support and cooperation of all of us. That is why I am pleased not only because Canadians have supported this program from the outset but because they have not changed their minds since, despite the well financed and well organized hostility of our opponents.
What is to be feared is not that willing Canadians will finally take a negative stand as a result of the continued propaganda of groups which serve particular interests, but that public support weakens because some people would be led to conclude, on the strength of favourable statistics on the cost of living, that the fight is already won, or because others, reassured by the same figures-I will quote them in a moment-would feel that this problem is not as serious and consequently that restraints are no longer necessary. Both attitudes, if they were to become widespread, might be fatal to the success of our program. This is why those who are in a position to influence public opinion have such a responsibility. Those who, among influent and academic people, contribute to make people believe that it is less important today than last October to strongly restrain prices, salaries and public expenditures are doing the nation a very bad service.
Of course I am gratified that the increase since last year in the consumer price index declined to 8.9 per cent in April and May from 10.6 per cent in October. I am pleased that the seasonally adjusted CPI, which had increased at an annual rate of 11.7 per cent in the six months prior to last October, declined to 6.4 per cent between October and
[Mr. Trudeau.)
May. While this sharp rate of decline is very welcome, I am the first to admit that it is not due solely to the anti-inflation program, and that it is not sustainable over the longterm in the absence of some basic structural reforms in the economy.
I have said many times before that success in the fight against inflation is not to be looked for in short-term movements of the CPI, but in the progress we make in effecting necessary changes in our attitudes, expectations and economic institutions. That takes time. If we do not give ourselves the time by reaffirming our resolve to see this battle through to the end, we cannot succeed. I realize that in the context of the double-digit inflation which Canada has suffered for the past couple of years, the 8 per cent rate which we confidently expect to reach this year must seem to many people like the fulfilment of a dream, negating the need to continue the struggle.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: A bad dream.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: A bad dream, as the hon. member opposite mumbled.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I did not mumble. I said it quite distinctly.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member dreams quite distinctly. I apologize.
It is because of the potentially dangerous consequences of such an attitude that I am appealing today to all who have an influence over public opinion to tell it like it is. I realize that in order to sustain public support for the anti-inflation program it is necessary for the people to understand not only that it must remain in force until it is successful, but it is also necessary for them to see that the program is fair.
In furtherance of that second objective, the government has consistently and seriously offered to make changes in the rules when we are convinced that such changes will contribute to greater equity. Our desire to be fair is the reason wage settlements above the arithmetic guidelines have been allowed in special cases. But it is important to note that even with those exceptions above the arithmetic guidelines, settlements subject to the Anti-Inflation Board's jurisdiction have shown an average increase of only 12.1 per cent. This compares with settlements which were running at average rates of about 18 per cent during the first three quarters of 1975.
I wish to stress that point. More and more we hear people-usually they are theorists-say that inflation was going to come down anyhow and the government only brought the program in to take the credit. Inflation was not going to come down anyhow. They say that now because it has been coming down. Settlements have been reduced from an average of 18 per cent in the first three quarters of 1975 to an average of 12.1 per cent since we brought the controls program in.
The desire to be fair is the reason behind changes in pricing regulations announced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) on budget night. We are confident that with the new rules all companies will be treated more equitably. No one in the government has ever claimed that restrictions on the way we do business in this country are
June 10, 1976

attractive to us or easy to apply. We have claimed only that such restrictions are necessary and can work. Mr. Speaker, they are working and they continue to be necessary. They are working because millions of Canadians have generously subordinated immediate self-interest to the longer-term common good of the nation. In that spirit of generosity lies the greatest hope that the program will continue to attract the support of Canadians and will be ultimately successful.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it never occurred to me, when I was slated to be the first speaker for the Conservative party this afternoon, that it would be my lot to follow-and I say this in a neutral sense-the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). It is difficult to predict the course of events in this House. On this quiet, early summer afternoon I wish to make some comments on the budget and offer some suggestions.
The Prime Minister set a good example for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) by delivering a short speech. I say this as I wish to comment on the length and dullness of the budget speech; and I assure you I will not indulge in carping criticism. Although the minister's speech did little for the Canadian economy, it did something for me. Speaking as one who may have bored audiences, as I suffered throughout that marathon of platitudes which the minister delivered I felt purged of all sense of guilt. I no longer felt guilty for what I may have inflicted on my audiences during the past 25 years or so.
I am puzzled why the government House leader, whom I regard as an honest and straightforward man, would wish to see the speech televised. Perhaps the hon. gentleman wishes to destroy not only the House of Commons but Canadian television as well. The truth is that the speech would never have been made on TV. Some generously describe the speech as realistic. A more accurate adjective is "soporific." I do not believe anyone could be that dull for so long without really trying. I know that I could not have been so dull for so long without working hard at it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You must be trying now.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not know if the minister was trying to put the House of Commons to sleep. I suppose the government's strategy is to tranquillize the Canadian people. Its strategy is also to leave it to the Americans to bring prosperity to Canadians after the next election: Do not raise any disturbing issues in Canada. Prepare your ground well with a few well chosen fights against the big, bad wolves, like certain big labour interests and certain special interests in the country. We saw the Prime Minister start to prepare that ground very nicely this afternoon.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It surely indicates something about this government, and in fact this country, that the Minister of Finance could have delivered that fatuous speech in the year 1976 in the world as it really exists. I am afraid it says something about the Canadian people. Some of them think that speech was not too bad because there was not anything in it to disturb them. I wondered that night, and I still wonder, whether the minister and I are living in the same world. Is he right to ignore the reality that I see, and
The Budget-Mr. Stanfield
content himself with a policy of inertia associated with some tricks, devices and sleight-of-hand such as monkeying with the estimates, unemployment insurance and controls?
I wish to say a few words about the tricks. The Prime Minister emphasized the importance of telling it as it is. There is no need for me to dwell on the basic dishonesty of the government on the issue of controls. The government and its supporters have shown a degree of cynicism that was previously not thought possible in this country. It is just as simple as that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Prime Minister spoke this afternoon about those members of parliament who are not prepared to help the little fellow whom they were elected to support. I ask the Prime Minister seriously, does he remember anything at all of what he said in 1974? Does he really expect anybody to take him seriously when he attacks any member of this House for failure to defend the little fellow or defend controls?
Consider what the government is doing in the area of unemployment insurance. Changes are being adopted that the government resisted, fought against and repudiated, hoping to convince the electorate that they were prepared to be tough toward unemployment insurance and hoping that the whole issue of the cost of unemployment insurance would quieten down and go away. That is the whole point. Consider the sleight-of-hand with the spending estimates. The Prime Minister made a big fuss, pleading for support for the efforts of the government to cut back on its expenditures. As far back as December last, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) was swearing by everything that is holy that spending for the year ending March 31 last would not be more than 16 per cent higher than in the previous year. He stuck to that story in a pamphlet issued to us in April, just a couple of months ago.
On budget night, however, we learned that spending during the last fiscal year was in fact 18 per cent higher than in the previous year; some $700 million higher than the President of the Treasury Board swore it would be. That may have made a monkey out of the President of the Treasury Board, but it was very convenient for the Minister of Finance and the government as a whole. Having spent that money last year, they not only do not have to spend it this year but it gives them a better basis for comparison in terms of this year's spending. It enables the Minister of Finance to say that expenditures this fiscal year will not grow faster than the gross national product, estimated by him to be about 14 per cent.
The government spent hundreds of millions of dollars during the fiscal year ending March last. It advanced hundreds of millions of dollars to Crown corporations toward the end of that fiscal year, hundreds of millions of dollars which did not need to be advanced or spent in that fiscal year. The government seems to have deliberately inflated last year's spending so that it will look better this year. Thsi is the sort of jigging around, tinkering and dishonesty which one has come to expect from this government.
Some may say I am making a big fuss about very little. What difference, they may ask, does it really make wheth-
14378

June 10, 1976
The Budget-Mr. Stanfield
er the government spent money in the last fiscal year or the current fiscal year? Just this, Mr. Speaker. Quite apart from making a fool of the President of Treasury Board- and that is his business, with all his fine talk-it puts the Minister of Finance and the government in a position where they may well argue this time next year that expenditure growth did not exceed the growth of the gross national product during this fiscal year. It is just more manipulation.
The Prime Minister pleads for us to co-operate with them in their very earnest effort to control expenditures. He does this, of course, completely forgetting the totally irresponsible commitments made by the government during the election campaign. How can anybody take the Prime Minister seriously? Who can have any confidence, now, that this government will do what it says it will do, that its word is worth the paper on which it is written? Who can really believe that this government believes in anything?
This destruction of confidence is serious. Our challenge in Canada, as in other western democracies, goes far beyond working our way out of this recession. If we look around us, we see that western-style democracies and economies are under attack for lacking a sense of purpose, direction and cohesion. They are under attack for being too materialistic and lacking ideals, under attack for the range of their inequalities, inflation and unemployment.
In Canada, today, we lack a sense of common purpose. Distrust is prevalent. There is distrust of big business, big labour and big government. Citizens do not believe their national government is telling them the truth. Unfortunately, they are too often correct in that regard. The Minister of Finance is not to blame for all of this. However, this is the context in which he ought to have prepared his budget, although you would never recognize that from reading his speech.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) emphasized the need for a budget to set objectives for a period substantially longer than the year for which this budget has provided. We must improve our economic policies. We must re-establish trust between the citizen and his national government. We must ease, rather than aggravate, tension and confrontation that exists within our country.
I am not suggesting that we should abandon our institutions because those institutions are under attack. I am not suggesting that we should subject ourselves, as the Prime Minister said this afternoon, to deep-seated structural reform. The kind of talk indulged in by the Prime Minister around the end of the year is both incoherent and unsettling for many Canadians. He did not do much here this afternoon to throw any light on that question. Of course our institutions must evolve as conditions change. However, our system of a mixed economy, with heavy reliance on private enterprise, is better for us than anything we see abroad. That system may not be the best for certain developing countries, but it is best for us.
Government ownership has a role to play, providing certain national services as our history and our experience shows us. However, public ownership as a means of giving people control of their economy has been shown to be a gigantic illusion. I suspect the most difficult corporations for government to control are Crown corporations where

we see a paradoxical lack of control by the government, associated with great difficulty by those corporations in any hard decisions taken.
I say that our system is best for us. However, if we are to preserve it, we must see that it works satisfactorily. It is not working satisfactorily. This is partly due to external conditions, but it is dishonest to blame most of our troubles on the rest of the world, as the Prime Minister and the government have been doing for the past several years. What we need in the post-control period is not more government intervention but more restricted, intelligent, honest and better-defined intervention.
We should define the aims and priorities of government policy for the years ahead. The Leader of the Opposition has emphasized the importance of this. Not only have governments been expanding too rapidly, but they have been unable to solve or deal effectively with the problems they suggested they could solve. The national government in particular has been trying to do so many things that it has not done anything well. This has led to disillusionment and distress. Moreover, government has been taking an increasing proportion of the gross national product, and this in turn has generated inflationary pressures. Then, again, we see the federal government launch, with the provinces, costly programs which the national government now wishes to stick the provincial governments with, thus increasing distrust between the federal and provincial governments. I shall not elaborate on the con game involved in this; I have done so before.
Let me sum up in this way. The federal government has plenty to answer for. Instead of the Prime Minister coming to us and asking us to tell it as it is; instead of coming to us and seeking our support for some program of restraint, let the government tell it as it is, let the government try to be honest with the people. Certainly, the government must slow down the rate of growth of its expenditures if it does not wish to foster continuing inflation as taxpayers try to maintain their position after taxes.
It is clearly not good enough for the federal government to transfer costs to the provinces. That may ease the financial position of the federal government, but it solves nothing. Moreover, it places a heavy strain on confederation. We should recognize that the increasing share of the gross national product taken by the government presents a basic problem for our economy and our society. If that is what the Prime Minister was saying this afternoon, though he did not put it in those terms, I would agree with him. We must face that issue.
I think the hon. member for York-Simcoe did face it. He put before the House a number of proposals for large cuts in expenditures. It is true he did suggest using a small part of that money for certain specific purposes about which the Prime Minister made fun this afternoon. If the Prime Minister and members opposite are serious about the importance of controlling the rate of growth of government expenditures, the situation has gone far beyond hurling challenges at the opposition to say what we would cut. It has gone far beyond that. We must face this problem of the government taking more and more of the gross national product. But we should not regard government restraint as
June 10, 1976

being in itself a policy of economic management, though this is crucial if we are to preserve our mixed economy, with its heavy reliance on private enterprise, and if our citizens are to regain confidence in what the government says it can do and in what it does.
But I emphasize that government restraint, of itself, will not cause our economy to work satisfactorily. Government restraint is only a precondition. Flexible fiscal and economic policies, as opposed to rigid doctrinaire conceptions, will continue to be essential tools of economic management.
It may have been naive to believe that Keynesian techniques could achieve perfection, that they could produce a perfectly balanced economy with full employment and no inflation. But it would be even more naive to believe that our economy would regulate itself if only the government would control itself, important though that is. Surely we are not going to revert to a pre-Keynesian world. I remember what that world was like, and I do not wish to go back to it. Surely we are going to learn from our post-war experience and not simply throw it out of the window because we have made mistakes. Let us learn from our mistakes. We might even go back and reread Keynes, who never advocated bigger and bigger governments taking an ever-increasing share of a gross national product. In any event, we still need flexible fiscal and monetary tools for economic management, associated with a longer-term policy of economic restraint.
The question is: what additional tools will we need to provide the stability and growth required to enable our institutions to work? That is the question which is worth discussing, not some murky question about changing our institutions. Nearly everyone agrees that price and income controls are not a permanent solution, that they can only be used effectively to deflate inflationary expectations. I say, after long and considerable thought, that the length of the program of controls adopted by the government is both stupid and tragic.
I am sorry the Prime Minister is not in the chamber to hear me say this, but I hope my remarks will be brought to his attention, for what they may be worth. I say the duration of the control program contemplated by the government is both stupid and tragic. In the first place, controls will not work satisfactorily for that length of time. Then, the restriction on collective bargaining, for example, for so long a period will create fear and resentment among organized labour which will subject the economy to severe and unnecessary strain. I say to members of the government over there, "Please stop thinking of maintaining controls for three years or more." I say this is an irresponsible attitude, partly because the government probably has no intention of maintaining controls for that period of time any more than it had any intention of not imposing controls when it was arguing that controls should not be imposed.
The correct policy of the government would be to emphasize its firm intention to drop controls as soon as possible and seek the co-operation of labour, business and other economic groups. The correct policy at this time is for the government to give labour and business an incentive to prove that controls are not necessary. Maintaining the position that the controls are to be kept in place engenders
The Budget-Mr. Stanfield
confrontation and tension. The control operation carried out by the government is cynical and is certainly harmful as far as the aspect of its duration is concerned. Controls will not provide a solution to anything except in terms of deflating inflationary expectations on a short-term basis. Nor will controls take care of any competitive disadvantage which may exist in the manufacturing sector of our industry.
The Economic Council has already outlined the reasons for our competitive difficulties in this world of large trading blocs. One problem basically is that, with few exceptions, our manufacturing industries do not have free access to large markets and consequently are not competitive with manufacturing industries which do have free access to large markets. The Economic Council has documented this difficulty.
Why do we not face this problem? Why do we try to pretend that we can perhaps overcome these competitive disadvantages by the imposition of controls? The problem is real, it exists, it will not go away; controls will not drive it away. We will not get rid of it just by cutting or controlling government expenditures. We will not drive this problem away through any approach of Canadian ownership. Nor will we solve the problem by adopting miscellaneous programs to encourage research and development. We will only solve this problem by attacking it in the way the Economic Council indicated.
This, however, is not my main point this afternoon, Mr. Speaker. The main question is: what direction should the government be taking? What direction are we taking? There has been debate about where we should go in the post-controls period. With all due humility, I express the view this afternoon-it is a very simple approach basically, though certainly not easy to carry out-that we should make another effort to run our economy along what I would call orthodox post-war lines; that is to say, we should try to get back to where we were before the government became overcommitted. There is much more force to this than just trying to put the clock back.
I should like to see us adopt a firm determination to reduce somewhat the proportion of the gross national product going to governments in Canada. I say that without any delusions about its difficulties. Associated with this move, however, I wish to see neither the adoption of rigid concepts, such as the necessity of a balanced budget every year, on the one hand, nor, on the other hand, resort to Galbraithian concepts, analyses and solutions.
I should like to see us take another crack at the approaches that seemed to work reasonably well after the war and which we have moved away from substantially during the past ten years. That, I think, is a simple, realistic approach that is worth trying. I believe that if the government were to back off somewhat in terms of expenditures and what it is trying to do in this country-such as to stop taking, for example, more of the working man's pay in taxes, and if the government and the Bank of Canada were to abandon the sort of stop-go policies that we have had in recent years-and took a somewhat longer-term view of economic policy, realizing that policies take time to take effect and have the additional advantage of creating
95570-101/2

June 10, 1976
The Budget-Mr. Martin
an atmosphere of more certainty for those involved in our economy, the workingman as well as the businessman-the Leader of the Opposition referred to this-we might achieve, not Utopia but something we could live with. I think it is worth trying and it is urgent that we try it. I believe that all Canadians generally would support this kind of effort.
I am not this afternoon attempting to write a blueprint. My time will soon expire. Certainly, anything I have said this afternoon would have to be supplemented by specific programs, such as attacks on structural unemployment. Nor am I suggesting conditions have not changed in the last ten years, that life in Canada 10, 15 or 20 years ago was the same and that our economy in that period was working perfectly, because I know it was not.
My basic point is that our post-war economic policies worked reasonably well until we got off the track; until, as I have put it, the government became overcommitted, not simply in terms of what it was spending but in terms of what it was trying to do, usually without success. I believe we should make a very determined effort to get back on the track, that the national government should outline a firm, believable set of objectives and policies for, say, the next five years, and try to convince the Canadian people that it is both serious and determined to carry out those policies. One of those policies, of course, would be a very firm attitude toward the rate of inflation, having clearly and firmly delineated its direction. We would then follow the course that had been charted.
I must say that I have not seen evidence that this government is capable of that, and if it is not capable of such an effort, or if it lacks the credibility to put forward such an effort, then the people of Canada will most certainly turn to the Leader of the Opposition for the kind of straightforward, challenging leadership which our country needs. I want to say to my hon. friends opposite, and through them to the Prime Minister, that I believe trickery has run its course in Canada.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to participate in this third budget debate since becoming a member of parliament. I should like to say at the outset that I have never been prouder to be associated with a finance minister and his budget presentation than in this particular case. I think we should all be aware that Canada is in the midst of some troubled times and that there is, indeed, the need for a steady hand on the rudder. I believe that our current finance minister has indicated very clearly that that steady hand is now being applied. I
I think it is worth remembering at this time, Mr. Speaker, as we enter a phase with a new finance minister, that he is joining a group of seven able and capable finance ministers which successive Liberal governments in this country, under four prime ministers, have placed in this onerous responsibility since the early days of World War II. I suggest each has acquitted their responsibility with a degree of ability and aplomb that I suggest has been the pride of Canadians and has had much to do with the continuing strength of successive Liberal governments over 30 years of this 36-year period.

I think it is significant, in the context of today's problems, Mr. Speaker, to bear in mind the importance that must be attached to the direction being given in the area of economic policies. The success of past finance ministers under Liberal governments has brought us through various periods, including a general period in which the population of the country has doubled. It has brought us through a wartime period, a crisis that has never before or since been equalled.
