It has brought us through a post-war boom, with all its ensuing difficulty as the economy moved ahead at a very rapid and unusual rate.
Liberal government finance ministers were then called upon to take over following a six-year period of Conservative rule during which our national and international reputation, which had been built up so successfully over past years in the area of the management of our economic affairs, was brought to a new low point and almost completely destroyed.
A more recent situation facing the country, of which we are all aware, has been the raging inflation that has beset Canada, and the need eventually to impose strong, central controls when it became evident that voluntary measures were not going to suffice. Finally, it was under a Liberal government that a finance minister has been responsible for implementing a most difficult and challenging set of amendments to our Income Tax Act, which has resulted in a greater degree of equity and fairness under our over-all taxation system.
These were some of the challenges faced by the government and by men of the stature of Ilsley and Abbott, both of whom held the finance minister portfolio for a period of some 14 years, and by people of the stature of Harris and of Gordon, the man who, in spite of problems besetting him and his government, was the single Canadian in high political office who was finally able successfully to pinpoint and bring into public focus one of our most continuing and besetting national problems, the degree of control over our Canadian economy exerted by people beyond our borders. The list goes on.
It is with this background, and in this context of 30 of the past 36 years, that our current Finance Minister, a man of proven ability and strength of character, as evidenced in his previous portfolios, particularly that of energy, mines and resources where I came to know him best, now takes over during an exceedingly difficult period. I suggest he has approached his first budget in his current mandate as Canada's Minister of Finance with a background that is second to none.
On the other side of the coin, what has parliament to offer? At the present time, the financial critic of the official opposition is spending a good deal of his time comparing fiscal expenditures with those of the past 100 years. It seems to me this is an exercise equally as futile as an endeavour to point out that General Motors is today an inefficient operation because its capital expenditures are so much greater than at the time that organization was built up. It is so ridiculous a comparison as to be discountable without any further thought on the part of any Canadian to attempt to follow the rationale of the finance critic of the official opposition.
June 10, 1976

The position of that finance critic is one which I think we must assume, under the parliamentary system, does indeed involve responsibility to bring intelligent criticism to bear on government economic policies as brought forward in a statement so important as the budget. While I do not envy the task of the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens)-it is an arduous task he has been given, to poke holes in an honest and straightforward finance policy brought forward by such an experienced and able minister as the hon. member for Rosedale-I must, however, take him to task for seeking sensationalism in his unfounded accusations, based as they are on the potential media value of the rhetoric contained in them rather than on their actual material content.
He mentioned the so-called 7 per cent growth factor which apparently has been lost over the past two years. Has he examined the picture in other western industrialized countries over the same time? Obviously not. Or if he has, for purposes of his own choosing he has refrained from including these comparisons in his speech. I must assume that he is both too intelligent a person and one who properly prides himself on the research capabilities of his office not to have appreciated that the real GNP for OECD countries dropped by 2 per cent in 1975, far from any gain at all, let alone a 7 per cent gain, and that as a result of, and contributing to this decline in economic activity, was a 6 per cent drop in over-all volume of world trade.
It is inconceivable for a responsible person to suggest that Canada, a country which lives by trading, could remain insulated from this worldwide trend and be expected to fly completely in the other direction, particularly to the extent suggested by the hon. member, the official opposition's financial critic. On one hand the hon. member for York-Simcoe complains of the extent of government control in the economy-and I presume he is referring to all levels of government, including the massive involvement of the government sponsored by his own party in Ontario in the affairs of that province-while on the other hand he moans about the lack of further government involvement in the federal economy in 1976 in his reference to what he chooses to call a "heal thyself" philosophy that he attributes to the federal government's position in relation to economic matters within the country at the present time.
He simply cannot have it both ways. The member indicates concern over what he regards as no real stimulus to employment. Yet he must be aware of the intent of the government to use any funds saved by the changes in the unemployment insurance legislation for job-creation programs. This will obviously operate as a form of stimulus. This may turn out to be something the opposition financial critic may find difficult to accept, being a seemingly confirmed anti-stimulant where the stimulus is to originate with the government.
Mr. Speaker, it is extremely difficult to really know where the hon. member stands or even to adequately define the side of the fence on which he appears to sit. The hon. member goes on to talk about lack of tax cuts and a probably horrendous deficit. Surely, tax cuts would result in an even higher deficit. Once again his economic arithmetic is difficult to fathom. The opposition financial critic indicates that we are counting too heavily on the U.S.
The Budget-Mr. Martin
economy to cure the Canadian economy of its ills. Again, as a businessman, surely he understands the position of the United States as Canada's largest customer. Is it not rational to assume that an improvement in the financial condition of your largest customer is bound to help your situation, when you are indeed its main provider of merchandise?
His reference to lotteries is nothing but a cheap shot. If, indeed, the lotteries of the day at both federal and provincial levels are, as he indicates, a poor remnant of what went on in the seventeenth century, one must assume that the lotteries of those days represented real bonanzas, based on the current success of the current Olympic series of lotteries. Here, again, the official opposition's financial critic is obviously seeking a point that lacks substance, in his attempt to make a publicity score on the government. This sort of meaningless criticism, once again, does him and his party little or no credit and the Canadian people, I suggest, simply will not buy it.
The arguments of the member for York-Simcoe on the anti-inflation program are similarly disturbing.
Mr. Speaker, he continues to argue for the implementation of the controls some 18 months earlier. Yet it seems to me that the government of the day, and the people of Canada, demonstrated quite clearly that they were not prepared to go for controls at that time without benefit of further attempts at consultation among government, labour and industry in a final effort to see if some voluntary means could be found to achieve the desired objective. As stated on many occasions, and surely as heard and noted by the hon. member for York-Simcoe, such efforts at voluntary resolution were not successful.
In the interim, the rates of inflation grew beyond all reasonable limits, reached double-digit rates and thus demanded more concerted and direct involvement by government than voluntary means could possibly have provided. Yet we have the spectacle of the hon. member for York-Simcoe, the official opposition's financial critic, leading his group in opposing that controls legislation when it was finally brought into the House. As to the post-controls period, the financial critic for the Conservative party decries the absence of meaningful discussion over this. Yet what has his own personal contribution been in this direction? When our distinguished Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made even the slightest reference to changes that might be necessary in the future, the best that spokesman for the Conservative party could do was dash off in a form of blind hysteria. I ask whether this really can be considered a responsible position. In my view, it cannot.
I could go on and on analysing and answering criticisms levelled by the hon. member for York-Simcoe in his capacity as the official opposition's financial critic. However, I would like to move for a few minutes to comments made even more recently in this past week by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark).
In one area-that of proposed changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act-the distinguished Leader of the Opposition on the one hand indicates general concurrence with the position advocated by the Minister of Finance

June 10, 1976
The Budget-Mr. Martin
(Mr. Macdonald), but then later in his speech equivocates as to his position when he further examines the matter.
The hon. Leader of the Opposition indicates that the minister fails to provide leadership. Surely this is far from the case, Mr. Speaker. Any real understanding of the term leadership will appreciate that there is a time and a place for holding a firm hand on the rudder and charting a course that lies straight ahead. Stated in another form one might say that, when in a small boat on rough waters and surrounded by alligators, it is no time to stand up and move around. I suggest that the present Minister of Finance, the hon. member for Rosedale, has shown a most direct and meaningful act of leadership in bringing down a budget that might quite fairly be described in a general sense as neutral in its over-all impact on the Canadian economy, a most appropriate stance at this particular time, in my view.
I could continue to pick apart many of the specific criticisms made by the Leader of the Opposition in his speech earlier this week. However, I feel that in fairness I must respect the fact that this is his first opportunity to react to government leadership in the area of Canada's economy, in his new and responsible role as leader of his party. Although the Minister of Finance was also presenting his first budget in his new portfolio, I think his most creditable performance must at least in part be attributable to his extensive background in major positions of responsibility within the present government-in each of which he has acquitted himself with a high degree of ability and success. I do appreciate that the Leader of the Opposition has not had the opportunity for serving in anywhere near equivalent positions of responsibility or experience, and no doubt we can expect more from him in the years ahead as he entrenches himself in the role of leader of the party that I am sure Canadians will be pleased to leave in its current position of official opposition for many years in the future.
I have chosen to enunciate in my comments today the underlying strength which I think has been evident in the positions taken and the leadership shown by finance ministers in Liberal governments since World War II. I say again that into this picture enters our current Minister of Finance as he presents his initial budget before the House of Commons and the nation at large. I am sure the House recognizes the obvious ability of our new minister to follow in the illustrious steps of his predecessors. Nowhere is this more in evidence than in the seeming inability of the opposition to come forward with any real, meaningful criticism during this budget debate.
Turning for a moment to the immediate area of the economy that must continue to be of concern to Canadians I want to speak briefly on the matter of the balance of payments situation. In 1973 our current account with other countries was in balance. In 1975 the situation had deteriorated to a $5 billion deficit. In 1976 we are hoping that this deficit can be reduced to $4 billion. Mr. Speaker, we all understand the extenuating and world-wide circumstances that have led to this unfortunate state of affairs. The severe drop in the rate of increase of our 1975 exports to our two major trading partners; the international and national problems in the area of oil and gas-resulting in significant contraction of our exports in these commodi-

ties; our continuing deficit in the non-merchandize trade area; all of these contributed in a significant way to the $5 billion deficit which had then to be made up through the importation of substantial amounts of capital-both of short and long term nature. Unfortunately this capital has both to be serviced and repaid in future years, and it really provides an unsatisfactory solution to the problem over the long term.
It is important to point out that this current account deficit was occurring at a time when our Canadian economy continued to perform better than those of most other countries. In other words, Mr. Speaker, the $5 billion cash problem is there, but I believe there is every reason to be optimistic in view of our buoyant economy. Surely methods will be found to offset this substantial cash deficit problem. Certainly improvements in the area of merchandize exports to our major trading partners, as their economies improve, will help substantially. The point is that the cash deficit problem is there and must continue to receive the concerted attention of government and persons in the private sector.
I think it is significant to note that as we discuss this current budget the rate of unemployment has dropped- slightly it is true-but nevertheless the drop from 7.4 per cent to 7.1 per cent is most certainly in the right direction.
I would like to make a brief reference to the features of the budget relating to unemployment insurance, I might add, features that I heartily endorse. By uniting the Manpower and unemployment insurance programs, by increasing the work requirements from 8 to 12 weeks, by more directly tying benefits to the number of weeks worked and granting extended benefits according to regional economic conditions, the cost of the insurance program to taxpayers will be lowered at no risk to its equity. The Canadian unemployment insurance program has been hailed as one of the most advanced in the world. The changes which have been announced will help to reduce the opportunities to violate the intent of the program.
The integration of unemployment and Manpower services will result in improved enforcement of the provision that recipients be actively seeking work. I think that is important, and the length and eligibility requirement should discourage over-reliance on unemployment insurance as a principal source of income. Like other forms of justice, social justice must not only be fair but must be seen to be fair if it is to retain the support of society as a whole.
In conclusion, there are no claims that this budget would be a panacea for all our economic problems. However, the decision not to attempt extensive remedies should not be confused with indecisiveness. Rather, it represents a mature recognition of the limits of effective government intervention and of the importance of individual initiative. That problems will persist, there can be no doubt. Neither an unemployment level of 7.1 per cent nor an inflation rate which approaches 9 per cent is compatible with a healthy economy. Both undermine the foundations of an open society. The increased levels of investment which are essential if we are to avoid an early relapse are likely to await further improvements in business confidence.
The demand for housing continues to outstrip the supply. Credit conditions play a particularly important
June 10, 1976

role in the housing sector, and mortgage rates which are near the 12 per cent level make it all the more difficult to finance the construction or purchase of a home.
I might add that I do not share the views of those who suggest that the average Canadian should no longer be expected to own his own home. Whenever the opportunity has been available, people have unequivocally demonstrated their preference for their own piece of property and their own backyard. It is therefore essential that there be further improvements in the housing industry.
There are many positive signs on the economic horizon. A careful review of the minister's speech and accompanying documents most certainly gives legitimate cause for an optimistic if cautious attitude on the part of all Canadians. It is this kind of positive attitude that we on this side of the House feel is the appropriate and justifiable stance to hold. I am personally thankful that the prophets of doom and gloom, epitomized in the little thought out and almost desperate tone of the official critics of the opposition, do indeed occupy the benches opposite.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is great to get into this debate finally after waiting for so many days. The fact that so many cabinet ministers have spoken in this debate is an indication to me of its weakness. I do not believe the House has witnessed so many cabinet participants in a budget debate for many years.
The intervention of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) today can be classified as a painful exercise in generalized vagueness. In fact if the parade of cabinet ministers continues, we may have a new entry for the Guinness Book of Records for the most cabinet ministers to speak in support of a budget which was so lacking in content that it needed their contribution to prop it up.
Recently the Prime Minister was quoted as saying that it would take a miracle for the anti-inflation controls to be removed. Let us say that if the budget presented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) is any indication of the talents of the government, then we can be sure there are no miracle makers in its ranks.
This is really such a bare bones budget that one has difficulty separating the verbiage of the document from the measures which normally flow from budgets. Indeed, by 10.15 p.m. on budget night the media people in the lobby were putting their cameras and tape recorders to bed, and there has to be a message there. Watching some members of the front benches opposite, one could see them fighting off yawns.
One of the few good things in the budget was the removal of research and development from the Anti-Inflation Board regulations. This was hardly a stroke of genius because research and development should never have been placed under the AIB regulations in the first place. We will never know the full extent of the damage to the development of products in Canada. We could not calculate the number of projects which would have been undertaken but were either cancelled or moved out of the country. As it stands today, research and development projects will have to be approved by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce before they will be allowed as an expense item,
The Budget-Mr. Kempling
and I am not too confident that that is the best procedure to follow.
Let me deal with a few items in the budget. Under the heading of energy conservation the minister announced a tax of $100 on automobile air conditioners. Any competent automotive engineer will tell us that an air conditioner uses the same amount of horsepower as power steering. In fact when in use automobile air conditioners take less than one mile per gallon from performance. If you have the wrong tire pressure in your automobile tires that can rob you of more than one mile per gallon and create a tremendous safety hazard as well.
The weight tax on automobiles must be questioned. Surely the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, which obviously put this tax in the budget, must realize the lead time required for the design of an automobile. Of course I am not surprised that the minister of that department did not think it out because he is part of the energy problem, not part of the solution.
Earlier this year the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) announced that government policy, in line with that of the United States, was to set a target of 24 miles per gallon fleet average for cars by 1980, and here again we have a conflict between the two ministers.
This budget increases the weight tax in stages to 1979. Bearing in mind the lead time required for design, and bearing in mind that the industry has accepted the 24 miles per gallon standard and adopted it as an industry standard, why have we chosen to complicate the problem further by adding a further tax?
We have a rationalized North American automobile industry, to some extent, and now we may be heading for a separate standard for Canada as distinct from the United States. While I appreciate the need for conserving energy I believe it could be accomplished in other ways without interference in the design and production of automobiles. We find the motor vehicle safety standards have added more than 1,000 pounds to an automobile.
In fact to look at the weight of a vehicle alone as the criterion for saving fuel shows the lack of in-depth study done by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources and the Department of Transport. It is obvious to anyone dealing with motor vehicles that aerodynamics, tires, axle ratios, carburetion, engine displacement, and so on can have more effect on the efficiency of the engine performance than the weight of the vehicle. In many instances a small, light weight engine is less efficient than a larger, heavier engine.
When one considers the impact on our domestic industry and how our trade balance is affected when the industry is not at top production, one can only conclude that the provisions for additional taxation are inappropriate at this time.
The real disappointment in the budget is that the government missed a real opportunity to add a measure of confidence that would show our economy is really recovering, that inflation is being contained, and unemployment is being reduced.
Instead, we have another budget deficit of more than $5 billion, a trade deficit in high technology product of $9

June 10,1976
The Budget-Mr. Kempling
billion, and no meaningful reduction in unemployment. In fact it is forecast that we will have an increase in unemployment before the end of this year, and that is tragic. The tragedy in all the economic problems we face is that it could be so different. When we travel out of the country we are told how fortunate we are in Canada with all our resources. Yet within the country we are being told we are running out of resources.
Various members on the government front bench have stated that the recovery of our economy is directly related to the recovery of the American economy. While in Japan a few weeks ago, Japanese cabinet ministers with whom we discussed the question indicated that the recovery of their economy depended to a great extent on the recovery of the American economy. In Japan I picked up an Australian newspaper and read that the Prime Minister of Australia stated that their economic recovery depended upon the recovery of the American economy. If we read the comments in the OECD releases, we will find that they continually refer to the European economic recovery linked to the recovery of the American economy.
It would seem to me that we should be working closely with the Americans to see that our economy not only recovers in step with theirs but that we put in place complementary taxation and tariff measures to see that both our economies remain strong and buoyant. Rationalization of taxation is an urgent priority for the manufacturing sector.
We have no industrial strategy. In fact much of the profit earned by industry since 1971 is a pure paper profit. The combined effect of inventory inflation and a rate of depreciation on assets that is inadequate to recover the replacement of that asset has created levels of profitability that are fictitious. In many cases companies have to borrow to pay the tax bill. The net result is that most businesses face cash flow problems. Decisions to replace machinery are deferred because of lack of cash and increased replacement cost. Plant expansion has been held off because of increased cost, lack of cash, and the high cost of borrowed money.
When you spin off the combined effect of inflated inventory prices, unrealistic depreciation allowances, lack of adequate cash to operate, and high interest rates for borrowing, you realize the opportunity missed by the government to put in place some legislation that would build a sound foundation for an economic recovery. Once in place, that type of legislation can be adjusted to achieve the national objectives of a strong secondary industrial base.
Canada will for the forseeable future be a trader in rocks and logs in the international market place. The amount of processing of our mineral resources we are able to accomplish will depend upon the acceptance of those resources in the market place. There are those who like to comment on the economy and who would have us refuse to ship our mineral resources unless they are partially or completely processed. That is an unrealistic approach. We are not the only country in the world with mineral resources for sale. We have to compete for orders in a market that is flexible and moving. Our labour rates are amongst the highest in the world. To offset this we must be more productive and more efficient in our business process. Our transportation, because of the distances involved, must be the best and

most efficient to offset the distances to markets. It follows, then, that we have to operate in an atmosphere as free from government interference as possible.
The most urgent negotiation the federal government should undertake is with the provinces to work out a taxation formula to maximize the development of our mineral resources. But hand in hand with this is the development of a secondary industrial base, not only to complement the mineral industry but also to produce more of the products we import.
Each year we see the number of companies involved in manufacturing declining. Many companies find they can purchase the products they were manufacturing from a source outside the country, and merely act as a sales agent and marketing arm. There are more and more manufacturers becoming marketing organizations. It usually starts with a position that says, "We will round out our line of products with imports." From there they move to calculate the capital cost of new plant and machinery research and development against the cost of acquiring a product offshore. You can go through industry after industry and find this happening. In fact a large portion of products manufactured in Canada are aligned against similar products from countries that are classified as Third World countries that have labour rates only a fraction of our rates.
Looking at the decline in the manufacturing sector of our economy, one can only say that there is a death wish in the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce that virtually all manufacturing cease in this country and that we become a net importer of products of other countries forever.
Certainly a look at the textile industry is a classic case in point. Our manufacturers' share of the Canadian market is dropping and has reached a level that they only enjoy 46 per cent of the domestic market. Only 6 per cent of the available domestic market is covered by quotas. In order to claim damage from imported textiles the manufacturers can appeal to the textile board, but the process is complicated and lengthy. By the time a case is heard it is too late for action to be taken.
By comparison the United States textile manufacturers have about 90 per cent of their domestic market reserved for them. The United States government has negotiated 19 separate agreements on textile quotas with various countries that produce fibres, woven and knitted products, flat goods, and apparel.
The net result of all this is that we find the Canadian textile industry in general will not invest in new plant facilities, and will only upgrade and maintain the better and newer production facilities. Plants that should be replaced will be closed down and more unemployment will result. Certainly the people responsible for including, in the first instance, research and development in the AntiInflation Board's regulations, and restricting the level of expenditures by a formula classifying research and development with donations to charity, promotion and advertising, displayed plain stupidity.
It is this type of bureaucratic stupidity that has frustrated manufacturing in Canada for years. We need, first, a complete overhaul and review of our taxation system. It
June 10, 1976

must be compared with that of our major trading partners to see that we are not placing our manufacturing industry in a non-competitive position because of inequities in our taxation system.
We must then examine the pricing of inventories and take a look at the method of calculating depreciation. Manufacturing profits should be stripped of inflation factors, and the profits should reflect true profits. To offset high interest rates a serious study of depreciation methods and an appropriate adjustment will do much to increase the cash flow in a business.
Profits that are earned and reinvested should not be subject to taxation. This would help the cash flow problem facing many businesses today.
Needless to say I am deeply disappointed that the budget did not reflect some of these points. We have so much potential in this country. I find it discouraging, and feel the sense of frustration that there is in this country with a government that has so little imagination that, at a time when other economies are advancing, we are still playing the short term game of finance. Is it any wonder that after the budget presentation when we asked people in business, "What did you think of the budget?", they replied, "What budget?"
There is a basic weakness in the departmental structure of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. Perhaps the weakness is the fact that industry is included with trade in one department. Perhaps we would be better served in Canada if industry were separated from trade and we could then have them pursue their separate goals. Certainly a visit to the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce confirms this. Talk to the people at Industry, Trade and Commerce about a product, and the first and most urgent question is whether or not it has export potential. If you say you want to serve a domestic market they lose interest.
In other words the heavy emphasis is on trade. Industry itself is only of secondary concern to the people in the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. Question the people at the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce about product development in Canada and you are surrounded with classic bureaucratic buzz words such as world scale, economies of scale, export-export-export. You end up frustrated and discouraged.
There has never been any real co-ordination between the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, and the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. A case in point is that there is at present a backlog of 370 cases to be heard by the Opposition Board of the Registrar of Trade Marks. Under normal circumstances the Opposition Board would rule on about 60 cases a year. At the present time the trade marks office is dealing with cases presented for adjudication three years ago. Only the registrar can give a ruling on these cases, but the new registrar is on a year's immersion course to learn French. Consequently when he returns he will be looking at more than six years of backlog. What an intolerable situation! It requires an amendment to the Trade Marks Act to allow person other than the registrar to act on his behalf.
The Budget-Mr. Kempling
When you look at the combined effect of all the disincentives to the business community, it is any wonder there is dissatisfaction and frustration? Let us for a moment add up the problems they face. The Anti-Inflation Board has more than 3,000 wage settlements to rule on; inflation is creating false profits that are being taxed at too high a level; the combined effect of federal and provincial taxes and royalties is holding back expansion of our non-energy resource industries; inventory pricing under existing regulations does not allow for an inflation factor; depreciation allowances do not reflect the replacement cost of capital assets; there is a basic tax penalty for Canadian manufacturers as compared to our major trading partners; before phase one of the competition legislation has had a chance to work, we will be looking at phase two; interest rates are the highest of any country of the western world; our productivity is amongst the lowest of any of the O.E.C.D. countries; we have a six year backlog of trade mark cases to be considered by the Opposition Board under the Trade Marks Act; working capital is so short that some companies are borrowing money to pay their tax bills to the federal government; we lost 11 million man years due to strikes in 1975; we lost more than 11 million man years due to alcoholism and drug use in industry in 1975; research and development are at the lowest level they have ever been.
Only two countries on the O.E.C.D. list have lower research and development than Canada; we had, until this budget, research and development subjected to AIB regulations and formulae. This alone caused cancellation of many projects. It has taken four years after the realization that we had an energy supply problem for the government to act on expense deductions for exploration costs. While we welcome the announcement in the budget we must ask, along with other Canadians, "Why did it take so long for you to act?"
We face more and more intrusion in the private sector by the federal government. Add to all the foregoing, the year-end musings of the Prime Minister on the economy, and subsequent statements, and you will begin to see the depths of despair and frustration of the business community.
Many cabinet ministers who have spoken said that the official opposition has offered no solutions but pointed out legislative weaknesses. If you examine the points I have just mentioned you must agree that solutions to most, if not all of them, could have been included in the budget. Too much goes to the government. In fact these suggestions would have gone a long way toward stimulating employment and helping to reduce the level of unemployment in the country.
Inflation can be beaten, but the action that has been taken so far I do not believe has made the impact it could have made. Our trade deficit and balance of payments problem, in spite of the buoyant words of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Jamieson), will be with us for some time. In fact his speech reminded me of a man whistling in a graveyard trying to keep his spirits up.
I have tried to set forth the real facts and problems as I see them. I have spent most of my life in business. I have had to look at the realities of economic life. If I had to choose a board of directors from the government benches I

June 10, 1976
The Budget-Mr. Maine
would be hard pressed to find one person to whom I would offer that position of trust. From the Prime Minister down, there is hardly anyone who would qualify based on their eight years of lack lustre performance. This budget reflects the lack of talent available.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again I should like to bring to the attention of the House and the Canadian people the importance to Canada's economy of science and technology, which in turn rest on a foundation of research and development.
I was pleased to learn that the new budget removes approved expenditures for research and development from the list of restricted expenses under the Anti-Inflation Act, expecially so since I made representations to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) and emphasized this point strongly in my speech during the recent opposition day debate on science and technology. I am glad that the government showed a sensitive and sensible response to an important matter when it was brought to its attention.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It was a beginning.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Two major aspects of science and technology in our economy are vital: harnessing it and controlling it. One without the other does nothing to improve either our standard of living or the health of our economy.
The harnessing of science and technology is done in the laboratory. To this end we spend millions of dollars annually to train scientists in our universities. We have expertise in many high-technology-content areas, but we rarely reap the benefits from this knowledge via its application because we do not control the use of that knowledge. If we are to derive benefit from scientific research work, the results must be commercialized and thereby translated into the Gross National Product. The "brain drain" about which we heard so much in the early sixties remains a serious problem. There are very few significant industrial research and development operations in Canada.
If by chance a multinational corporation does become interested in a product of Canadian technology, it is unlikely that much, if any, financial benefit will be realized by Canada. It is the practice of most multinationals based in the United States to carry out virtually all research and development in American labs and limit the Canadian operation strictly to manufacturing. The auto industry provides a very good example of that type of operation. All of the research and development work in the automotive industry is done in Detroit. All that is left for the Canadian operation is assembly line jobs, while jobs which should be going to our university graduates do not exist in this country.
Occasionally there has developed in Canada a research and development facility rivalling the best in the world. One of these is the RCA Limited Research Laboratories in Montreal, part of RCA Limited. There is no better example of the problem of Canadian control of science and technology than the announcement by RCA corporation that it is closing down these labs. RCA Limited is owned 100 per cent by RCA International Development Corporation in

New York. The Canadian company has 20 directors, ten of whom are U.S. nationals. The president of RCA Limited, Mr. G. Denton Clark, is a native of Montreal who has taken out United States citizenship. The company dates back to the turn of the century, became part of RCA during the 1920's, was for many years known as RCA Victor, and in 1968 became RCA Limited. In 1975 the sales volume of RCA Limited was approximately $175 million. At least 75 per cent was in consumer products or components for consumer products. Of the remaining 25 per cent a substantial amount was sales to the federal government or to Crown corporations.
For many years RCA corporation prospered under the direction of David Sarnoff, who built the organization into the giant multinational it is today. Following Sarnoff's retirement in 1970, his son, Robert Sarnoff, became president of RCA corporation. The young Sarnoff, for whatever reasons, was unable to provide the quality of leadership his father had shown. He was replaced as president in 1971 by Andrew L. Conrad, who now also serves as chairman of the board since Robert Sarnoff's resignation from RCA last fall.
Before Mr. Clark became president in 1973, the president of RCA Limited functioned largely as an administrative head. Effective line authority over the five divisional vice presidents was exercised by the corresponding executive vice presidents at the headquarters of RCA corporation in New York. With Mr. Clark as president, this situation appeared to change. The new president attempted to establish full functional line authority over the five operating divisions. In what was viewed by the government to be a significant move, the research and development laboratories were elevated to the status of an autonomous division reporting directly to the president.
In March, 1975, Mr. Denton Clark indicated to the government that the future direction of RCA Limited would emphasize Canadian autonomy, a world-wide product mandate, high technology and Canadian design capability, and the expansion of business. In an apparent reversal of Mr. Clark's earlier position, RCA announced on March 18, 1976, a restructuring of RCA Limited, "as part of an international program at RCA corporation to make its product divisions more efficient and profitable by giving them direct control of their world-wide operations."
RCA issued a further press release in April stating that, "Consistent with RCA's restructuring program, RCA Limited is undertaking a major realignment of its research and development activities." In other words, the research and development laboratories will be closed down at the end of this year, or by the end of the first quarter of 1977 at the latest. Some of the work done by the laboratories will be transferred to other divisions within the company, but only about 30 per cent of the scientists now engaged in research and development will be assigned positions in those divisions. However, those will not be research positions and will not be innovating the expertise developed at the research centre.
RCA Limited has made good use of the incentives programs which are available to industry through the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. The company has, during the past ten years, received at least $20 million in outright government assistance for research and develop-
June 10, 1976

ment. In addition it has benefited from $67 million of financing provided by CIDA and the Export Development Corporation toward sales to other countries through RCA Limited's government and commercial systems division, one of the five divisions in the company. Without this government assistance these foreign sales would not have been made.
What has been a successful and highly respected scientific research centre in Canada is now to be disbanded and abandoned because Ed Griffiths, an executive vice president of RCA corporation and president of RCA electronics and diversified businesses, decided that such a move would increase profits for the parent company and streamline its international operation. Mr. Griffiths was responsible for restructuring the Canadian Hertz rent-a-car company, an RCA subsidiary, so that control was centralized more completely at the American head office, leaving little autonomy for the Canadian operation. Apparently because that move was financially effective it was felt that similar actions should be taken with RCA Limited. I maintain that no matter what economic sense this realignment may make to the American parent company, such high-handed measures, disregarding Canada's needs and priorities, should not take place or be allowed to take place.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Most hon. members are aware that the government updated last year its guidelines for good corporate citizenship for foreign companies operating in Canada. Those guidelines state that foreign-controlled firms in Canada should pursue a high degree of autonomy in the exercise of decision-making and risk-taking functions, including innovative activity and the marketing of any resulting new products. RCA Limited was committed to function according to that principle. That commitment has, as I have shown, been rescinded by the parent corporation.
The guidelines also ask that companies develop as an integral part of the Canadian operation an autonomous capability for technological innovation, including research, development, engineering, industrial design and pre-production activities. Here again the actions of RCA corporation show no regard for that principle.
Furthermore the guidelines suggest that the companies foster a Canadian outlook within management, as well as enlarged career opportunities within Canada, by promoting Canadians to senior and middle management positions and by including a majority of Canadians on boards of directors of all Canadian companies, in accordance with the spirit of federal legislative initiatives. The board of directors of RCA Limited does not have a majority of Canadian members. Neither does the company offer expanded career opportunities within Canada when it closes down a successful operation that will almost certainly force brilliant Canadian scientists to take employment in the United States.
What is to be done? RCA Corporation should review its decision in the context not only of profitability but also in the wider context of Canada's national interest bearing in mind the large amount of Canadian taxpayers' dollars that have assisted the company in achieving its reputation and
The Budget-Mr. Mazankowski sales. RCA Limited has been successful in establishing an excellent technical capability in satellite subsystem design. The recent award of the Telesat contract to RCA Limited enabled its satellite group to remain in business in Canada, and its continued viability will depend on government support.
If the company is not prepared to reverse this retrograde decision, the government should not give any further subsidy to a company which has demonstrated that it will not abide by the "New Principles of International Business Conduct", as published by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce in July, 1975. Canadian consumers, too, should consider whether they should purchase products from a company that is not prepared to be a good Canadian corporate citizen.
As 75 per cent of the company's sales come from consumer products, primarily TV sales, if RCA does not change its policy, I would urge Canadians not to buy RCA. I repeat, do not buy RCA products-boycott RCA if RCA Corporation closes its research and development labs. Fight fire with fire. If RCA wants to attack Canada's future, let Canada attack RCA's future!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There is no point in the government taking measures to encourage industrial research and development if foreign multinationals such as RCA are not prepared to support Canadian research operations. But, since our standard of living is directly related to the harnessing of research and development and will be even more so in the future, it is absolutely essential that we have and maintain a viable industrial research and development community in Canada if we are to have any control of our own future.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as my colleague, the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kempling), indicated, this is a rather record-breaking debate in terms of participation by cabinet ministers. They have indeed been brave souls, trying diligently to make the best of this budget, hopefully trying to make it a saleable product.
I was very impressed by the attempt of the hon. member for Scarborough West (Mr. Martin) to try to sell the sizzle in the budget, the sizzle that is not there. A number of members have participated in this debate, including the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Jamieson), the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) and other brave souls.
I listened very closely yesterday to the speech by the President of Treasury Board. He ran out of steam about half way through, talking directly about the budget. He switched to debating the Official Languages Act and policy. His comments seemed to run counter to the report of the languages commissioner.
The President of the Treasury Board went on at great length suggesting that the critics of government expenditure controls were ill informed. I trust he was not including in that category the Auditor General, having regard to the rather stinging indictment the Auditor General made about government budgetary control, improper accounting methods, and a dearth of clear-cut understandable infor-

June 10, 1976
The Budget-Mr. Mazankowski
mation contained in the estimates and the public accounts. That is very clearly documented. It is something of which the government, and indeed all members of parliament, should take serious cognizance.
In my view parliament must have a better awareness of government's anticipated spending and government's intentions both in the short and long term. Further, adequate provisions and procedures must be established in order properly and effectively to examine and scrutinize all government expenditures.
The former Leader of the Opposition, the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield), today dwelt at great length on the cynicism and lack of trust that pervade society with respect to our parliamentary and other democratic institutions. It is something we must all concern ourselves with if we are going to preserve the kind of credibility our institutions deserve and, with it, the kind of support we must have in order that our institutions will function in an orderly and proper manner.
The budget that we are debating has been described in many ways. Don McGillivary of Southam News described it as a drifting, dreaming budget in the midst of multiplying economic problems. Doug Fisher referred to it as 90 minutes of rhetorical drivel. He suggested the government did not have two ideas to rub together. He further suggested that the manner in which the budget was presented was tantamount to a non-relevant ritual. I think we all agree there were a lot of words in the budget, perhaps a lot of unnecessary words. I think we can further agree that the speech was honed in such a way as to preserve the government's own self interest.
I see my good friend, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), in the Chamber. Some people refer to him these days as the "Minister of sour milk and rotten eggs", but I would not do that. He is indeed a very unique Minister of Agriculture. The fact that we taunt each other in the House from time to time does not in any way affect our personal regard for one another.
The Minister of Agriculture has been under a fair amount of pressure, and under a lot of heat lately. He adopts the same profile as the others. When things are going well in agriculture, he is the first to take credit. If things go sour and we have a rotten egg or sour milk problem, who does he blame? He blames the provinces. It is not the fault of the Department of Agriculture or the government.

speechtext: Typical Grit trick.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If they had done what I told them, there would be no problem.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There he goes again. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) indicates that the farmers are getting enough and they should thank him.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They are the highest paid in the world. Heward Grafftey said we should lower the pay.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am surprised that the Minister of Agriculture has not engaged in this debate. I can only presume it is because there is nothing positive in this budget to help agriculture in this country.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Just ask the pork producers; they will tell you.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They are the best off farmers in Canada.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would love to get involved in an agricultural debate, but unfortunately I have to speak on other things today. There is nothing I would love to talk about more than the "blue tongue Superbull."
We need only look at the attitude the government has taken when it expresses great satisfaction over the fact that we survived with a zero growth rate in this country last year. That has been described as a successful achievement. As the leader of my party pointed out in his remarks-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Which one?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We have a number of leaders. Together we are building a team that will lead this country out of the doldrums, and back to prosperity.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As our leader has pointed out, the difference between our party and the governing Liberal party is the absence of any clear determination of growth, the absence of any clear direction. I think it well worth while drawing attention to what our leader stated as was reported in Hansard at page 14284, "We see sound economic growth not as a contradiction to inflation control but as a prime requisite for the control of inflation in the long term." In that context I should like to quote a passage from the latest edition of The Economist, that of May 22, 1976. This is from an article entitled "Out of Slump."
In 1974 the world's six largest industrial economies marched roughly in step into slump. These big six are America, Japan, West Germany, France, Britain and Italy, which together account for 80 per cent of the output of the 24 rich countries in the Organization for Economic Corporation and Development. In 1975 two of the big six turned back up again early (America and Japan) while three others (France, Britain and Italy) turned back up again late. But by the end of 1975, industrial output in all six was rising again.
In January-March, 1976, recovery continued and each of the big six achieved faster industrial growth than its longer term trend. On this reckoning, the slump is over and the boom has begun. Everywhere idle plant and capacity are being brought back into use. Everywhere unemployment has stopped rising, and almost everywhere it should soon be steadily reduced.
In theory this should be the start of a long and strong boom. The world has a lot of lost ground to recover. Do the impossibly huge industrial growth rates necessary to get the world back on trend mean that there is no danger of overheating-of overstrain in capacity in any of the big six until 1981 at least? Not quite.
I think that sets out the international scene succinctly. It is obvious that recovery internationally is well under way. It seems to me that the budget we are discussing is not tuned in to the realities of the recovery on the international scene-that we have failed to take advantage of what might well be a long and sustained boom.
Look at the government's position with respect to spending. Here again we find the government patting itself on the back for the manner in which it says it is cutting back
June 10, 1976

or controlling federal expenditure. I should like to examine that aspect in some detail, but I will repeat once again that this budget is clearly not a good budget; it fails to include measures to encourage productivity or stimulate sales abroad despite the fact that our industrial plant is operating at less than 80 per cent of capacity.
It has been said over and over again in this debate, but it still bears repetition, that the government relies essentially on the recovery of the United States and its other trading partners. It intends to rely also upon the Anti-Inflation Board whose staff has now increased to 853 in an effort to deal with a backlog of 3,000 wage cases and to reduce delays which have made it an increasing target of criticism. The budget is completely lacking in vision of the full potential of this country. I find it amusing, having regard to the curt attitude the government has taken toward the United States that it should now be relying on that country as its saviour.
A word, now, about the importance of the private sector. The Prime Minister and some of his colleagues had all but written off the private sector last December, but it has suddenly become the key factor again. It is consoling that some ministers like the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey) should be coming out in defence of the private enterprise system, and I hope some of their colleagues will engage in the same crusade.
What about the reckless spending habits of the government and, in particular, the position of the President of the Treasury Board who is going about the country trying to convince Canadians that the government has become the epitome of restraint and good economic management? The fact that it is content to live with a further deficit of $4.5 billion shows us how phony and misleading it is. I think this reflects a blatant failure on the part of the government to control its own spending which, in my view, continues to be one of the main factors contributing to inflation.
The government has clearly demonstrated its inability to forecast accurately its expenditures and revenues. Review the record. On November 18, 1974, finance minister Turner told Canadians that he expected a deficit of $1 billion in the financial year ending March 31, 1976. Mr. Turner returned to the House with a new budget on June 23, 1975, and revealed that the $1 billion deficit he had planned earlier was in fact to be $3.2 billion. The estimate had gone awry, he said, because he had over-estimated revenues by nearly $2 billion, having taken an over-optimistic view of the economy. Despite the drastic revision of the expected deficit of the June 23 budget, evidence mounted during the fall of 1975 that the federal government had lost control of the deficit. Presented with evidence showing that the deficit would climb even higher than Mr. Turner's estimate of June 23, 1975, the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) refused to comment. He said it would be of little value to comment on such projections.
May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
At six o'clock the House took recess.
The Budget-Mr. Mazankowski

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 8 p.m.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at six o'clock I was pointing out the dismal record that the government has had in its ability to forecast. I was also leading up to the point that the Minister of Finance was not left with a very glamorous situation. While the former minister of finance may have been a glamour boy, he did not have the propensity for being able to put the nation's economic house in order. We are now faced over there with a new version, a version in the name of "Thumper". Whether he can put our economic house in order remains a leading question, but it is little wonder that he refuses to say what the predicted deficit will be.
In his budget speech of May 25 the Minister of Finance revealed that the deficit would be $4.1 billion in 1976, $900 million over the June 23, 1975, estimate. This time the fault lay not in inaccurate economic forecasting but in the fact that federal expenditures had overshot their target by close to $1 billion. The finance minister chose not to tell Canadians that the budgetary deficit had quadrupled in size since the first estimate of November 18, 1974. To make such a comment would have revealed both the wilful deceptions of previous federal economic forecasting as well as the incompetence of the present administration in controlling its own spending.
We have only to turn the clock back to the campaign of 1974, May and June, to ask how the government can stand up in a very sanctimonious fashion and preach restraint and responsibility? During the 1974 election campaign this was the government that so recklessly threw money around. Its members made election promises amounting to billions of dollars, Mr. Speaker, of your money and mine, simply to buy votes.
Today the Prime Minister stood up in this House and said, "We have to level with the Canadian people". He appealed to all members of parliament to be honest and to tell the story as it really is, and to tell it particularly to the little people. I can assure hon. members opposite and you, Sir, that many Canadians did not ask for the extravagances which were promised during the election campaign of 1974, but in the name of power, and only in the name of power, did this irresponsible, power hungry bunch scandalously pilfer the Canadian taxpayers' money.
The President of the Treasury Board failed to deal with this particular point in his remarks yesterday, and I am glad to see that he has now come into the House. He failed to justify the startling figures on the basis that they were political. It was a political game rather than an honest economic game. This particular view is shared by many Canadians, including a well known Liberal by the name of Douglas H. Fullerton who, in the Ottawa Citizen for March 8, in an article entitled "Dear Pierre: Who Said We Wanted All Those Goodies?" wrote as follows:
Come off it, Pierre, did we the people really ask for all those goodies your government showered on us these past eight years?
I'm awfully tired of hearing you say, as you did again recently in Vancouver, that the enormous rise in federal spending since you became prime minister has occurred because of the insistent and growing demands of an expectant public for more government handouts.

June 10, 1976
The Budget-Mr. Mazankowski
This is a phony argument, a smokescreen designed to obscure the truth. Most of your new or expanded programs were concocted by a group of your colleagues, the "liberal" or spending wing, perhaps more appropriately designed as the "drunken sailors". With your support, their schemes were powered through cabinet and caucus, despite the doubts of more cautious ministers and members.
I am not challenging the motives of this spending lobby, which I suspect range from a humanitarian desire to benefit the weaker members of our society, down to instinctual political or personal urges for recognition, glory or re-election. What is at issue is that they are much less a response to a need felt by the public than the collective decisions of a small but powerful group at the top, who believed that they knew what was best for the country.
This is elaborated further by the former auditor general in an article appearing in the Globe and Mail for Wednesday, April 28.1 quote him as follows:
Spending public money "seems to have become almost the exclusive preoccupation of the government, with the politicians spending the people's tax money almost solely to buy votes to retain power, with little regard for parliament and no regard at all for the concept of balancing the budget or living within the country's means ...
Unlike businesses which have to meet payrolls and make profits or face disasters, governments can never face bankruptcy so long as they have an unlimited blank cheque on the pockets of the taxpayers of the country.
Yesterday we had a long dissertation from the President of the Treasury Board, who has been making a lot of sweeping statements recently. He generated a lot of publicity across the country. Maclean's referred to him as "Mr. No". He has also been referred to as the fastest gun in the east. Members on both sides of the House, I know, have a great amount of admiration for the minister's capacity and integrity, but we know very well that he is very political; he is a cagey individual, and he is very canny when it comes to manoeuvring and manipulating figures. I suppose his training in the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has served him well in that regard. But we know very well that in justifying government expenditure the minister has used deferrals. He used the business of transferring or borrowing authority.
We see a new technique in the formation of Loto Canada by which the minister is using an estimate to enact legislation which in effect establishes a Crown corporation, outlining its purpose and its method of financing, so we know very well that the minister is very capable. However, as the Globe and Mail has suggested in an article on Monday, May 24, some of his practices are somewhat deceptive.
The President of the Treasury Board has talked a good line about restraint, but surely with the record of increase in government spending by this administration since it took office there is a lot of room for trimming government fat. I must say that, because of the juggling of figures and the manipulation, many Canadians are not convinced that the government has seriously cut back on federal government expenditures. It has not been able to live within its own forecasts and its own predictions. On February 18, 1976, the President of the Treasury Board, during the tabling of his estimates for 1976-77, stated in the House as follows:
Government expenditures in 1975-76 will be held to 16 per cent or less over 1974-75.

He stated further:
I am pleased to say that there is now every indication that this target will be achieved.
I must say that this is 1 per cent over his prediction in February, 1975, when he said he would keep expenditures down to a 15 per cent level. As late as April 27, 1976, less than one month before the budget was brought down, in an address to the Toronto Metropolitan Board of Trade he heaped praise upon himself for cutting the percentage increase of 16 per cent during the last fiscal year. That was less than a month before the budget was brought down.
As I said earlier, the minister reminds me of the Minister of Agriculture who heaps praise upon himself. I am sorry the Minister of Agriculture is not here. He is probably mourning over the fact that his good friend, Beryl Plump-tre, has resigned. I think she was a political asset to the Minister of Agriculture.
The minister said further, "I will not fudge or juggle statistics", but that is precisely what he is doing. While the minister purported in the same speech just one month before the budget, to have had effective control-he declared that he managed to hold spending to 16 per cent for 1975-76-what did we see on budget night? We saw that increase rise to 18 per cent, which amounts to more than peanuts, it amounts to some $725 million. We have not received a satisfactory explanation for that.
The President of the Treasury Board waffled around the subject yesterday but, in my opinion, the explanation is far from satisfactory. If this money was spent in 1975-76, why is it included in the estimates for 1976-77? Should not the figure of $42,150,000,000 be reduced by $725 million? This is tantamount to the Minister of Finance and the President of the Treasury Board hoodwinking the Canadian people into believing that they will restrain their spending in 1976-77 to 14 per cent over the previous fiscal year. This is another example of the government's manipulating and juggling figures. Its record of forecasting and the methods that it employs make it very difficult to place any credence in its forecasting ability. If this is what the Canadian people have from their new planning, programming and budgeting system, I am sorry to say that we are in for very dismal days ahead. Perhaps that is why the Auditor General took such a dim view of the government's accounting procedures.
If we look carefully at the 1976-77 estimates we find some rather revealing information that the government has not acted with restraint in areas where it could and should have. If we compare the 1976-77 estimates with the forecasted expenditures for 1975-76 we find that the government has stated that the major components of the roughly $4.7 billion increase, which amounts to 14 per cent for total standard objects, are transfer payments and other spending items which are beyond the government's control. The most cursory examination of total spending by standard objects indicates that this statement is ridiculous and nonsensical. Increased spending on grants, contributions, and transfer payments in fact accounts for $1,944,228,000, or 41.5 per cent of the increase. But there are a number of areas in which a more realistic approach would produce significant savings.
Let us look at a number of items. For example, in the area of salaries and wages there has been an increase in
June 10, 1976

1976-77 over the last fiscal year of $687,305,000. This is an increase of 13.6 per cent, or a 14.7 per cent increase of the total amount exceeding the expenditures of the last fiscal year. In personnel costs there has been an increase of $179,546,000, that is, 18.4 per cent over the previous year. In rentals there has been an increase of $50,759,000 or 18 per cent over the previous year. In public debt charges there has been an increase of $875,000,000, a 23.1 per cent increase over the previous year. In all other expenditures, a sort of umbrella group, there has been an increase of $392,444,000, amounting to 36.4 per cent over the last fiscal year.
It is interesting to look at these expenditures in terms of specific government activities. Most of these are highly controllable. Administration, for example, is controllable. We can go into that in quite some detail. The administrative operative expenses will cost at least $1,358,176,000 in the fiscal year 1976-77. This is an increase of $143,226,000 over actual expenditures in 1975-76, or 11.8 per cent. Some of the increases are astounding. There is much that can be done in this area and that is not being done.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in his budget speech given on Tuesday, March 25, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) stated the following:
No miracle drug exists to provide an instant cure to these economic ills. It will take time and patience to restore price stability and a high level of output and employment. This approach is evident in our monetary policy, our fiscal policy, our expenditure policy, our energy policy and our control policy. In all of these fields, drastic action to yield quick results would be highly disruptive, damaging to the interests of the groups most affected and unlikely to be sustainable.
Mr. Speaker, such is the philosophy underlying the budget now under consideration, a budget instilled with a healthy realism which truly shows the well-understood role of a government in the management of community affairs.
Mr. Speaker, and oft repeated French adage states that the knack of governing is to see ahead. It is also to try and determine where the true interests of the people lie, and above all to have the courage to go to the bottom of things in the search for solutions to society's problems. It seems to me the main quality of this government in these circumstances is they do not try to hide the facts from the Canadian people, they treat them as adults. The government also show they believe in Canadians, because they invite them to take part in the fight against our current economic troubles.
In the budget, the Minister of Finance stated and I quote:
Indeed, all Canadians have their roles to play in the achievement of our economic goals.
Mr. Speaker, clearly it is in the interest of workers themselves to join in the fight against inflation, because one way or another they are going to suffer most in an inflationary period. Let me say that while wages and salaries accounted for 74.9 per cent of national revenues in the first quarter of 1974, they had declined to 70.2 per cent only in the third quarter of the same year. That proportion seems to have maintained during 1975.
The Budget-Mr. Duclos
As for corporations, their profits rose from 11.2 to 17.6 per cent of national revenues between 1971 and 1974, an inflationary period. How can anyone blame the government for seeing to it that the rate of price increases be abated, while wishing for an upswing in the Canadian economy.
Mr. Speaker, it used to be that government had to remain entrapped in the vicious circle either of fighting unemployment at the cost of stimulated inflation, or fighting price increases at the expense of employment but those times are over. As the governor of the Bank of Canada suggested on May 29, 1975 to the members of the Canadian Association of Life Insurance Companies, and I quote:
The time has come for everybody to realize those two complementary aspects, to be united if we are to have stability and orderly progress in the economy, rather than contradictory objectives impossible to reach together.
Clearly, Mr. Speaker, a government concerned only with their popularity would have yielded to the temptation to introduce a very expansionary budget. But in so doing, they would have escaped their responsibilities. The danger must be perceived that considerably higher rates of unemployment and inflation as we are now facing might befall us if no measures were taken to fight inflation and maintain Canada's competitive position vis-a-vis the United States, which account for two thirds of our international trade.
In this connection, one must bear in mind that during the third quarter of 1975, just before the implementation of the anti-inflation program, the collective wage agreements signed in Canada provided an average salary increase of 16.8 per cent or about twice the increase awarded in the United States. If this trend had continued, we would have experienced at the same time disastrous unemployment and inflation rates, and that had to be avoided at all costs. Therefore, we must rejoice in the fact that the inflation rate has been brought back to 6.3 per cent during the first six months of the anti-inflation program while it reached 11.7 per cent during the six previous months. Salary increases have been reduced to an average of 11 per cent since the program is in force, and that can only improve our competitive position on foreign markets on which Canada relies for a number of jobs.
Mr. Speaker, whatever some people may say, it does not appear advisable in the overall economic situation to sacrifice the fight against inflation for the one on unemployment, because, and I quote once again the Governor of The Bank of Canada:
In due course, it appears that what we get for a slight reduction in the unemployment rate-here again only for some time-is not an additional amount of inflation but indeed a fast and accelerating inflationary upswing to which there is no end in sight.
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to review all the measures contained in the last budget. However, I would at least like to bring to light the uplifting from $100,000 to $150,000 of the annual profit ceiling under which small businesses can take advantage of a reduced taxation rate, as well as the increase to $750,000 of the cumulative maximum under which businesses can be taxed at this rate. In my opinion, this is a measure which was needed if the incipient economic recovery is to appear still more vigorously in the coming months. I am more especially glad as the government is thus bringing a solution to a problem I had person-

June 10, 1976
The Budget-Mr. Duclos
ally brought to the attention of the Minister of Finance last April in the House. Indeed we must recall that as a result of the provisions of the Anti-inflation Act concerning the payment of dividends by corporations, many corporations might have lost their eligibility for that reduced rate of taxation because they would not be able to pay their shareholders all the dividends they had to pay in order not to reach the cumulative limit which was only $500,000. In taking these measures, the government shows its concern for our small business and its desire to use it as a decisive factor of the economic recovery which will create the employment and the prosperity all Canadians want.
I previously pointed out the sense of responsibility of the government, which does not hesitate to strike at the root of the problem and which prefers to risk being unpopular in the short run so as to ensure the well-being of the people in the long run. There is no better example of that sense of responsibility than the difficult decision made recently to raise the price of crude oil. Of course, it is a measure which strikes the consumer directly, and which may look inconsistent with the government's concern for the fight against inflation. Still, it had no other choice but to so encourage the people into moderating their consumption of a nonrenewable resource, while by the same token freeing additional amounts to speed up exploration in the field of traditional oil in western Canada and its tar sands. Because the fiscal treatment of oil companies should encourage them strongly to reinvest their profits instead of increasing the dividends paid their shareolders, I support that decision.
It is imperative that the people know that Canadian oil reserves are not limitless, that our country runs the risk of becoming dependent in less than ten years, on imports from the Middle East or Venezuela, if explorations in Canada are not stepped up. Then, we will have to pay the price exacted by the producing countries. If the past is any indication of the future, this cost could very well be prohibitive and lead us, for a few years at least, to yearning for 1976 price levels; let us not forget that oil products are still relatively low-priced in Canada, when one knows that in western Europe, a gallon of ordinary gas costs between $1.60 and $2.
In this respect, Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out that it is essentially because of the federal affiliation that Quebecers can obtain oil products at a substantially lesser price, a price which will reach $9.05 a barrel starting July 1 and which is less than the price prevailing on the international market, which is between $11 and $12 a barrel.
This single price policy is possible only because the federal government gives generous subsidies-the cost in 1975-76 is estimated at $1.6 billion-to refineries of eastern Canada in general and Quebec in particular, so that they can sell gasoline and heating oil for a significantly lesser price than what they would normally have to charge in relation to international costs of crude petroleum.
