Mr. Speaker, shortly after the federal-provincial energy conference in April 1975, the director of the Montreal Newspaper Le Devoir, Mr. Claude Ryan, wrote this, and I quote:
Just as the fact of belonging to the Canadian federal community enabled provinces such as Quebec and Ontario to go through the crisis resulting from the spectacular rise in the international price of oil, without being too affected so can the ten Canadian provinces view their energy future with confidence if they stay together instead of separating.
And he added very appropriately, quote:
The most important thing is that a country has the wealth which enables it to be sure it will enjoy a great variety of energy resources and maximum security of supply. These are the guarantees offered by the Canadian challenge but they would not be available to a separate province.
Mr. Speaker, there are some ideas worth thinking over in these few lines, for those in Quebec who are tempted by the apparently captivating adventure of the establishment of an independent state, for which Quebecers generally and the workers particularly may be left to pick up the tab.
I do hope that while letting the crude oil price get nearer the international levels in the next few years, a substantial differential be maintained and that, as far as possible, the single price oil policy be maintained in Canada as a whole. Otherwise, one of the most forceful arguments in Quebec in favour of Canadian federalism would lose all its meaning.
Mr. Speaker, I think it would be timely to review briefly why, in spite of the considerable benefits the federal formula brings to Quebecers, too many of them remain skeptical about the possibility for them to assert themselves as a cultural group different from the majority of Canadians. Fortunately, Mr. Speaker, most Quebecers clearly see the advantages provided by the federal system or they are at least open to a frank and honest discussion. It is the latter group, Mr. Speaker, that we must convince once and for all in the years to come of the profitability of federalism and of the possibility for Quebecers to assert themselves culturally, socially and economically in such a political framework.
Mr. Speaker, during the debate on the Speech from the Throne in October 1974, the Prime Minister stated that he hoped an agreement would soon be reached with all the provinces towards the repatriation of the constitution. That was almost two years ago but unfortunately little progress has been achieved, chiefly on account of the Quebec government's opposition. However, it seems to me that the amendment formula which was adopted in Victoria in 1971, providing for regional veto powers, one of them for Quebec, was an improvement over the current constitutional practice which requires unanimity rule for any amendment concerning the delimitation of constitutional jurisdictions. One could not reasonably claim that the repatriation of the Canadian constitution would, under those conditions, seriously affect the basic rights of Quebec.
Besides, Mr. Speaker, it is regrettable that the Quebec government is somehow seeking to trade its agreement as to the repatriation of the constitution for a constitutional review, which would inevitably lead to an increase in its constitutional powers. Therefore I hope that Quebec will
June 10, 1976

renounce what sounds very much like blackmail and give its assent to the repatriation of the constitution. Thus it would help create a more serene and favourable climate in view of a future federal provincial conference which would consider the matter of sharing constitutional powers, which is obviously most important for the province of Quebec. However, it is imperative that the federal government show unequivocally in the next months its strong intention to pursue more vigorously than ever its objective by strengthening slightly the role of French-speaking officials in the management of the business of this country to promote the full development of French culture and the use of French in Canada, particularly in Quebec. If not, the people of Quebec will be right in turning to the government of their province and the latter will be justified in taking all available means to get a new sharing of the constitutional jurisdictions which will satisfy it.
We must say, Mr. Speaker, that if the present sharing of powers does not seem satisfactory, because of the extraordinary behaviour and the untiring devotion of Quebecers in the government who make sure that Quebec gets its share and that it is not affected in its vital interests, it is not impossible than an electoral accident could deeply change the Canadian political checkerboard and lessen the role of Quebecers on the federal scene. I think it is normal that such a possibility is the main concern of several Quebecers and that they are anxious to give to the Quebec government the necessary means enabling it to modify even more the destiny of Quebec in case the voice of French-speaking people would disappear from the federal scene.
However, Mr. Speaker, I think that all these negotiations to review the system of the sharing of powers must be undertaken in a real cooperative spirit and must at least take care that the quality of the services offered to all Canadians will be maintained. We must also see to it that they will not generate an irreversible process of gradual erosion of the powers of the federal government leading to some kind of disappearance of the presence of Quebec on the federal level. If French-speaking people could expect to be equitably represented in the senior positions of the federal public service, the possibility of a setback of Quebecers on the political level would not be so serious. Unfortunately, it is clear that, in spite of the important progress that has been made in almost ten years, the efforts made to promote French-speaking people to the senior positions of the public service have not been as fruitful as expected. If the number of French-speaking persons in the senior pos-iions of the Public Service Commission, the Privy Council, the Secretary of State and in some other departments is adequate, the situaton is far from satisfactory in some others, and I would like my friends of the opposition to listen carefully to some figures I would like to give. For example, in the Department of National Defence, only one senior officer out of 28 is French-speaking; in the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, three French-speaking persons have been promoted to senior positions out of a total of 67; in the Department of Finance, 2 out of 32, in the Department of Agriculture, 5 out of 79, and in the Department of the Environment, 10 out of 127-
The Budget-Mr. Duclos

I am sorry that they are prejudiced in this way, but this is an attitude that we must consider and which should in fact urge the federal government to be more enthusiastic when French-speaking people show an interest in a career in the federal government.
How can we ask French Canadians to play a role in federal administration if, in spite of their university degrees and their experience on the labour market, they are not sure that their offer of service will be well received. The government says that there are not enough French Canadians in the public service. It is supposed to be very difficult to find competent French Canadians, but if one shows some interest, he is treated with indifference.
I know that the government can count on the suppport of our Social Credit colleagues and on the open-mindedness of the NDP members on this matter, but I would like especially the official opposition to make a positive and determined stand on this matter instead of being satisfied with supporting the government half-heartedly.
I am sometimes surprised, Mr. Speaker, to hear certain members of the official opposition. From what they say, it seems that it is the French Canadians who have taken over everything in the federal public service. I hope that the few figures that I have submitted to the House will make them reflect on this and that they will take the trouble to read the last annual report of the Public Service Commission which contains very significant statistics in this matter.

June 10, 1976

Therein lies an obligation that we all have, a kind of political contract with French-speaking Canadians under which they would reject separatism and the federal parliament would guarantee the right to French Canadians to communicate with and work in the federal administration in the French language. speechtext: The Chair recognizes the hon. member for Greenwood. Is it agreed that each member will speak for 20 minutes?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we will try to stick to that suggestion.

I feel that this debate is about to end and that probably nearly everything which needs to be said about the budget has been said. But I wish to make a few comments on what, after all, is an important central event in the life of parliament.
In my view the budget introduced few significant changes. It lacked any sense of social justice and failed to move in the direction of equity. The view which I and, I think, my party hold is that the budget should be the instrument for bringing about social justice and promoting equity. I share the view expressed by Lord Keynes, the famous British economist, who recommended redistribution of income in the direction of equality, partly on the ethical ground that extremes of wealth and poverty were disgraceful but also because the poor spent more of their income than the rich.
I was going to quote the words of other famous men, the words of Tawney and Matthew Arnold, but will not do so now. Both said that a system founded on inequality is against nature and breaks down. I think we are seeing the breakdown of our system which is based on inequality. My quarrel with the budget is that it fails to reverse this trend. For example, let us consider unemployment.
Over 700,000 Canadians are out of work. I strongly suspect that when students seek to enter the labour force, the figures will get worse. What has the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) done about this? He has done nothing, as far as I can make out. He rests his case on shallow optimism about the American economy. He anticipates it will continue to expand and that this will have the direct effect of promoting in the neighbourhood of 250,000 new jobs in Canada. One is assuming a great deal when one assumes the American economy will continue to expand. In any event, there is little link between American expansion and the Canadian economy. I remind the House that we will have 300,000 people entering the labour market next year; therefore, even on the basis of the Minister of Finance's assumptions, we will have a larger number of unemployed than before. What should be done about this question?
In my view the Minister of Finance should substantially cut the personal income tax for those whose incomes are below $15,000. This would have a dual effect. It would not only be a way of equalizing wealth between rich and poor but would stimulate the economy. People on lower incomes spend a greater proportion of their incomes than the rich do. As Lord Keynes pointed out, an excellent way to stimulate aggregate demand is to tax the rich to employ the poor. The budget does not touch on this.
It is suggested by some, including the Minister of Finance-I think the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said much the same this afternoon-that such a tax cut would be inflationary. This argument ignores that our economy is only working at 80 per cent of capacity, and if we were to use the now unused 20 per cent capacity the effect might well be a reduction of inflation. The minister ignored the fact that in an economy working at close to capacity there will be less unemployment, less money going out in unemployment insurance payments, an increased supply of goods and services, and a reduction in welfare costs.
The next thing on which I wish to comment in the budget is the proposal to increase the number of weeks of employment required to qualify for UIC and the decline in
June 10, 1976

the duration of benefits. Here again the so-called remedy of the Minister of Finance strikes at those who can least afford it. I refer to the people in the maritime provinces and Quebec where there is little opportunity to qualify for the present eight-week requirement. There will be even less opportunity to qualify if the period is extended to 12 weeks. The effects of these proposals will drive those people on to welfare rolls and increase the burdens of municipalities and provinces which can least afford them. Surely we in this House have learned that the welfare of all regions of Canada is of vital interest to all Canadians.
The question may be asked, if we are to seek full employment, for what types of employment must we plan? I maintain the view that where private industry cannot provide the necessary jobs it is up to public enterprise to step in. There are very great needs in our country; I will not list them all. We need public housing at rents and prices people can afford. There is an urgent need in metro areas, such as my own, for the extension of rapid transit. So far the government has completely failed to live up to its promises to assist the development of public transit, promises made in the last election campaign.
There are one or two things in the budget of which I approve. The first is the higher taxes on large cars. This measure is designed to conserve energy. I wonder if enough has been done. I am inclined to think that a reduction in the tax on small cars would have been a better incentive to conserve energy over the years.
I heartily agree with the increased tax exemption for small businessmen. The limit to which businessmen are eligible to pay the small business rate of 25 per cent tax is doubled. Small businessmen are a group in the community who have been particularly damaged by inflation and urgently need the assistance provided for them by the budget change.
I also approve of the increase in the child care deduction. I wish the government would proceed vigorously to carry out the recommendations of the Status of Women Committee which recommended a major federal investment in day care centres. On the other hand I do not agree that the government was wise in allowing tax exemptions for an increased range of registered personal pension plans. This is a change to assist the well-to-do and not the people who need it most.
I have tried to study the proposed changes in the prices and incomes policy. The objection which we have in this party to the government's anti-inflation measures is that the prices and incomes policy was effective to some extent in stabilizing wages and salaries but it left profits virtually intact. The Prime Minister this afternoon almost seemed to acknowledge this fact. I suspect that after the changes it will remain ineffective in respect to prices and profits. One obvious reason is that a large number of prices are exempt, such as energy, most food, and the price of imports. The price of housing has not been effectively controlled. These are major items.
I suppose that the object of the proposed changes is to give at least the impression of more effective control of prices and profits. I am afraid that the effort will be ineffective. One reason for this is the extraordinary com-
The Budget-Mr. Brewin
plications of the system. These invite evasion by those who can afford a skilled accountant and other expert advice. The mysteries of transfer payments give rise to serious doubts whether these technical changes will be an effective instrument of control. The Department of National Revenue has been unable to control large multinational corporations, and without an army of investigators far exceeding the present staff of 853 the Anti-Inflation Board has no way to assess the figures found in financial statements of these large corporations engaged in intra-corporate trade.
I now want to turn to the external aspects of the budget. The Minister of Finance in his budget speech did indeed make reference to the new economic order, but I think Canadians still have a long way to go before they appreciate the importance of the revolutionary changes affecting the world trade system. Canada depends upon trade; trade in the ultimate analysis depends on world stability and prosperity. There is an increasing recognition all over the world of the need for change in the way in which international trade is conducted. This has given rise to a series of international meetings. The main actors and promoters of the new economic order have been the victims of under development who have suffered on an immense scale from ever-worsening destitution and malnutrition. The Prime Minister himself observed in his famous address at the Mansion House, London, and I quote:
These nations seek no piecemeal adjustments but a comprehensive restructuring of all the components. The response of the industrialized countries can be no less well prepared or no less comprehensive in scope.
What is sought from us now is not aid, although in the least developed countries that remains a major factor. What is needed is to promote agriculture in the Third World, and to improve trade opportunities so that the Third World can earn for itself the means of developing itself. What we are talking about then are not fringe benefits but the basic necessities of life such as food, shelter, and clothing. What is required is to meet the basic needs of mankind in the foreseeable future on a global scale.
To this end a number of conferences under the auspices of the United Nations have met. The latest one we discussed today, the UNCTAD IV conference at Nairobi. It is notable that in all of these conferences the participants recognized the inter-dependence of nations in solving the basic problems of mankind, and the urgent need for the political will in both developed and developing countries to make the necessary changes.
Another thing which seemed to be common to all of these conferences was the conviction expressed by knowledgeable men and women from all over the world that the problems of the world could, in fact, be met by international co-operation and the necessary political will.
The Canadian government has clearly indicated its acceptance of the basic notions behind the new economic order. In his address to UNCTAD IV, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) spoke of the need for action "with an unprecedented sense of urgency". He went on to say:

June 10, 1976
The Budget-Miss Campbell
I believe we have passed the stage of analysis and assessment of issue. We must now get together to devise workable and dynamic solutions, and solutions mean action.
Some observers at the conference felt that, at Nairobi, Canada did not take an effective lead and offered no solution but only more talk. I will not discuss UNCTAD further because it was discussed today. However, there is a long course ahead of us where important structural changes are required to be made. We must organize new machinery, such as the common fund to stabilize the price of commodities.
I am aware of course that programs in this field will be sought during the coming year, and no doubt for many years to come. It is of course wrong to assume that commodities are the only subject that is the concern of the new economic order. It is concerned with trade liberalization policies. It is concerned with the transfer of technology, and is still concerned with adequate aid transfers.
It is sometimes asked what is the real basis for Canada's concern about these matters. The real basis is a dual one. On one side is enlightened self interest. This requires that the strong, positive demands of two thirds of the world's people be heard and acted on. This is essential to stability. The other is the basic notion of human compassion and brotherhood. It is perhaps old fashioned to mention this, but it remains that some such moral imperative is an essential ingredient if we are to have effective action.
I had intended to mention the subject of justice to our native peoples, but I do not have enough time to do that. I will conclude by repeating that I have found the budget uninspiring and inadequate. It fails to move in the direction of social justice. It deals inadequately with the major problem of external trade whose urgency was expressed the other day by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Jamieson). I can only hope that if the minister has another chance to bring in a budget, it will be a much better one.

speakeroldname: Miss Coline Campbell (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to rise tonight to speak in the budget debate. I would first like to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) on what I consider a very good budget for the times. One might have the great desire to get into all sorts of expansionary ideas and projects, and certainly as a member of parliament it would be very nice to have more federal money circulating in my constituency. However, it seems to me that it is very important to allow existing programs to take hold fully. I refer to the anti-inflation program established last October.
At that time all Canadians were asked to abide by the guidelines for prices and incomes, and we made provisions for mandatory controls over the larger economic units in our economy. The essential purpose was to change expectations, and to bring about a quicker response to the program as a whole so that the fiscal, monetary, and other general policies would in fact bring about real growth and declining inflation. We have seen the program become operational in the last few months and we have actually seen it taking effect. It would not do at this time to introduce programs which might disturb the full operation of the government's attack on inflation. The importance of all

Canadians co-operating in this program was reiterated in the Prime Minister's speech on the budget today.
Nevertheless there are some areas in the budget which I should like to discuss and with respect to which I may, hopefully, introduce some new thoughts. The one-parent family or the working mother will welcome the changes set forth under the day care provisions which allow a deduction for child care of $1,000 per child up to a total of $4,000 per family. Many people will not be directly affected by this concession, but for those concerned about the cost of child care this will be a welcome measure.
I also welcome the new tax provisions concerning oil and gas exploration. Such a means of equalizing power costs will be particularly attractive should oil be discovered and the Maritimes become an exporter of energy. I understand that a similar concession is given to the coal industry. Let me remind hon. members that we have a source of energy in coal. Not only could this provide energy but it would also provide work for people in Cape Breton and other areas in Nova Scotia. Let us take a look at it. The challenge is there. My sources tell me we still have a great amount to use up.
The budget provides that a taxpayer will henceforth be able to write off exploration costs at a rate of 100 per cent-up from 30 per cent as it presently stands. This concession became operative as of budget night and will remain in force until July 1, 1979. Until now, only the principal business taxpayers could claim a 100 per cent write-off of exploration costs. The new provision will also apply to funds received under provincial incentive programs in connection with drilling and exploration. As one who comes from a province where, at present, we are right in the difficult situation of relying on an oil-based power system due to the low cost of oil less than three years ago, I welcome these tax advantages and look forward to the use of coal and to the discovery of commercially viable oil resources off the Atlantic sea coast.
However, let us not think the discovery of oil will ease our problems over the long term. The Atlantic provinces and Quebec must make arrangements between themselves to provide a mutually beneficial and fully operational grid power system.
The federal government has offered financial support for the development of alternative power sources and it is up to the provinces to take advantage of this program. The provinces wish to continue jurisdiction over energy and thus they should come forward with new proposals. In this regard I am particularly anxious to see action taken to harness Fundy tidal power if this is possible.
Canada has always been a country which seemed to be able to get around its difficulties. In 1867 the areas came together and, as provinces, dedicated themselves to working together for the good of all. This has occurred over many years; it happened with respect to the rail and air transport industries; in connection with the oil and gas pipeline in the West; in equalization grants to the provinces; in support for the arts, humanities, and sciences; in education; with the CBC; with our social insurance programs, and in all principal areas of our national life.
June 10, 1976

The federal government provides services of unique importance to the unity of this country; this is what Confederation is largely about. Surely at this point it is not up to the federal government to say to one province, "Find your own solution." This is particularly the case should the solution lie in co-operation not only with the federal government but perhaps with four or five other provinces, all of which must get together if a particular difficulty is to be solved. Let me say, Mr. Speaker, that the sooner this is done the better it will be for Canada.
I should like to turn now to the subject of employment and the labour force. We often hear of the high unemployment rate in the Atlantic provinces. We also know that the figures mentioned are true and we look forward to the amendments which are to be introduced to the Unemployment Insurance Act. However, one does not solve this problem by increasing the number of weeks a person must work in order to qualify. Surely what we need to solve the problem are incentives which would help get all those people back to work.
We know that approximately 50 per cent of those presently receiving benefit can find those four extra weeks quite easily and will do so as soon as they are forced to take such action. But what of the others? As I say, I look forward to the amendments to the UIC Act in the fall. We welcome the assurances from the government that there will be programs of retraining and job creation-that the money which has circulated in the area will continue to be there. We are looking to see incentives which will enable existing operations to find new jobs for these people, along with the incentive already provided by the federal government.
Let us remember, Mr. Speaker, that there are abuses of the present system and that it is not only the working people who are responsible for them. There are employers who will not take a person who comes knocking at the door because they are scared that if they refused to say that the applicant is not suitable he will, when engaged, fail to provide efficient service. Employers therefore prefer to state that the applicant is not fit for the job rather than engage the services of a possibly unwilling worker. The system certainly has its faults and the one I have mentioned is probably the greatest-an employer is afraid to say openly to an applicant for a job that the job is available when he knows that the applicant is really not anxious to stop receiving UIC benefits.
On the other hand in some areas it is very hard for employers to compete in the employee market bearing in mind the amount of UIC benefits possible applicants for work are receiving. Usually it is persons from outside the community who receive these high amounts of unemployment insurance benefit.
I do not want to give the impression that we should jeopardize an unemployed person's UIC benefits if he has earned them at a particular level and would receive the same amount if he returned to the work force, when there is no job available for him. However, over an extended period of time perhaps it would encourage people to get back into the work force if the rates were reduced to the minimum wage thereby enabling an applicant to compete for jobs which are available in the area. I therefore welcome the indication of the Minister of Finance that the
The Budget-Miss Campbell
Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) will introduce a further change relating to unemployment insurance benefits, that is to say, the number of weeks during which benefits may be drawn will be more directly related to the number of weeks worked and that, in addition, regional extended benefits will be related in a more sensitive manner to the level of regional unemployment. I look forward to taking part in the discussion of these proposals.
The budget has been criticized by the opposition as failing to bring forth new housing programs or incentives to business. I have been a member of parliament for not quite two years but I know the government has brought in a number of housing programs. Consider, for example, the Assisted Home Ownership Program. Under this program, a couple, regardless of income, who are buying or building a new house under the qualifying limit, which is $31,000 in my area, are eligible for loan assistance to reduce their mortgage interest rate to 8 per cent. Those with children and needing additional help to keep monthly payments below 25 per cent of their income may qualify for outright subsidies of up to $750 annually.
We have programs such as the Neighbourhood Improvement Program available to a great many municipalities. There are 16 municipalities in Nova Scotia which have taken part in this scheme. One of them is in Yarmouth, in my constituency. I should like to see more use being made by Nova Scotians of these programs, and I look forward to seeing residential rehabilitation assistance programs in full use.
[DOT] <2110)
I also realize that an agreement has been signed by the province of Nova Scotia with the federal government designating the rest of the province-that is, the rural areas including municipalities of less than 2,500 population-as eligible for residential rehabilitation assistance programs. It is up to the municipalities to take advantage of these programs. Included in this designation in Nova Scotia are a number of areas selected for priority assistance. I am under the impression that some problems still remain to be worked out before commitments can be made, particularly program delivery arrangements for provincial assistance. However, negotiations on these matters are proceeding and I hope it will not be too long before the full impact of these housing programs is felt.
These programs, Mr. Speaker, show progress in the housing industry, and I hope that anyone with housing problems will go after their municipality, their provincial and federal representatives, to ensure that the full benefit of these housing programs are taken advantage of, not only in Nova Scotia but in Canada in general.
In so far as business incentives are concerned, Mr. Speaker, opposition members claim we have not provided measures to stimulate capital investment. This government provided in the last budget manufacturing incentives, investment tax credits. Other programs provide financing directly, such as to small business. In the province of Nova Scotia in the first three months of 1975 there were eight loans to small businesses, whereas in the same period this year there were 30. The amount last year was $66,240, compared with the amount this year of $487,146.

June 10, 1976
The Budget-Miss Campbell
With regard to farm improvement loans, in the same period last year, namely the first three months, there were 48 loans made in Nova Scotia, and 48 in the first three months of this year. However, the amount lent last year was $191,537 compared with $262,435 this year. As far as the fishing industry is concerned, there were 208 loans granted in Nova Scotia during the period April, 1974, to March,
1975,	totalling $1,505,251. Between April, 1975, and March,
1976,	there were 197 loans-this was a poor year for expansion, particularly in the groundfish industry-for a total of $1,300,773. However, loans in the first quarter of this year ending March, 1976, totalled 50, amounting to $282,021.
These measures have been provided to sustain high levels of business investment in Canada. We are looking at productivity as a government, Mr. Speaker. People, business, and Canada as a whole must get into these programs. We have reached a maturity; let us take it from there and make a success of what we have.
This budget also increases the amount of corporate profits allowed for the small business tax reductions. Canadian controlled private corporations are entitled to pay tax at a reduced rate, subject to an annual limit on their profits. For 1972-73 the limits were $50,000 to $400,000 per annum in total. In 1974 they were raised to $100,000 to $500,000; and effective for 1976 the Minister of Finance in his recent budget announced the limits will be further increased, ranging from $150,000 to a total of $750,000. This can only create incentives for small business in the Atlantic area and will help these small businesses to continue and expand.
Another welcome announcement has been the increase in the maximum annual deduction for registered pension retirement plans from $2,500 to $3,500. This measure will be welcomed by all those who are saving for their retirement.
A new step was taken by the government last Friday when it announced that it would be proclaiming jurisdiction over fishing rights extending out to 200 miles from our coast. This is to take effect as of January 1, 1977. We have had bilateral negotiations and have tied up some 88 per cent of the operations of foreign fleets within this 200 mile limit.
What will this do for the Atlantic provinces? It can only provide new industry and ideas. It is also time that the government regarded fish as a natural resource. We do not have to look elsewhere if we have a 200 mile limit. Businesses will grow and the fishery will develop. We have allowed foreigners to fish off our shore, but a lot of these fishermen have been fishing these grounds for some time alongside our own fishermen.
With regard to tariffs, we have a tariff on finished fish products that leave Canada but no tariff on unfinished products. When we are negotiating tariffs with other countries, perhaps we should consider imposing a tariff on unfinished products as an incentive to finish our products in Canada.
I realize we have agreed to take only 20 minutes and perhaps I have overstepped my time.

Thank you. This budget has been crit-ized by the opposition as not being expansionary. I suggest

that this is a time when we ought to examine the programs we already have in existence in an attempt to make our economy work. At a time when we are trying to make our anti-inflation program work we should not try new, expansionary ideas; the programs we have, I suggest, will probably work if given the opportunity.
I was very pleased to be given this opportunity this evening to speak in this debate, Mr. Speaker. Since my 20 minutes have expired I will say thank you, and resume my seat.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased once again to take part in a budget debate, especially since I seem to have the distinction of closing this memorable debate on this memorable budget, which will be remembered forever for its nothingness. However, if I stick strictly to the contents of the budget itself, I will probably be finished before I have hardly begun. I say that because the budget is as shallow and as celluloid a budget as we have ever seen, and as a result it has very quickly become known as the "no budget budget".
This budget is what we get at a time when sweeping new proposals and policies are required, in fact are vital, if the downward economic trend that we are facing is to be reversed. But all this and more has been said by my colleagues who have spoken before me, none better than by the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Clark) in his very forceful yet eloquent address just a couple of days ago.
Instead of expounding on the obvious deficiencies in the budget itself, I would like to take this opportunity to express my thoughts about a part of our economic process, a part that must surely form the backbone of our economic way of life. I am, of course, referring to small business, which many believe is slowly but surely disappearing under this government.
This small firm sector which generally seems to be ignored and bypassed by governments is responsible for employing over 50 per cent of our labour force. This high figure was substantiated several years ago by the minister of energy who was then the minister of industry, trade and commerce, when he stated in this House:
Almost 60 per cent of our entire labour force-two thirds of Canadians work for businesses employing 15 persons or less. Most of these businesses are owned and managed by Canadians and provide a means of developing greater Canadian participation in our country's growth.
Although it is admitted that by far the largest and possibly the most important sector of our economy is in fact the small firm sector, the government continues to expound on philosophies it established some 20 years ago by concentrating most if not all its efforts on bigness, bigger and costlier governments, bigger and stronger units, and larger and fewer multinational corporations as well as merger oriented enterprises, while small business as we know it is possibly heading toward extinction.
The government has gone so far in its centralization of power that it has nearly reached the stage of allowing a few to monopolize our over-all economy. The Canadian Labour Congress, for example, has been allowed to become so powerful that just recently it reached the height of impertinence when it threatened the government, and
June 10, 1976

therefore the public at large, by suggesting that unless it were given a key role to play in running the nation it would call a national strike. This is the way things operate in most communist countries, obviously not to the advantage of their people. In any event, they hold all this concentrated power, and yet the CLC controls only approximately 20 per cent of the labour force compared to over 50 per cent in the small firms sector.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Nonsense.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: 1 notice that my socialist, if not communist, friends are getting upset because they would like nothing better than state ownership and control. If that is so, they can go back to Cuba or Russia.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Absolute tripe.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yet the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) did not even mention small business in his speech on the budget earlier this week. He does, however, from time to time outside the House indicate the seriousness of problems relating to the small businessman, as he did in a recent speech to the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. But I believe this is only a means of pacifying the hungry. If the minister were sincere in his casual concern for the small business community, then he would back his statements by appropriate legislation in order to show his sincerity. Promises alone mean nothing unless they are backed by action, and action is nowhere to be seen as far as the government is concerned.
As for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) I do not think he even knows small business exists. The only mention in his budget which was in any way connected to even medium sized firms was an increase in the amount of net profits eligible for a lower tax rate. Not only will this affect less than 1 per cent of the business community but the truly small businessman whose net profits are below $100,000 a year remains on the list of the ignored so far as the government is concerned.
I would like to point out some of the problems or deficiencies that exist between governments and small business, but before doing so let me say that I hope I will not be labelled a pessimist or a cynic, as I was by the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey) a few weeks ago during my objective questioning on Olympic financing because I will now, as I did them then, base my points on facts and precedents, and therefore if I am to be labelled anything by anyone I suggest that the word realist would be far more appropriate.
First, however, let us clarify by means of a definition who we are talking about when we mention the small firms sector. The government's definition of small business, an active business income, has created considerable room for dispute which involves the usual cost of accountants and lawyers for the businessman and of civil servants for the government.
I believe that a far better working definition, perhaps oversimplified to some extent, would be that a small firm is one that is owner-managed. There are always exceptions, of course, for specific programs where arbitrary size limits would have to be decided upon. However, at this time for
The Budget-Mr. Jelinek
the sake of simplicity let us assume that the so called small business sector would fall into the owner-managed category. Even without the exceptions, by using this definition we can be sure that we are including 99 per cent of all small firms in that category.
Let me begin with high interest rates and the over-all banking system as it relates to this "owner-managed" segment of our business community. It is a well known fact that a small independent firm is at a great disadvantage against conglomerates and multi-national corporations when it comes to money supply. Although there are thousands of chartered bank branches across this country and the government has the Federal Business Development Bank, which is a carry over from the Industrial Development Bank, established supposedly for the purpose of assisting Canadian firms in their expansion programs; our banking system still remains one of the least competitive organizations in the world, afraid to take the least amount of risk when compared to the banking system in the United States, for example. A sort of a monopoly by the big "10" seems to be in existence within the money institutions, supported and protected by the government. The branches and their managers virtually have their hands tied when it comes to credit decisions, as their credit levels are limited by head office at uniform levels, thus eliminating any possible fluctuation for the sake of a healthy competitive atmosphere.
What is even worse is that American and other foreign subsidiaries can come into Canada and purchase Canadian firms and businesses which may have remained in the hands of Canadians, without ever using their own capital. The foreign company, by simply using its parent company in the United States or elsewhere as collateral, is able to generate a loan from a Canadian bank with no real problems. In many cases it is able to obtain the loan from the same Canadian bank that more often than not had refused the same Canadian plant further credit for necessary expansion. I know this as a fact as I have gone through this whole cycle myself.
In short, as it now stands, a U.S. or foreign enterprise can in fact buy out a Canadian firm without ever having to bring a red cent into Canada. From time to time we cry foul, or independence, and rightly so, but we as Canadians cry foul often without doing anything about it. The best comparison I can make is the way we cry and complain every four years when, as a nation, we do not bring back enough or any medals from the Olympic Games. Unfortunately this year will not be any different, so we complain, but during the subsequent four years we as Canadian citizens, as media, as governments, do next to nothing to assist, morally or otherwise, those few athletes who continue to give all their energies as well as their souls to specific goals for this country, and that is just one typical comparison with the small independent businessman in Canada and the government's attitude to him.
Yet still on the money end, while governments continue to turn their backs on small business and from time to time throw a bone in their direction just to keep them pacified, Canada has lent almost $1.5 billion to 57 foreign countries in the last ten years alone, for little or no interest. These are not figures I am making up, Mr. Speaker, they are figures that the government itself has confirmed. Some of

June 10, 1976
The Budget-Mr. Jelinek
these loans are even made to communist countries with no termination dates set, and they continue to be made while thousands of small businesses survive in this type of political atmosphere. How is it that Cuba, for example, can borrow millions of dollars at a rate of 3% while many small Canadian firms have to fight and beg, and collateral their gold fillings, in an attempt to obtain reasonable financing-say around 12%-many to no avail? No wonder the unemployment situation is a disaster, with three quarters of a million Canadians unemployed. Mr. Speaker, there is no better, no cheaper, and no quicker potential employment opportunity than by way of the small firm sector of our economy. The government must take appropriate steps to utilize this sector for economical make-work programs, by initiating and imposing comprehensive and realistic incentives for this very important industrial and economic community for the benefit of all Canadians.
Now let us move to a more specific problem, the problem dealing with the swamp of bureaucratic paperwork which governments continue to impose on all business establishments. There are the conventional tax papers, refund forms, application papers, questionnaires, licence forms, and on and on goes the list. There is general agreement that some of these forms have no justification for existing, and in fact many have become obsolete, sometimes tied to legislative bills which are no longer in effect. However, the forms continue to circulate, causing unnecessary demands at great expense to governments and business establishments. Meanwhile the filing cabinets of the nation bulge, often with incorrect and incomplete information. The only consolation is that most files gather dust, rarely to be used again.
The answer to this problem is simple: all we have to do is follow the example of the United States and initiate an immediate reduction of 10 per cent of government forms every few years or so. The result would be an unbelievable saving in dollars to the taxpayer and would certainly reduce considerably the nuisance, even harassment, that the small firm is expected to bear.
Surely if the government is prepared to wait for the United States economic upswing to bring us out of our doldrums, the least we could do would be to borrow some of their effective methods, which are obviously working for them, and could just as well work for Canada.
With regard to labels and packaging our labelling legislation is yet another horrendous bureaucratic and complicated mess. It is of little, if any advantage to anyone and unquestionably a big hindrance to the small manufacturer. To point out a very quick example, a manufacturer in northern British Columbia distributing goods from, say, the United States within the borders of the province of B.C. alone must go through the expense of relabelling and repackaging his product at a very great expense. The same can be said for manufacturing in central Quebec, or in any other area of this regionally complex nation. The act should and must be simplified.
One of the more intricate problems for some businesses-and I suppose every individual has this problem to a certain extent-is one which relates to the existing tax complexities. It is bad enough for individuals, but for small

businesses it is a nightmare and a real deterrent to expansion. The entire Income Tax Act should be rewritten so that it would be comprehendable to the taxpayer. This may seem like a large and burdensome order, but from the viewpoint of a small business the administration of the tax laws has become as critical as the laws themselves. It is a double cost to the taxpayer who must indirectly pay for bureaucratic administration and then pay again for advisers to deal with the problems directly affecting him.
If the small businessman had unlimited funds, as most multinational corporations do, there would be fewer tax problems for him to worry about. He could set days aside to confer with tax advisers, supervisors, and evaluators from Revenue Canada, but only to find that simple solutions are no longer available in this respect. Of course the small businessman has other things on his mind, for example, mere survival, let alone keeping up with product development, research, employment, cash flow, expansion and so on.
I could produce a long list of specific tax examples which apply to the small firms sector in a harmful way, but because of my time limitation I will just give one sample. It relates to the small businessman who in many cases must depend on his spouse to take part in his business endeavours. It so happens that because of the weird tax laws which are in existence it is cheaper for the business proprietor to live with a woman working for him rather than to marry her. I can vouch for the fact that wives can be just as expensive as girlfriends, but that is no reason for this specific tax law to continue. The point of the matter is that if they marry his business income is all taxable, and if they do not, he can deduct her salary. Then if they do decide to marry after all, they will need to incorporate so that she can be employed by the business. In other words, it is more economical to live with a mistress than it is to marry her. Strange as this example may seem, it is a true fact, and it affects tens of thousands of Canadians struggling to carry on their business ventures under existing tax complications.
The fact that the budget is a no budget naturally came as a surprise to many, but the fact that the budget in no way deals with Canada's current number one problem surely must have shocked all. I am of course referring to the housing situation as it now stands and the fact that the average young family can no longer purchase a home. This lack of positive action by the government in the field of housing does not only affect the small firms sector, but indeed all Canadians. Surely if the government was not prepared to reduce the tax on building materials, at least further concessions should have been introduced in respect to insulating materials, just to name one example.
We talk and preach about the serious need for energy conservation, and rightly so, yet modern homes are built without the least bit of thought about conserving energy. It is a known fact that properly designed and insulated homes will use less energy, as far as heating and air conditioning are concerned, than the types of homes which are now being constructed in various developments across Canada.
I had the privilege of attending a recent NATO conference at which it was established that those nations which impose stricter controls on building construction in respect
June 10, 1976

of energy conservation are the same nations which are ahead in the energy conservation field, and Canada unfortunately is not among them. It seems to me that the government has its priorities mixed up when it comes to controls.
Having just mentioned air conditioning, I am prompted to reflect on why the Minister of Finance saw fit to include in his budget a surtax on automobile air conditioners when the amount of energy consumed by air conditioning is less than one half of 1 per cent. The only answer must be that once again this is simply another example of pacification, this time for the benefit of energy conservationists who have a right to be concerned.
If I may, I would now like to take this opportunity to make some suggestions and recommendations which I hope will be considered in a serious manner.
It is no secret that government, whether in a restraint period or not, is by far the largest purchaser of goods and talent, but the bulk of the contracts go to a concentrated group of elite corporations and individuals, usually in the multinational range. In this regard it is time that the government followed the examples set by Japan and others by initiating set-aside programs in its purchasing for the purpose of contracting them to the competitive small firms sector. It is time the government took immediate steps to reduce the costly bureaucratic paperwork onslaught I mentioned earlier. It is time to simplify our legislation with regard to labelling and packaging, and it is time to rewrite the Income Tax Act for the sake of simplification and saving.
It is time the government took away the right to strike from those individuals and groups working in essential services. It is no secret that one of the major factors behind the low productivity figures in Canada is the fact that millions of working man-days are lost as a result of strikes, many of them illegal, and many of them within essential or government services.
Two recent polls indicate strong support for such a proposal. Of roughly 5,000 business establishments polled on a national basis 91 per cent favoured the idea of taking away the right to strike within essential services. On a more local level, of those constituents from my riding of High Park-Humber Valley who answered a recent questionnaire, 94 per cent supported such a move. Many of them work in essential services themselves.
It is also time the government followed its anti-inflation guidelines and reduced its spending in accordance with those guidelines. Our finance critic, the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), outlined in his budget remarks how we could realistically reduce government spending by at least $1 billion.
It is time for the government to encourage, by way of co-operation in research and development, the formation of a small firms consortium. This system of business co-ops in West Germany, Japan, and elsewhere is a tremendous advantage to the small firms taking part with respect to buying, selling, financing, sharing facilities, and so on.
It is also time for the government to initiate cautious but realistic and meaningful incentives for the primary purpose of increasing productivity. It' is time the government encouraged, through tax incentives, a far greater amount
The Budget-Mr. Jelinek
of secondary manufacturing within Canada rather than selling our national resources abroad for the sake of improving our international trade balance.
In short, the time has come for the government to change its attitude toward centralization of business, unions, and governments as well, and to take the necessary steps, some of which I have outlined, for the purpose of preserving a competitive business community which forms the basis of the free market system.
I have tried to outline some of the problems, along with some remedies, that relate to the small firms sector of our economy and, believe me, I have only scratched the surface. If we want this sector to survive within our society, as indeed we do, then immediate action by the federal government must be taken, for the small business community is what the free enterprise system is all about. It is what this country was built on and what this country can prosper by. Other countries which presently are more fortunate than Canada in regard to unemployment, inflation, productivity, and other areas by which the standard of success and happiness is judged, have all concentrated their economic energies toward their small firms sectors within their industrial way of life.
Japan, Belgium, West Germany, not to mention the United States and others, are all in far better shape economically speaking than Canada, and one of the primary reasons is because in those countries their governments are dedicated toward the betterment and continual growth of the small firms sector, thereby assuring the survival and success of the free market system in particular, and free enterprise as a whole. We cannot allow the Prime Minister to change the free market system in this country. If the Prime Minister believes that the free market system does not work, as he so clearly stated late last year, then may I remind him that if indeed free enterprise is having its problems in this country it certainly has nothing to do with the system itself but rather with the stranglehold that he and his government have had on that system for the past decade or so.
I see I still have about five minutes left, Mr. Speaker, so in order to close on a not too serious note I should like to read to you a very simple but significant story put out by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business. It simplifies the realities of our economic society to a children's fairy tale, but the reason I decided to end my address today by reading this story is because, more than anything that has been printed lately regarding the problems within our economy, this story signifies reality and comes right to the point in a way that even members and supporters of the New Democratic Party will understand-I hope.
Before I read it, however, let me set the stage by introducing the characters in the story and equating them to the real life segments of our society. First, there is the Little Red Rooster who should be equated to a typical small businessman in a free society. The cow will play the part of the union leaders, the duck will be the NDP oriented working man, and the goose is a socialist Liberal-is there any other? And lastly the farmer represents the cabinet. Allow me to read from this pamphlet put out by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, which

speechtext:
If you guys had been quiet over there I might have been finished. Here is the story. Once upon a time there was a Little Red Rooster who scratched about and uncovered some grains of wheat. He called his barnyard neighbours and said, "If we work together and plant this wheat, we will have some fine bread to eat. Who will help me plant the wheat?" "Not I," said the Cow. You remember who the cow was. "Not I," said the Duck. "Not

I," said the Goose. "Then I will," said the Little Red Rooster and he did.
After the wheat started growing, the ground turned dry and there was no rain in sight. "Who will help me water the wheat?", said the Little Red Rooster. "Not I," said the Goose. "I'd lose my workman's compensation," said the Cow. "Equal rights," said the Duck. "Then I will," said the Little Red Rooster and he did.
The wheat grew tall and ripened into golden grain. "Who will help me reap the wheat?" asked the Little Red Rooster. "I'm waiting for a guaranteed annual wage," said the goose. "Not I," said the Duck. "Out of my classification," said the Cow. "Then I will," said the Little Red Rooster and he did.
When it came time to grind the flour, "Not I," said the Cow. "I'd lose my unemployment insurance," said the Duck.
When it came time to bake the bread, "That's overtime for me," said the Cow. "I'm a dropout and never learned how," said the Duck. "If I'm the only one helping, that's discrimination," said the Goose.
"Then I will," said the Little Red Rooster and he did. He baked five loaves of fine bread and held them up for his neighbours to see.
"I want some," said the Cow. "I want some," said the Duck. "I demand my share," said the Goose. That is the NDP.
"No," said the Little Red Rooster. "I can rest for a while and eat five loaves myself."
"Excess profits," cried the Cow. "Capitalist leech," screamed the Duck. "Equal rights," screamed the Goose. And they hurriedly painted picket signs and marched around the Little Red Rooster, singing, "We shall overcome." And they did.
For when the Farmer-that is the cabinet-came to investigate the commotion, he said, "You must not be greedy, Little Red Rooster. Look at the oppressed Cow. Look at the disadvantaged Duck. Look at the underprivileged Goose. You are guilty of making second-class citizens of them."
"But I earned the bread," protested the Little Red Rooster.
"Exactly," the wise Farmer said. "That is the wonderful free enterprise system; anybody in the barnyard can earn as much as he wants. You should be happy to have all this freedom. In other barnyards, you would have to give all your loaves to the Farmer. Here you give four loaves to your suffering neighbours."
And they lived happily ever after. Including the Little Red Rooster, who smiled and crowed, "I am grateful. I am grateful."
But his neighbours wondered why he never baked any more bread.
The point of this story is that it is time to wake up to the fact that unemployment insurance has increased five times since 1971 and government spending has increased five times in the past ten years. The unemployment deficit has reached a staggering $4 billion, not to mention the unacceptably high unemployment figures and the highest infla-
June 10, 1976

tion rate in history. So wake up Canada-there is no free lunch.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in taking part in this debate, I wish to emphasize some aspects of the budget proposed by the present government and that seem very logical, wise and adapted to the general situation of the Canadian economy a well as to the needs of the area that I represent, the south shore of Montreal.
Without coming back in detail on every point contained in the precise statement of the minister (Mr. Macdonald), I wish to comment briefly on the general context of that budget which is as follows: it is made up of a delicate web of contradictory situations. It represents the middle phase of an economic cycle. We are not entirely out of the depressive phase of the last economic cycle and we are not yet at the apex of the recovery which follows automatically any recession in each four or five year cycle. This is why the opposition can only make general criticisms which consequently are irresponsible. Those criticisms are general and out of context. As we all know the years 1974 and 1975 were the worst years of the recession in our economy since the 30's. In unprecedented and extremely concrete fashion, they reflected for every citizen what happened internationally, events which cannot possibly be underestimated in the restrictive context of a national electoral quarrel-a new planetary awareness both distressing and beneficial at the same time.
The last years have lit up new alarm signals on the controls panel of our planet. We realized as never before the limit of our resources. We noted, even us, the privileged citizens of a wealthy country, a large country new and rich, the fragility of the economic and environmental balance of the world.
We also understood the message of Carl Sagan, the American astronomer and physicist responsible for the message sent to the stars by Mariner 8. Our planet is small and limited and while we are broadening our conscience at the universal level we must look for new forms of organization on this earth and evaluate immediately its resources in the spirit of interdependency so favoured by the economists Galbraith and Myrdal. This is the meaning of the two years of recession which we have just experienced. They mean deep realignments on a world-wide basis between developed and underdeveloped countries, rich and poor ones, young and old ones, heavily populated and almost empty ones such as ours.
In spite of its privileged position in the world, Canada has known the consequences of an economic crisis which has affected every one of its partners. Due to some persistent behaviours of its citizens, especially the rapidly growing significance of wage increases as a deflation factor of the yearly inflation rate, Canada has been prompted to react, to strengthen some controls and to impose others enabling it to anticipate the future and maintain a real stability. By the way, while all or almost all industrialized countries reported a real reduction of their national production, Canada maintained during the past years an average growth of 1 per cent on a two-year basis.
The Budget-Mr. B. Loiselle
While the unemployment rates were reaching 10 per cent in the United States, including incredible rates of 16 per cent in Connecticut and 23 per cent in the States of New England, Canada for its part was always maintaining unemployment rates lower than 8 per cent. At the same time, the unemployed of our country enjoyed services and benefits whose realism and efficiency drew the admiration of all industrialized countries. For me, the general criticism expressed by the opposition in its motions of non-confidence are shabby and show an alarming chauvinism. They form, I think, an incredible condemnation of the policy carried out by the majority of our major commercial partners in the free world that were unable to match the stability of Canada in the recent crisis.
Indeed, if the opposition is not satisfied with an actual increase in the purchasing power of Canadian citizens, a real employment growth, a gradual increase in oil prices and a sustained national productivity, I wonder what strong criticisms they would make as regards the American government which enables the United States to undergo a real slowdown in productivity, the Japanese government which had to face inflation rates ranging from 10 to 20 per cent and the British government which must constantly appeal to the International Monetary Fund to keep afloat what is left of the strong pound sterling. I wonder what else the opposition want and to what model they were referring when they restlessly attacked the behaviour of the government of Canada during the recent events.
They were probably referring to a hypothetical country located in a solar system with which they are the only ones to maintain a constant relationship. I humbly suggest that Canada got out of the recent crisis with distinction and that the Canadian government was largely responsible for the relatively good performance of our economy through its strong and responsible approaches which were constantly adjusted to reality rather than to the requirements of a restrictive theory. And this year, it continues to act according to its principles.
We might have, between two alternatives, either applied brakes and more severely restricted our expenditures by relying on the economy recovery to ensure as best as we could a fair distribution of wealth. As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) said, this would have amounted to clearly ignoring the most disadvantaged segments of society whose improving status necessarily depends on suppletive government action. Or we might have brought forward a largely expansionist budget, ignoring the fact that we can expect a better recovery than was forecast in Canada, under the pretence of stimulating our weakened economy.
But we had to respect the traditional balance of the economy. We decided not to feed inflation thanks to expansionist measures and important tax reductions, but at the same time not to demand further sacrifices from the citizens, under the pretence that consumption has remained at a high level and that it is impossible to cut expenditures that are attributed to it in our society.
This budget strikes a difficult balance between expansion and belt-tightening. It is an intermediate budget, with significant amounts still allocated to items that will require less funds starting from next year because the effort is done now. It also takes into account the real and

significant results obtained mainly through the Anti-Inflation Board. It is now projected the inflation rate for 1976 will be below 8 per cent, certainly a more acceptable figure than the 11 or 9 per cent figures of preceeding years. This budget takes into account the key action by the Anti-Inflation Board since its inception. It also introduces a delicate transition before the termination and change of certain programs, and finally it undertakes major structural changes originating from important policy statements such as those made by the Economic Council of Canada.
I would like to stress at this point why this budget seems to me both acceptable and in line with certain major aspects of the situation in Quebec, namely economic development-more especially that of small and medium businesses-the improvement of manpower programs and progressive changes in the employment insurance, and finally the energy issue. On the matter of economic development, I note firstly that this budget does not affect the regional development incentives programs.
Despite the significant progress experienced during the 1970-74 economic cycle, and the bulk of favourable trends now experienced by the Quebec economy, that province is still faced with important structural problems that were keenly emphasized in the last DREE report in March 1976. Although Quebec has caught up in real terms on most aspects, its economy is still plagued by traditional industrial traits that must be rapidly changed to bring the province to the level of Ontario or the Canadian average.
We may therefore hope in that context that all this year and all along the 1976-1977 fiscal year the DREE programs take into account that basic requirement, by allocating significant funds to industrial reconstruction efforts that are complemented at the provincial level by a determined and specific action policy. However, I see in this budget a special emphasis on the growth of small and medium businesses, clearly the ones that denote the highest level of local and regional enterprise.
The provisions designed to increase deductible benefits for tax purposes to $150,000, and set their total amount at $750,000, are first of all a type of realist indexing to the cost of living.
